knowledge_statements.title: Optimal-Face Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Optimal assignment face represented by the equality graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\in\mathbb Z_{\ge1}\), let \([n]=\{1,ldots,n\}\), and let \(C=(c_{ij})\in\mathbb R^{n\times n}\). Define \(B_n=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge0}^{n\times n}:\sum_{j\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }i\in[n],\ \sum_{i\in[n]}x_{ij}=1\text{ for every }j\in[n]\}\). For any optimal dual solution \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\), let \(H\) be the bipartite graph on two copies of \([n]\) with \(E(H)=\{ij:c_{ij}=u_i+v_j\}\). The optimal face is \[F^*=\{x\in B_n:x_{ij}=0\text{ whenever }ij\notin E(H)\}=\operatorname{conv}\{\mathbf 1_M:M\text{ is a perfect matching of }H\}.\] Consequently, \(F^*\) is the perfect-matching polytope of \(H\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any optimal dual solution, the optimal assignment face consists exactly of the doubly stochastic matrices supported on zero-reduced-cost edges, and it is the convex hull of the perfect matchings in that equality graph.
assumptions_latex: \((u,v)\in\mathbb R^n\times\mathbb R^n\) is an optimal dual solution.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F^*\) is the perfect-matching polytope of the equality graph \(H\).

notation.meaning: The optimal face of the assignment polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Breaking Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lexicographic perturbation of a finite assignment problem without changing its primary optimum.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal A\) be the finite set of feasible assignments, let \(c:\mathcal A\to\mathbb R\), and order the assignment edges as \(e_1,\ldots,e_m\). Define \(c_\varepsilon(A)=c(A)+\sum_{e_i\in A}\varepsilon^i\). There exists \(\varepsilon_0>0\) such that, for every \(0<\varepsilon<\varepsilon_0\), every minimizer of \(c_\varepsilon\) minimizes \(c\); moreover, the perturbed problem has the unique minimizer whose incidence vector is lexicographically smallest among the \(c\)-optimal assignments, with respect to the stated edge order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For all sufficiently small positive perturbation parameters, primary optimality is preserved and the unique selected assignment is the one with lexicographically smallest incidence vector among the original cost-optimal assignments.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmin}_{A\in\mathcal A}c_\varepsilon(A)=\{A^{\mathrm{lex}}\}\subseteq\operatorname*{argmin}_{A\in\mathcal A}c(A)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Tight-Edge Matching Certificates and Label Update
knowledge_statements.scope_note: States two termination certificates and the feasible label update that creates an additional tight edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let G be a graph, c:E(G)\to\mathbb R, and z\in\mathbb R^{V(G)} satisfy z_v+z_w\le c(e) for every e=\{v,w\}\in E(G). Let G_z=(V(G),\{e=\{v,w\}\in E(G):z_v+z_w=c(e)\}), let M be a matching in G_z, and let F be a maximal alternating forest in G_z with respect to M, with inner vertices X and outer vertices Y. Then: (a) if M is perfect, it is a minimum-weight perfect matching in G; (b) if \Gamma_G(y)\subseteq X for every y\in Y, then M is a maximum matching in G; (c) otherwise, define \varepsilon=\min\!\left\{\min_{e=\{v,w\}\in E(G[Y])}\frac{c(e)-z_v-z_w}{2},\min_{e=\{v,w\}\in\delta_G(Y)\cap\delta_G(V(F))}\bigl(c(e)-z_v-z_w\bigr)\right\} and set z'_v=z_v-\varepsilon for v\in X, z'_v=z_v+\varepsilon for v\in Y, and z'_v=z_v for v\notin V(F). Then z'_v+z'_w\le c(e) for every e=\{v,w\}\in E(G), M\cup E(F)\subseteq E(G_{z'}), and \Gamma_{G_{z'}}(y)\setminus X\ne\varnothing for some y\in Y.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For feasible vertex labels, consider the tight-edge graph and a maximal alternating forest for a tight matching. A perfect matching is minimum-weight perfect; the stated neighborhood condition certifies maximum cardinality; otherwise, the minimum-slack label update remains feasible, preserves the matching and forest edges as tight, and creates a tight neighbor outside the inner set for some outer vertex.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a graph and }c:E(G)\to\mathbb R
z\in\mathbb R^{V(G)}\text{ satisfies }z_v+z_w\le c(e)\text{ for every }e=\{v,w\}\in E(G)
F\text{ is a maximal alternating forest in }G_z\text{ with respect to }M
X\text{ and }Y\text{ are respectively the inner and outer vertex sets of }F
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \bigl[M\text{ perfect}\Rightarrow M\text{ is minimum-weight perfect}\bigr]\land\bigl[(\forall y\in Y,\Gamma_G(y)\subseteq X)\Rightarrow M\text{ is maximum}\bigr]\land\bigl[\text{otherwise the stated }z'\text{ is feasible, preserves }M\cup E(F)\text{ as tight, and creates the stated new tight adjacency}\bigr]

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Structural invariants of the weighted matching algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous invariants holding at every stage of the specified weighted matching algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: At every stage, define X(j):=\{v\in V(G):j\in\{b^1(v),\ldots,b^{k_v}(v)\}\} and \mathcal B:=\{X(j):1\le j\le K\}\cup\{\{v\}:v\in V(G)\}. Then: (a) \mathcal B is laminar; the sets V_r:=\{v:\rho^{k_v}(v)=r\} with \rho^{k_r}(r)=r are exactly its maximal elements, are each uniformly outer, inner, or out-of-forest, and carry blossoms with base r; (b) the edges \{x,\mu(x)\} form a matching M containing a near-perfect matching in every member of \mathcal B; (c) the maintained \mu- and \varphi-data associated with each X(b) describe an M-alternating ear decomposition of G[X(b)]; (d) all designated matching, \varphi-, and maximal-inner-blossom connector edges are tight; (e) the designated edges form a general blossom forest F with respect to M, consistently with the vertex marks; (f) contracting the maximal sub-blossoms of any B\in\mathcal B with |B|>1 yields a circuit; and (g) for every outer vertex v, \operatorname{TREEPATH} returns an M-alternating v-r path, where r is the root of v's tree in F.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At every stage, the maintained blossom sets form a laminar family with uniformly marked maximal blossoms. The mate edges form a matching that is near-perfect within every blossom; the stored data describe alternating ear decompositions; the designated edges are tight and form a mark-consistent general blossom forest; contraction of maximal sub-blossoms yields a circuit; and TREEPATH returns an alternating path from each outer vertex to its tree root.
assumptions_latex: \text{The specified weighted matching algorithm is at an arbitrary stage.}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{All structural properties (a)--(g) concerning }\mathcal B,M,\text{ ear decompositions, tightness, }F,\text{ contraction, and }\operatorname{TREEPATH}\text{ hold.}

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Perfect matchings in finite undirected graphs, including nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is perfect if every vertex of \(G\) is incident with exactly one edge of \(M\). Equivalently, the endpoint sets of the edges in \(M\) partition \(V\), so \[|M|=|V|/2.\] Consequently, existence of a perfect matching requires \(|V|\) to be even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A perfect matching consists of vertex-disjoint edges covering every vertex exactly once; therefore the graph must have even order.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: V=\biguplus_{e\in M}e\quad\text{and}\quad |M|=|V|/2

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Matching Structure at a Tight Tutte–Berge Set
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Here \(\nu(G)\) is the maximum matching cardinality and q_G(X) is the number of odd connected components of G-X.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(X\subseteq V(G)\) satisfy \[|V(G)|-2\nu(G)=q_G(X)-|X|.\] Then every maximum matching of \(G\) restricts to a perfect matching in each even connected component of \(G-X\), restricts to a near-perfect matching in each odd connected component of \(G-X\), and matches every vertex of \(X\) to a vertex in a distinct odd connected component of \(G-X\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If X attains the Tutte–Berge deficiency, every maximum matching is perfect on each even component of G-X, near-perfect on each odd component, and matches all vertices of X into distinct odd components.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Covered and exposed vertices; perfect matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-coverage terminology and the definition of a perfect matching in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph and let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching. For \(v\in V\), the vertex \(v\) is covered by \(M\) if \(v\in e\) for some \(e\in M\), and is exposed by \(M\) otherwise. The matching \(M\) is perfect if every vertex of \(G\) is covered by \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Let G be a graph and M a matching in G. A vertex is covered by M if it belongs to an edge of M, and exposed otherwise. The matching M is perfect if it covers every vertex of G.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \forall v\in V:\quad v\text{ is covered by }M\iff \exists e\in M\text{ such that }v\in e;\qquad v\text{ is exposed by }M\iff \nexists e\in M\text{ such that }v\in e;\qquad M\text{ is perfect}\iff \forall v\in V\,\exists e\in M\text{ such that }v\in e.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Near-perfect matchings under the one-exposed-vertex convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. A matching \(M\subseteq E\) is near-perfect if exactly one vertex is not incident with an edge of \(M\). Thus \(|V|\) is odd and \[|M|=(|V|-1)/2.\] If \(v\) is the unique exposed vertex, then \(M\) is a perfect matching of the vertex-deleted graph \(G-v\); conversely, every perfect matching of \(G-v\) is near-perfect in \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A near-perfect matching leaves exactly one vertex exposed, equivalently becoming perfect after that vertex is deleted.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is near-perfect with exposed vertex }v\iff M\text{ is perfect in }G-v

knowledge_statements.title: Parity-Controlled Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity restriction on the vertices left uncovered by a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(U(M)\) be the set of vertices not covered by \(M\). Since every matching edge covers exactly two vertices, \[|U(M)|=|V|-2|M|\quad\text{and hence}\quad |U(M)|\equiv |V|\pmod 2.\] Therefore a perfect matching can occur only when \(|V|\) is even, while a matching with exactly one exposed vertex can occur only when \(|V|\) is odd.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every matching leaves a number of exposed vertices having the same parity as the graph order.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: |U(M)|=|V|-2|M|\equiv |V|\pmod 2

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight matching without a prescribed cardinality in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\). The weight of a matching \(M\) is \(w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\). A maximum-weight matching is any matching \(M^*\) satisfying \[w(M^*)=\max\left\{\sum_{e\in M}w(e):M\subseteq E\text{ is a matching}\right\}.\] Under this unconstrained convention, negative-weight edges need not be selected and the empty matching is feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A maximum-weight matching maximizes the sum of selected edge weights; its cardinality is not fixed.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: w(M^*)=\max\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching in }G\}

notation.meaning: sum of weights of matching edges

children.title: Minimum-Cost General-Graph Matching

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum-Cost General-Graph Matching
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-cost matching over an explicitly specified feasible matching family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(c:E\to\mathbb R\), and let \(\mathcal F\) be a nonempty family of matchings encoding the required cardinality or coverage. For \(M\in\mathcal F\), set \(c(M)=\sum_{e\in M}c(e)\). A minimum-cost matching is any \(M^*\in\mathcal F\) satisfying \[c(M^*)=\min_{M\in\mathcal F}c(M).\] Specifying \(\mathcal F\) is essential because the unconstrained empty matching may otherwise be optimal.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A minimum-cost matching minimizes total edge cost within a stated nonempty family that fixes the intended cardinality or coverage regime.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^*\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal F}\sum_{e\in M}c(e)

children.title: Weight–Cost Transformation
children.top_down_role: Objective transformations connecting weight maximization with cost minimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Weight–Cost Transformation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Affine equivalence of weight maximization and cost minimization at fixed cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), fix \(k\ge 0\), and define \(c(e)=C-w(e)\) for a constant \(C\in\mathbb R\). For every matching \(M\) with \(|M|=k\), \[c(M)=\sum_{e\in M}(C-w(e))=kC-w(M).\] Hence, over the family \(\mathcal M_k\) of size-\(k\) matchings, maximizing \(w(M)\) and minimizing \(c(M)\) have exactly the same optimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For fixed-size matchings, replacing each weight by a constant minus that weight converts maximum weight into minimum cost without changing optimizers.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \operatorname*{argmax}_{M\in\mathcal M_k}w(M)=\operatorname*{argmin}_{M\in\mathcal M_k}c(M)

notation.meaning: family of matchings having exactly k edges

knowledge_statements.title: Cardinality-Constrained Weighting
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum-weight optimization restricted to matchings of a prescribed size.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(w:E\to\mathbb R\), and choose an integer \(k\) with \(0\le k\le\nu(G)\). A cardinality-constrained maximum-weight matching is a matching \(M_k^*\) satisfying \[|M_k^*|=k\quad\text{and}\quad w(M_k^*)=\max\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching and }|M|=k\}.\] The constraint prevents changes in cardinality from being traded against edge weight.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The problem selects a maximum-weight matching among exactly those matchings containing a prescribed number of edges.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M_k^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{w(M):M\text{ is a matching},\ |M|=k\}

knowledge_statements.title: Matching with Prescribed Vertex Coverage
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact characterization of a prescribed set as the covered vertices of a matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(S\subseteq V\). A matching \(M\) covers exactly \(S\) when the union of the endpoint sets of its edges equals \(S\). Such a matching exists if and only if the induced subgraph \(G[S]\) has a perfect matching. Equivalently, there is a matching \(M\subseteq E(G[S])\) with \[|M|=|S|/2.\] In particular, \(|S|\) must be even.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exactly the vertices in S can be covered by a matching precisely when the induced graph on S has a perfect matching.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \exists M\text{ with covered vertex set }S\iff G[S]\text{ has a perfect matching}

notation.meaning: prescribed set of vertices to be covered

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Maximum-Matching Optimality Is Preserved by Blossom Shrinking
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence under an externally incident even alternating path to the blossom base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, \(M\) a matching, and \(C\) a blossom with base \(r\). Suppose an \(M\)-alternating \(v\)-\(r\) path \(Q\) of even length starts at a vertex \(v\) exposed by \(M\) and satisfies \(E(Q)\cap E(C)=\varnothing\). If \(G'\) and \(M'\) are obtained by shrinking \(V(C)\) to one vertex, then \(M\) is maximum in \(G\) if and only if \(M'\) is maximum in \(G'\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an exposed vertex is connected to a blossom's base by an even alternating path using no blossom edge, contracting the blossom preserves maximum-matching optimality in both directions.

C\text{ is a blossom with base }r
Q\text{ is an even-length }M\text{-alternating path from an }M\text{-exposed vertex }v\text{ to }r
(G',M')\text{ is obtained by shrinking }V(C)\text{ to one vertex}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is maximum in }G\iff M'\text{ is maximum in }G'.

knowledge_statements.title: Berge Augmenting-Path Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Berge’s optimality criterion for matchings in finite general graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(M\subseteq E\) be a matching. An \(M\)-augmenting path is a simple path whose endpoints are uncovered by \(M\) and whose edges alternate between \(E\setminus M\) and \(M\), beginning and ending outside \(M\). Then \(M\) is a maximum-cardinality matching if and only if no \(M\)-augmenting path exists in \(G\). If such a path \(P\) exists, \(M\triangle E(P)\) is a matching of cardinality \(|M|+1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is maximum exactly when it admits no alternating path joining two exposed vertices; flipping such a path increases cardinality by one.
assumptions_latex: G=(V,E)\text{ is a finite undirected graph}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M\text{ is maximum-cardinality}\iff G\text{ has no }M\text{-augmenting path}

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Paths
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Alternation is defined relative to a fixed matching in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(M\subseteq E\) a matching. A simple path \(P=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_k)\) with \(k\ge 1\) is \(M\)-alternating if consecutive edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\); equivalently, for every \(1\le i<k\), exactly one of \(e_i,e_{i+1}\) belongs to \(M\). It is \(M\)-augmenting if both endpoints are unmatched by \(M\) and \(e_1,e_k\notin M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A positive-length alternating path switches between matching and nonmatching edges. It is augmenting when both endpoints are unmatched and its first and last edges are outside the matching.
assumptions_latex: \(P\) is a simple path of length \(k\ge 1\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P\text{ is }M\text{-alternating}\iff |\{e_i,e_{i+1}\}\cap M|=1\text{ for every }1\le i<k.\)

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The cycle is simple and alternates relative to a fixed matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and \(M\subseteq E\) a matching. A simple cycle \(C=(v_0,e_1,v_1,\ldots,e_k,v_0)\) is \(M\)-alternating if, cyclically, exactly one edge of every consecutive pair belongs to \(M\). Consequently \(k\) is even and \(|E(C)\cap M|=|E(C)\setminus M|=k/2\). Replacing \(M\cap E(C)\) by \(E(C)\setminus M\) yields another matching of the same cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating cycle has matching and nonmatching edges in cyclic alternation. It is even, and flipping all its edges preserves matching feasibility and cardinality.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M' = M\mathbin{\triangle}E(C)\text{ is a matching and }|M'|=|M|.\)

children.title: Symmetric-Difference Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Component decompositions arising from comparison of two matchings.

knowledge_statements.title: Symmetric-Difference Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Component decomposition for two matchings in a finite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be matchings in a finite undirected graph \(G\). Every nontrivial connected component of the spanning subgraph \((V,M\mathbin{\triangle}N)\) is either a path or an even cycle, and its edges alternate between \(M\setminus N\) and \(N\setminus M\). Cycle components contain equally many edges of both matchings. A path component has equal counts or has one more edge from exactly one of \(M\) and \(N\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The symmetric difference of two matchings decomposes into edge-alternating paths and even cycles, with each path having matching-edge counts differing by at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\mathbin{\triangle}N\text{ is a vertex-disjoint union of alternating paths and even alternating cycles.}\)

notation.meaning: edges belonging to exactly one of the two matchings
spanning subgraph induced by the symmetric-difference edges

children.top_down_role: Transformations between matchings supported by alternating components.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Exchange Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasible exchanges are obtained by flipping alternating components.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M,N\) be matchings of a finite graph \(G\), and let \(K\) be a connected component of \(M\mathbin{\triangle}N\). Then \(M_K=M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)\) is a matching. Moreover, \(|M_K|-|M|=|E(K)\cap N|-|E(K)\cap M|\), which belongs to \(\{-1,0,1\}\). In particular, a component beginning and ending with edges of \(N\setminus M\) is an \(M\)-augmenting path and its flip increases cardinality by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Flipping any component of the symmetric difference of two matchings remains feasible; its cardinality change is minus one, zero, or one according to the component endpoints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)\text{ is a matching and }|M\mathbin{\triangle}E(K)|-|M|\in\{-1,0,1\}.\)

notation.meaning: matching obtained by flipping the edges of the component

children.title: Odd-Cycle Structure

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd alternating cycles are expressed as blossoms with a distinguished base.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a matching in a finite graph \(G\). An \(M\)-blossom cycle is a simple odd cycle \(C\) with a distinguished vertex \(b\), called its base, such that \(M\cap E(C)\) matches every vertex of \(V(C)\setminus\{b\}\) within \(C\). Thus the two cycle edges incident with \(b\) lie outside \(M\), while all remaining cycle edges alternate between outside and inside \(M\). The cycle minus \(b\) has a perfect matching supplied by \(M\cap E(C)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A blossom cycle is odd and has one base vertex; all other cycle vertices are paired by alternating matching edges within the cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\cap E(C)\text{ is a perfect matching of }C-b.\)

notation.meaning: base vertex of the blossom cycle

children.title: Blossom Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Odd alternating structures that obstruct direct augmenting-path search.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The obstruction concerns uncontracted alternating-tree search in nonbipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\) be an \(M\)-alternating search forest rooted at vertices exposed by \(M\). If an edge joins two even-level vertices in the same tree, their tree paths to the least common ancestor together with that edge form an odd \(M\)-blossom cycle. Unlike the bipartite case, this edge need not yield an augmenting path: the two paths can meet at the blossom base. Treating the cycle as an ordinary alternating path therefore makes the uncontracted search criterion invalid.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge between even-level vertices of one alternating tree can close an odd blossom rather than produce an augmenting path, invalidating the bipartite search rule.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) is an alternating forest rooted at exposed vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{An even--even search edge within one tree may certify an odd blossom, not an }M\text{-augmenting path.}\)

knowledge_statements.scope_note: The base is characterized intrinsically by the matching on the odd cycle.

knowledge_statements.title: Nested Blossom Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Laminarity applies to blossoms maintained by recursive contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a recursive blossom-contraction regime, regard each contracted blossom as the union of its represented original vertices. If a new blossom is formed in the current contracted graph, then every previously contracted blossom is either wholly contained in the new blossom or disjoint from it. Hence the represented blossom sets form a laminar family \(\mathcal B\): for all \(B_1,B_2\in\mathcal B\), either \(B_1\cap B_2=\varnothing\), \(B_1\subseteq B_2\), or \(B_2\subseteq B_1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Recursive contraction maintains blossoms as a laminar family: any two represented blossom sets are disjoint or one contains the other.
assumptions_latex: Blossoms are created after contracting all currently active blossoms.
Each contracted vertex represents its full set of original vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal B\text{ is laminar.}\)

notation.meaning: family of represented blossom vertex sets

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte One-Factor Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte's criterion for perfect matchings in finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, and for \(S\subseteq V\) let \(q(G-S)\) denote the number of connected components of \(G-S\) having odd order. Then \(G\) has a one-factor, equivalently a perfect matching, if and only if \(q(G-S)\le |S|\) for every \(S\subseteq V\). In particular, taking \(S=\varnothing\) shows that every connected component of a graph having a perfect matching has even order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph has a perfect matching exactly when deleting any vertex set leaves no more odd components than the number of deleted vertices. In particular, each connected component of such a graph has even order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ has a perfect matching}\iff q(G-S)\le |S|\text{ for every }S\subseteq V.\)

notation.meaning: number of odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph

knowledge_statements.title: Tutte–Berge Maximum-Matching Min–Max Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cardinality and deficiency forms of the finite-graph Tutte–Berge formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, let \(\nu(G)\) be its maximum matching cardinality, and let \(q(G-S)\) count the odd-order components of \(G-S\). Then
\[|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\bigl(q(G-S)-|S|\bigr).\]
Equivalently,
\[\nu(G)=\frac12\min_{S\subseteq V}\bigl(|V|+|S|-q(G-S)\bigr).\]
Thus a maximizing set \(S\) certifies the number of vertices necessarily exposed by every matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum matching size equals half the minimum of vertex count plus deleted-set size minus the number of resulting odd components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\{q(G-S)-|S|\}.\)

notation.meaning: maximum cardinality of a matching in the graph
number of odd-order components after deleting the vertex set

knowledge_statements.title: Matching Barriers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Barriers are maximizers in the Tutte–Berge deficiency formula.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\), define \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)\). A set \(S\subseteq V\) is a matching barrier if
\[q(G-S)-|S|=\operatorname{def}(G),\]
where \(q(G-S)\) is the number of odd-order components of \(G-S\). Thus a barrier attains the Tutte–Berge maximum. When \(G\) has a perfect matching, this reduces to \(q(G-S)=|S|\); conventions that require nonempty \(S\) should be stated separately.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching barrier is a vertex set attaining the maximum odd-component excess in the Tutte–Berge formula, and therefore witnessing the graph's matching deficiency.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(S\text{ is a barrier}\iff q(G-S)-|S|=|V|-2\nu(G).\)

notation.meaning: number of vertices left exposed by a maximum matching
number of odd-order components after deleting the set

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Component Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd components after vertex deletion provide a verifiable deficiency lower bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite, let \(S\subseteq V\), and let \(Q_1,\ldots,Q_q\) be the odd-order components of \(G-S\). For every matching \(M\), at most \(|S|\) of these components can send an \(M\)-edge to \(S\). Each remaining odd component has at least one vertex unmatched by \(M\). Consequently every matching exposes at least \(q-|S|\) vertices, and
\[|M|\le \frac{|V|-q+|S|}{2}.\]
The listed components and set \(S\) therefore form a directly checkable deficiency certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deleting a set that creates many odd components certifies unmatched vertices: every matching exposes at least the number of odd components minus the deleted-set size.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|V|-2|M|\ge q(G-S)-|S|\text{ for every matching }M.\)

notation.meaning: odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph Deficiency
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte–Berge representation of cardinality-matching deficiency in a finite undirected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\nu(G)\) be the maximum cardinality of a matching and let \(o(G-U)\) count the odd-order connected components of the vertex-deleted graph \(G-U\). The matching deficiency, equal to the minimum number of vertices left uncovered by a matching, satisfies
\[
\operatorname{def}(G):=|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{U\subseteq V}\bigl(o(G-U)-|U|\bigr).
\]
Thus every set \(U\subseteq V\) gives the lower bound \(\operatorname{def}(G)\ge o(G-U)-|U|\), and at least one set attains equality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The minimum number of unmatched vertices equals the maximum, over deleted vertex sets, of the number of resulting odd components minus the number deleted.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph; parallel edges are allowed and loops are irrelevant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{U\subseteq V}(o(G-U)-|U|)\).

notation.meaning: number of odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph
minimum number of vertices uncovered by a matching

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Deficiency Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Primal–dual certificate for the Tutte–Berge deficiency value.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A certificate that a matching \(M\) of a finite graph \(G=(V,E)\) is maximum consists of a set \(U\subseteq V\) such that
\[
|V|-2|M|=o(G-U)-|U|.
\]
The matching verifies \(\operatorname{def}(G)\le |V|-2|M|\), while the odd components verify \(\operatorname{def}(G)\ge o(G-U)-|U|\): after matching vertices of \(U\), at least \(o(G-U)-|U|\) odd components must retain an uncovered vertex. Equality certifies both that \(M\) is maximum and that \(U\) maximizes the deficiency expression.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching and a deleted vertex set certify optimality when their numbers of uncovered vertices and excess odd components are equal.
assumptions_latex: \(M\subseteq E\) is a matching and \(U\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(|V|-2|M|=o(G-U)-|U|\), then \(M\) is maximum and \(U\) is a maximum-deficiency set.

notation.meaning: vertex set furnishing the odd-component bound
number of odd-order components after deleting U

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical vertex decomposition and the resulting structure and cardinality of maximum matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph. Let \(Y\) be the set of vertices exposed by at least one maximum matching, let \(X\) be the set of neighbors of \(Y\) in \(V(G)\setminus Y\), and let \(W=V(G)\setminus(X\cup Y)\). Every maximum matching in \(G\) contains a perfect matching of \(G[W]\), near-perfect matchings of the connected components of \(G[Y]\), and edges matching all vertices of \(X\) to distinct connected components of \(G[Y]\). Every connected component of \(G[Y]\) is factor-critical, and \(2\nu(G)=|V(G)|-q_G(X)+|X|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Gallai–Edmonds partition consists of vertices exposed by some maximum matching, their outside neighbors, and the remaining vertices. Every maximum matching is perfect on the remaining part, near-perfect on each exposed-part component, and matches each neighboring vertex into a distinct such component. Those components are factor-critical, and the stated formula gives twice the maximum-matching cardinality.
assumptions_latex: Y=\{v\in V(G):v\text{ is exposed by at least one maximum matching}\}.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \begin{aligned}&\text{Every maximum matching contains a perfect matching of }G[W]\text{ and near-perfect matchings of every component of }G[Y],\\&\text{and matches all vertices of }X\text{ to distinct components of }G[Y];\\&\text{every component of }G[Y]\text{ is factor-critical};\\&2\nu(G)=|V(G)|-q_G(X)+|X|.\end{aligned}

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Vertex Partition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical Gallai–Edmonds partition determined by all maximum matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. Define \(D\) to be the set of vertices that are uncovered by at least one maximum matching of \(G\). Define
\[
A:=N_G(D)\setminus D,
\qquad
C:=V\setminus(A\cup D).
\]
The ordered triple \((D,A,C)\) is the Gallai–Edmonds partition. It is canonical because its definition depends only on \(G\), not on a selected maximum matching. Here \(N_G(D)\) comprises all vertices outside or inside \(D\) adjacent to a vertex of \(D\), with subtraction ensuring \(A\cap D=\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Vertices exposable by maximum matchings form D; their external neighbors form A; all remaining vertices form C.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((D,A,C)\) is a uniquely determined partition of \(V\).

notation.meaning: vertices missed by at least one maximum matching
neighbors of D lying outside D
vertices in neither D nor A

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Critical Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Factor-critical portion of the Gallai–Edmonds structure theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((D,A,C)\) be the Gallai–Edmonds partition of a finite graph \(G\). Every connected component \(H\) of the induced subgraph \(G[D]\) is factor-critical: for every vertex \(v\in V(H)\), the graph \(H-v\) has a perfect matching. Consequently, every maximum matching of \(G\) restricts to a near-perfect matching in each component of \(G[D]\), except that components receiving a matching edge from \(A\) can expose the endpoint incident with that edge before the edge is added.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every component induced by D remains perfectly matchable after deletion of any one of its vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For every component \(H\) of \(G[D]\) and every \(v\in V(H)\), the graph \(H-v\) has a perfect matching.

notation.meaning: subgraph induced by the Gallai–Edmonds set D

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition-Based Matching Methods
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Construction of a maximum matching from the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input \(G\) and its Gallai–Edmonds partition \((D,A,C)\). Find a perfect matching of \(G[C]\). In the bipartite incidence graph between \(A\) and the components of \(G[D]\), find a matching saturating \(A\). For each assigned pair \((a,H)\), choose an edge \(av\) with \(v\in V(H)\) and a perfect matching of \(H-v\). In every unassigned component \(H\), choose any vertex \(w\) and a perfect matching of \(H-w\). Output the union of these edges and matchings. The output is a maximum matching of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Match C perfectly, assign each A vertex to a distinct D-component, and use near-perfect matchings inside the factor-critical components.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph with Gallai–Edmonds partition \((D,A,C)\).
The component-incidence matching records an actual edge from each assigned \(a\in A\) to its assigned component.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The constructed union is a matching of cardinality \(\nu(G)\).

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Definition relative to a matching using maximal factor-critical blocks and their contracted alternating forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(M\) a matching in \(G\). A subgraph \(F\subseteq G\) is a general blossom forest with respect to \(M\) if \(V(F)=V_1\dot\cup\cdots\dot\cup V_k\), each induced subgraph \(F_i:=F[V_i]\) is a maximal factor-critical subgraph of \(F\) satisfying \(\lvert M\cap E(F_i)\rvert=(\lvert V_i\rvert-1)/2\), and contracting every \(V_i\) produces an alternating forest \(F'\). Each \(F_i\), and all its vertices, is outer or inner according as its contracted vertex is outer or inner in \(F'\). A general blossom forest is special if every inner blossom consists of one vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general blossom forest partitions its vertices into maximal factor-critical blocks that are internally matched except for one vertex, with simultaneous contraction producing an alternating forest. Blocks inherit outer or inner status from the contracted forest, and the blossom forest is special when every inner block is a singleton.
assumptions_latex: G\text{ is a graph and }M\text{ is a matching in }G
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: F\text{ is a general blossom forest iff the blocks }F[V_i]\text{ satisfy the stated maximal factor-critical and matching conditions and their contraction yields an alternating forest; }F\text{ is special iff every inner }V_i\text{ is a singleton.}

knowledge_statements.title: Alternating Forests
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search forest used by the cardinality version of Edmonds' blossom algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a matching \(M\) in a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), an alternating forest \(F\) is a rooted forest in which every root is uncovered by \(M\), and every root-to-vertex path alternates between edges outside \(M\) and edges in \(M\), beginning with an edge outside \(M\). Vertices at even depth are outer and vertices at odd depth are inner. Every inner vertex is covered by \(M\), and its unique incident edge in \(M\) joins it to its outer child; equivalently, every nonroot outer vertex is joined to its inner parent by an edge in \(M\). During search growth from an outer vertex, an unmatched edge to an unreached matched vertex adds that vertex as inner and its mate as outer. An unmatched edge to an exposed vertex instead yields an augmenting path and does not add that exposed vertex as an inner vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An alternating forest grows from exposed roots through unmatched-then-matched edge pairs; even-depth vertices are outer, odd-depth vertices are inner, and reaching another exposed vertex produces an augmenting path.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Every root-to-outer path has even length, every root-to-inner path has odd length, and every inner vertex has a unique matched outer child.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph and \(M\) a matching in \(G\). knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Detection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Same-tree outer–outer collision criterion for detecting a blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(F\) be an alternating forest for matching \(M\). Suppose a searched edge \(xy\notin M\) joins distinct outer vertices in the same tree, and let \(b\) be their lowest common ancestor in \(F\). The union of \(xy\), the tree path from \(b\) to \(x\), and the tree path from \(b\) to \(y\) is an odd cycle \(B\). Its edges alternate with respect to \(M\), except that the two cycle edges incident with the base \(b\) are outside \(M\). This cycle, together with base \(b\), is the detected blossom.

knowledge_statements.title: Forest Label Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Parity and mate invariants maintained by an Edmonds alternating search forest.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In an alternating forest \(F\) for matching \(M\), each root is exposed and outer. Every nonroot outer vertex has an inner parent joined to it by an edge of \(M\); every inner vertex has an outer parent joined to it by an edge outside \(M\), and its unique \(M\)-mate is its outer child. Hence an outer vertex has an even-length alternating path from its root, while an inner vertex has an odd-length alternating path. These labels are relative to the current contracted search graph and must be recomputed or inherited consistently after contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Outer and inner labels encode path parity, with matched edges linking each inner vertex to its unique outer child.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is an alternating forest generated from exposed roots for matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Outer vertices have even alternating root paths; inner vertices have odd alternating root paths and a unique matched outer child.

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Collision Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Case distinction for an unmatched edge scanned from an outer search vertex.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: When an edge \(xy\notin M\) is scanned from an outer vertex \(x\), apply the following cases. If \(y\) is unreached and matched, add \(y\) as inner and its mate as outer; if \(y\) is unreached and exposed, the root-to-\(x\) path followed by \(xy\) is augmenting. If \(y\) is outer in a different tree, concatenate the two root paths with \(xy\) to obtain an augmenting path. If \(y\) is outer in the same tree, detect and contract the resulting blossom. Edges to inner vertices require no growth under this scan rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An outer-edge scan either grows the forest, finds an augmenting path, detects a blossom, or produces no search change.

\(x\) is outer and \(xy\notin M\) is being scanned.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Contraction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shrinking a detected alternating blossom during augmenting-path search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a graph \(G\), matching \(M\), and a detected blossom \(B\) with base \(b\). Replace all vertices of \(B\) by one pseudovertex \(\beta\); delete loops and retain each edge between \(B\) and \(V(G)\setminus B\) as an edge incident with \(\beta\), preserving its original endpoint in \(B\) as metadata. Replace the internal matched edges of \(B\) by nothing and map any matching edge leaving the base to its corresponding edge at \(\beta\). In the contracted search, treat \(\beta\) as having the outer status formerly held by \(b\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Shrink the odd alternating cycle to an outer pseudovertex while retaining boundary-edge endpoints for later expansion.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is an odd alternating blossom detected relative to matching \(M\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure produces the contracted graph \(G/B\) and induced matching \(M/B\) used for continued search.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Expansion
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lifting a contracted augmenting path through an odd alternating blossom.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input an augmenting path \(P'\) for \(M/B\) in \(G/B\), together with the stored boundary endpoints of blossom \(B\). If \(P'\) avoids the pseudovertex \(\beta\), return the same path in \(G\). Otherwise replace the segment through \(\beta\) by the parity-compatible alternating arc of \(B\) joining the recorded boundary endpoint to the base or to the other recorded boundary endpoint. Choose the one of the two cycle arcs that preserves alternation with the entering and leaving edges. The resulting path \(P\) is augmenting for \(M\); output \(M\triangle E(P)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Replace a contracted pseudovertex on an augmenting path by the blossom arc whose parity preserves alternation, then augment.
assumptions_latex: \(B\) is a contracted odd alternating blossom for \(M\).
\(P'\) is an augmenting path for \(M/B\), with original boundary endpoints retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Expansion yields an \(M\)-augmenting path \(P\) in \(G\), and \(M\triangle E(P)\) has cardinality \(|M|+1\).

knowledge_statements.title: Contraction Invariants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Augmenting-path invariance under valid Edmonds blossom shrinking.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(B\) be a blossom detected in an alternating search for matching \(M\), and let \(G/B\) and \(M/B\) be obtained by valid blossom contraction. Then \(G\) contains an \(M\)-augmenting path if and only if \(G/B\) contains an \(M/B\)-augmenting path. Any contracted augmenting path can be expanded through \(B\) to an augmenting path in \(G\), while contraction maps an augmenting path in \(G\), after the standard simplification of repeated blossom crossings, to one in \(G/B\). Therefore contraction preserves the test that \(M\) is maximum and preserves the possibility of increasing its cardinality by one.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Valid blossom contraction preserves the existence of an augmenting path and hence preserves whether the current matching is maximum.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite undirected graph and \(M\) is a matching.
\(B\) is a valid alternating blossom produced by an Edmonds search.
\(G/B\) and \(M/B\) use the standard base-preserving contraction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A nested-blossom representation consists of a laminar family \(\mathcal B\) of odd vertex sets. Each nontrivial \(B\in\mathcal B\) stores a base \(b(B)\), an odd cyclic sequence of maximal proper child blossoms and singleton vertices, and the cycle edges joining consecutive children. Laminarity means that for \(B,C\in\mathcal B\), either \(B\cap C=\varnothing\), \(B\subseteq C\), or \(C\subseteq B\). Inclusion therefore forms a rooted forest. Recursively replacing every child by its stored cycle reconstructs \(B\), while the stored base and matching parity determine the alternating route used when an augmenting path is expanded.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nested blossoms form a laminar inclusion forest. Each blossom stores a base and an odd cycle of children, enabling recursive reconstruction and parity-correct expansion.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical unweighted general-graph Micali–Vazirani bound.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A phase begins by determining \(\ell(M)\), the minimum number of edges in an \(M\)-augmenting path, using alternating levels together with blossom formation. It then finds and augments along a maximal collection of vertex-disjoint augmenting paths of length \(\ell(M)\), represented and expanded through the phase's blossom structure. The phase ends when no augmenting path at that level remains. After augmentation, the next existing shortest augmenting path is longer. With linear-time search work \(O(m)\) per phase and \(O(\sqrt n)\) phases, the total running time is \(O(m\sqrt n)\), and termination with no augmenting path certifies maximum cardinality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Micali–Vazirani organizes general-graph matching into shortest-augmenting-path phases. Linear work per phase over at most square-root-many phases yields the classical O(m sqrt n) bound.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(M=\varnothing\). For each augmentation search, grow an alternating forest \(F\) from all \(M\)-exposed vertices. When an eligible edge reaches a new vertex, add the corresponding unmatched and matched forest edges. When it joins two appropriate outer vertices in one tree, contract the resulting odd alternating cycle and record it in \(\mathcal B\). When it joins outer vertices rooted at distinct exposed vertices, trace the forest paths and blossom records to obtain an augmenting path \(P\), replace \(M\) by \(M\triangle E(P)\), expand affected blossoms, and restart. If a complete search finds no augmenting path, output \(M\).

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Dual-adjustment iteration of Edmonds' weighted perfect-matching algorithm
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Describes one primal–dual iteration on the contracted tight-edge graph, including optimality, infeasibility, and bounded-update outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let $z$ be a feasible dual solution and let $G_z$ be the current contracted tight-edge graph. Compute a maximum-cardinality matching $M$ in $G_z$. If $M$ is perfect, expand it to a perfect matching of $G$ using only tight edges; under the maintained optimality conditions, this matching is optimal. Otherwise, form the Gallai--Edmonds decomposition $W,X,Y$ of $G_z$. If $B(v)\in\mathcal B$ is the vertex set contracted to $v$, decrease $z_{B(v)}$ by $\varepsilon$ for every $v\in X$, and for every connected component $C$ of $G_z[Y]$ increase $z_A$ by $\varepsilon$, where $A=\bigcup_{v\in C}B(v)$. Choose the largest $\varepsilon>0$ preserving dual feasibility. Tight matching edges remain tight, and
\[
\#\operatorname{cc}(G_z[Y])>|X|,
\]
so the dual objective increases by
\[
\varepsilon\bigl(\#\operatorname{cc}(G_z[Y])-|X|\bigr)\geq\varepsilon.
\]
If arbitrarily large $\varepsilon$ remains feasible, the dual LP is unbounded, the primal perfect-matching LP is infeasible, and $G$ has no perfect matching. Otherwise, update $G_z$ to reflect newly tight edges, contractions, and unpackings, and continue. The stated finiteness argument uses the fact that between augmentations every grow, shrink, or unpack step increases the number of outer vertices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a maximum matching in the current contracted tight-edge graph. If it is perfect, expand it through tight edges to obtain an optimal perfect matching. Otherwise, use the Gallai–Edmonds decomposition to decrease dual variables associated with X and increase variables associated with components of Y, taking the largest positive step that preserves dual feasibility. This preserves tight matching edges and raises the dual objective. If the step is unbounded, no perfect matching exists; otherwise new tight edges, contractions, or unpackings produce the next iteration. Finiteness is tied to growth in the number of outer vertices between augmentations.
assumptions_latex: z\text{ is feasible for the weighted perfect-matching dual}
G_z\text{ is the current contracted graph formed from tight edges}
B(v)\in\mathcal B\text{ denotes the vertex set contracted to }v
\text{The algorithm maintains the cited primal--dual optimality conditions}
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \text{The iteration returns an optimal perfect matching, certifies that no perfect matching exists when the dual step is unbounded, or performs a maximal dual-feasible update with strictly increased dual objective.}

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each vertex \(v\in V\), the equality constraint \(x(\delta(v))=1\) has a free dual variable \(y_v\in\mathbb R\). Together with odd-set variables, dual feasibility requires, for every edge \(uv\in E\), \[y_u+y_v+\sum_{\substack{S\subseteq V:\ |S|\text{ odd},\ uv\in E(S)}}z_S\ge w_{uv}.\] The vertex contribution to the reduced slack of \(uv\) is therefore \(y_u+y_v\). Translating one vertex coordinate changes all incident edge slacks uniformly, while feasibility is preserved exactly when every affected edge inequality remains nonnegative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each degree equality produces a free vertex dual variable. An edge receives the sum of its endpoint variables, so changing one coordinate uniformly changes all incident edge slacks.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The primal odd-set inequality is \[x(E(S))\le \frac{|S|-1}{2}.\] Its dual coordinate satisfies \(z_S\ge0\), contributes \(z_S\) to the covering inequality of every edge in \(E(S)\), contributes nothing to edges crossing \(\delta(S)\), and has objective coefficient \((|S|-1)/2\). Hence increasing \(z_S\) translates the dual load of all internal edges together. Complementary slackness implies that \(z_S>0\) can occur in an optimal complementary pair only when the matching uses exactly \((|S|-1)/2\) edges of \(E(S)\), equivalently exactly one matching edge crosses \(\delta(S)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd-set dual variable is nonnegative, prices every edge internal to that odd set, and can be positive complementarily only when the matching leaves exactly one vertex matched outward.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \(L_{uv}=y_u+y_v+\sum_{S:uv\in E(S)}z_S\). Dual feasibility gives \(L_e\ge w_e\) for every \(e\in E\). If \(L_e=w_e\) for every \(e\in M\), and \(z_S>0\) implies \(x(E(S))=(|S|-1)/2\), then all complementary-slackness products vanish. Consequently the primal weight \(\sum_{e\in M}w_e\) equals the dual objective \(\sum_{v\in V}y_v+\sum_S((|S|-1)/2)z_S\). Weak duality then certifies that \(M\) is a maximum-weight perfect matching and \((y,z)\) is dual-optimal.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Compute \(s_e=L_e-w_e\) and form \(E_0=\{e\in E:s_e=0\}\). Initialize an alternating forest at exposed vertices of the contracted graph. knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Maintain an alternating forest in \(G/\mathcal B\), treating each maximal blossom as one pseudovertex with the parity of its base. When a scanned tight edge joins two outer vertices in one search tree, trace their paths to the least common ancestor, contract the resulting odd alternating cycle, record its base and children, and continue on the new quotient. When a tight edge joins distinct exposed-root trees, concatenate their forest paths and that edge, then recursively expand every encountered blossom according to its stored entry, exit, and base. The resulting simple alternating path is used to augment \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search treats maximal blossoms as pseudovertex units. New odd cycles are contracted, while stored bases and child structure allow any discovered augmenting path to be expanded correctly.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Blossom Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Structural invariant of active blossoms in weighted equality-subgraph search.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For every edge \(e\) on the defining alternating cycle of \(B\), tightness means \(L_e=w_e\). The cycle is odd and has a distinguished base; its edges alternate between \(M\) and \(E\setminus M\) except at the base. With the base, child order, and attachment vertices retained, contraction preserves the alternating-search structure and the stored decomposition supplies parity-compatible lifts. Moreover, if a feasible perfect matching \(M^\star\) and the dual solution are complementary and \(z_B>0\), then \(|M^\star\cap E(B)|=(|B|-1)/2\), equivalently exactly one edge of \(M^\star\) crosses \(\delta(B)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A tight blossom is an odd alternating cycle of zero-slack edges with a stored base and decomposition, permitting contraction and later parity-correct lifting. In a complementary perfect matching, a positive blossom dual value forces exactly one matching edge to leave the blossom.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is finite, \(M\subseteq E\) is a matching, and \((y,z)\) is dual-feasible for the maximum-weight perfect-matching formulation.
\(B\subseteq V\) is an active odd blossom whose defining alternating cycle consists of tight edges and whose base, child order, and edge attachments are retained.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The blossom is an admissible contracted search unit; if a feasible perfect matching \(M^\star\) is complementary to the dual and \(z_B>0\), exactly one edge of \(M^\star\) crosses \(\delta(B)\).

children.title: Search-Stall Regimes

knowledge_statements.title: Search-Stall Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Search-stall condition stated independently of the sign convention used by a particular weighted-matching dual update.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A tight-edge search stalls when every tight edge incident with the outer set \(O\) has been scanned and none permits forest growth, blossom contraction, or augmentation. The stall condition alone is not an optimality certificate. To resume the search, the particular primal–dual algorithm must choose a nonzero update that preserves dual feasibility, nonnegativity of all constrained odd-set variables, and the tight equalities required by the current forest and matching. A maximal finite update ends when a previously slack search-relevant edge becomes tight or an active blossom variable reaches zero. The first event enlarges the equality-subgraph search, while the second permits the algorithm to dissolve or expand the affected blossom. If no such positive update is available, termination requires a separate optimality or infeasibility argument supplied by the selected algorithm.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Search stalls when all reachable tight edges have been exhausted without growth, contraction, or augmentation. A variant-specific feasible dual update must then create a relevant tight edge or reduce an active blossom price to zero; the absence of such an update is not by itself an optimality certificate.
assumptions_latex: \((y,z)\) is dual-feasible and an alternating tight-edge search has reached outer set \(O\) and inner set \(I\).
No currently tight edge permits forest growth, blossom contraction, or augmentation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Further search progress requires a feasible nonzero dual update that creates a new search-relevant tight edge or makes an active blossom variable zero; otherwise a separate terminality certificate is required.

children.title: Gabow Weighted-Matching Methods
children.top_down_role: Gabow-style combinatorial methods for weighted general-graph matching.

assumptions_latex: \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\) is an integral edge-weight function.
The objective is to find a matching maximizing \(w(M)=\sum_{e\in M}w(e)\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The final matching maximizes \(w(M)\) over all matchings of \(G\).

notation.meaning: Dual variables associated with vertices and contracted odd sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Generic exact integral-weight scaling template; the precise Gabow variant and its complexity remain source-dependent.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \(G=(V,E)\) and integral weights \(w\), initialize \(M=\varnothing\), feasible vertex and blossom dual variables \((y,z)\), and a scaling unit \(\delta\) determined by the leading weight bits. At each scale, form truncated weights \(w_\delta\), restore the prescribed approximate domination and tightness conditions for reduced costs, and repeatedly perform searches in the eligible-edge graph. Each search either augments \(M\), contracts an odd alternating blossom, expands a blossom whose dual reaches its boundary, or changes \((y,z)\) by the largest admissible dual adjustment. After no further augmentation is possible at that scale, refine \(w_\delta\), reduce \(\delta\), and continue. When the exact scale is reached, output \(M\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Process integral weights from coarse to fine while maintaining matching and blossom dual invariants; eligible-edge searches and dual adjustments yield an exact maximum-weight matching at the final scale.
knowledge_statements.title: Gabow Weighted-Matching Methods

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No evidence is cited, and the approximate domination, tightness, eligibility, and termination conditions depend on the particular Gabow scaling variant. The exact-optimality conclusion cannot be checked until a variant and supporting source are specified.

assumptions_latex: \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\) and \(|w(e)|\le W\) for every \(e\in E\).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=1+\lceil\log_2 W\rceil\). A binary weight-scaling regime chooses an initial power-of-two unit \(\delta_0\ge W\) and sets \(\delta_{k+1}=\delta_k/2\). At phase \(k\), the algorithm uses a truncated or rounded weight function \(w_k\) exposing the weight information resolved at unit \(\delta_k\), while preserving an approximate primal-dual optimality invariant whose error is proportional to \(\delta_k\). Once \(\delta_k\) reaches the unit scale, integrality converts the final approximate invariant into exact optimality. Consequently, only \(L\) binary refinement phases are required; multiplying all weights by a positive common integer changes numerical magnitudes but not the optimizing matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Binary scaling reveals integral weights one bit at a time. Weights bounded by W require at most one plus the ceiling of log base two of W phases.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A scaling phase at unit \(\delta\) consists of four logical operations. First, incorporate the next weight information and modify dual variables so approximate domination is restored. Second, construct the eligible graph \(H_\delta\) from edges meeting the phase's reduced-cost threshold. Third, run alternating-forest searches in \(H_\delta\), augmenting \(M\) when an augmenting path is found and maintaining odd blossoms by contraction and expansion. Fourth, when a search stalls, perform a maximal admissible dual adjustment; repeat until the phase termination condition holds. The resulting matching, blossom family, and dual variables satisfy the initialization invariant for scale \(\delta/2\). At the terminal integral scale, complementary slackness yields exact optimality.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each scale imports finer weight information, restores dual feasibility, searches eligible edges with blossom operations, and performs dual adjustments until the next scale can begin.
knowledge_statements.title: Scaling-Phase Structure

children.title: Numerical Weight Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Dependence on weight magnitude, integrality, or encoding.

knowledge_statements.title: Numerical Weight Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bit-length and overflow boundary for exact integral-weight implementations under an explicit sign-magnitude convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Suppose a signed integer is stored in sign-magnitude form using one sign bit and \(b-1\) magnitude bits. Such a word represents every integer of magnitude at most \(2^{b-1}-1\). Hence all input weights satisfying \(|w(e)|\le W\) are representable exactly if and only if \(W\le 2^{b-1}-1\), equivalently \(b\ge 1+\lceil\log_2(W+1)\rceil\). Because a matching contains at most \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor\) edges, its objective value has magnitude at most \(\lfloor n/2\rfloor W\); an objective accumulator therefore requires at least \(1+\lceil\log_2(\lfloor n/2\rfloor W+1)\rceil\) bits under the same convention. Scaled weights, reduced costs, and dual expressions require separate bounds. Overflow or inexact arithmetic can change eligibility tests and invalidate an optimality certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With one sign bit and b minus one magnitude bits, exact input storage requires b at least one plus the ceiling of log base two of W plus one. Matching-value accumulators and other derived quantities may require additional bits, and overflow can invalidate eligibility and optimality tests.
assumptions_latex: \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\) and \(|w(e)|\le W\) for every \(e\in E\), where \(W\ge 0\).
Signed integers use a sign-magnitude representation with one sign bit and \(b-1\) magnitude bits.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact input storage requires \(b\ge 1+\lceil\log_2(W+1)\rceil\), while an objective accumulator requires at least \(1+\lceil\log_2(\lfloor n/2\rfloor W+1)\rceil\) bits under the stated convention.

notation.meaning: Total number of bits in a sign-magnitude signed-integer word.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Store a weighted graph in a symmetric matrix \(A\), where \(A_{uv}=w(uv)\) when \(uv\in E\) and a distinguished sentinel denotes \(uv\notin E\). Edge existence and weight lookup then take \(O(1)\) time, the matrix occupies \(\Theta(n^2)\) words, and scanning every possible edge takes \(O(n^2)\) time. This representation statement does not by itself determine the total running time, which also depends on the number of searches and dual-adjustment events.

The representation occupies \(O(n+m)\) words, enumerates the edges incident with \(v\) in \(O(|L(v)|)\) time, and scans all stored edges in \(O(m)\) time. Sparse storage avoids inspecting nonedges, although priority queues or additional indices may be required to locate the next minimum-slack edge efficiently during primal-dual adjustments.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An integer-weight implementation is exact when every stored weight, scaled weight, reduced cost, dual variable, and objective accumulator is represented without overflow and every comparison is exact. Rational weights may be converted to integers by a common positive denominator, but the resulting encoding length, rather than numerical value alone, governs arithmetic cost.

children.title: Density–Encoding Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Performance interactions between graph density plus weight representation.

knowledge_statements.title: Density–Encoding Tradeoffs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Joint density and binary-encoding contribution to scan-based running time; the bound excludes non-scan work.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(L=1+\lceil\log_2 W\rceil\). If a binary scaling implementation performs \(s_k\) complete edge scans during phase \(k\), then its total scan time is \(O\!\left(m\sum_{k=1}^{L}s_k\right)\) with adjacency lists and \(O\!\left(n^2\sum_{k=1}^{L}s_k\right)\) with a matrix. Thus sparse storage improves the scan component when \(m=o(n^2)\) and searches avoid nonedges, whereas matrix storage has asymptotically commensurate size when \(m=\Theta(n^2)\). The number \(L\) records the binary weight-encoding contribution and is distinct from graph density. These bounds exclude blossom maintenance, priority operations, arithmetic bit cost, and other search or dual-update work.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Density determines the cost of each complete edge scan, while binary weight encoding determines the number of scaling phases. If phase k performs s sub k scans, the scan costs sum over those multiplicities; other algorithmic work must be charged separately.
assumptions_latex: \(w:E\to\mathbb Z\) satisfies \(|w(e)|\le W\) for every \(e\in E\), where \(W\ge1\).
The implementation uses \(L=1+\lceil\log_2 W\rceil\) binary scaling phases and performs \(s_k\ge0\) complete edge scans in phase \(k\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The scan time is \(O\!\left(m\sum_{k=1}^{L}s_k\right)\) with adjacency lists and \(O\!\left(n^2\sum_{k=1}^{L}s_k\right)\) with a matrix; these expressions do not bound the algorithm's non-scan work.

assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal M\) is the set of matchings and \(F(w)=\max_{M\in\mathcal M}\sum_{e\in M}w_e\).

source_refs.locator: Chapter 11. Weighted Matching p. 277

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function \(F:\mathbb R^E\to\mathbb R\), defined by \(F(w)=\max_{M\in\mathcal M}\langle w,\chi^M\rangle\), is convex, continuous, and piecewise linear because it is the maximum of finitely many linear functions. If \(M^*\) is optimal at \(w\), then for every perturbation \(d\in\mathbb R^E\), \[F(w+d)\ge F(w)+\langle d,\chi^{M^*}\rangle.\] Thus \(\chi^{M^*}\in\partial F(w)\). More generally, \(\partial F(w)\) is the convex hull of incidence vectors of all matchings optimal at \(w\). A unique optimum remains optimal under every sufficiently small perturbation that stays inside its normal cone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The optimal matching value is convex and piecewise linear in edge weights. Optimal matching incidence vectors are exactly the extreme data governing its local sensitivity.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The matching polytope \(P_M(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}\) is exactly \[\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E: x_e\ge 0\ \text{for all }e\in E,\quad x(\delta(v))\le 1\ \text{for all }v\in V,\quad x(E(S))\le \frac{|S|-1}{2}\ \text{for every odd }S\subseteq V\right\}.\] The odd-set inequalities may be restricted to odd sets with \(|S|\ge 3\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a graph, and let \(\mathcal A\) denote the odd-cardinality subsets of \(V\). Then
\[
\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^M:M\text{ is a matching of }G\}
=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:x(\delta(v))\le1\ (v\in V),\quad x(E(G[A]))\le\frac{|A|-1}{2}\ (A\in\mathcal A)\right\}.
\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The convex hull of all matching incidence vectors is exactly the set of nonnegative edge vectors satisfying every vertex-degree inequality and every odd-set inequality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Because \(P_{PM}(G)\) is a polytope, every nonempty face is exposed: there exist \(c\in\mathbb R^E\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\) such that \[F=\{x\in P_{PM}(G):\langle c,x\rangle=\alpha\},\qquad \alpha=\max_{x\in P_{PM}(G)}\langle c,x\rangle.\] Since the vertices of \(P_{PM}(G)\) are perfect-matching incidence vectors, \(F\) equals the convex hull of those \(\chi^M\) whose perfect matchings maximize \(c(M)\). knowledge_statements.title: Polytope Dimension Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dimensions of the matching and perfect-matching polytopes in their natural edge-coordinate spaces.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph. The matching polytope \(P_M(G)\subseteq\mathbb R^E\) is full-dimensional and satisfies \(\dim P_M(G)=|E|\). Suppose that \(G\) has a perfect matching, let \(E^*\) be the set of edges occurring in at least one perfect matching, and put \(H=(V,E^*)\). If \(b(H)\) is the number of bipartite connected components of \(H\), then the affine hull of \(P_{PM}(G)\) is defined by \(x_e=0\) for \(e\notin E^*\) and \(x(\delta_H(v))=1\) for \(v\in V\), and \[\dim P_{PM}(G)=|E^*|-|V|+b(H).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The matching polytope has dimension equal to the number of edges. If the graph has a perfect matching, the perfect-matching polytope has dimension equal to the number of allowed edges minus the number of vertices plus the number of bipartite connected components of the allowed-edge graph.
assumptions_latex: For the perfect-matching formula, \(G\) has at least one perfect matching.

notation.meaning: Edges contained in at least one perfect matching of G.

children.title: Odd-Set Inequality Family

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Set Inequality Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-cardinality constraints in Edmonds' description of the general matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), every matching-incidence vector satisfies, for each odd set \(S\subseteq V\), \[x(E(S))\leq \left\lfloor\frac{|S|}{2}\right\rfloor=\frac{|S|-1}{2}.\] Together with \(x_e\geq0\) for \(e\in E\) and \(x(\delta(v))\leq1\) for \(v\in V\), all these odd-set inequalities describe the matching polytope: \[P_M(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R^E: x\geq0,\ x(\delta(v))\leq1\ \text{for all }v,\ x(E(S))\leq\frac{|S|-1}{2}\ \text{for all odd }S\right\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd vertex set contains at most half its vertices, rounded down, as matching edges; these inequalities complete the matching-polytope description.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(E(S))\leq (|S|-1)/2\), and the displayed system defines \(P_M(G)\).

notation.meaning: Edges having both endpoints in S.

knowledge_statements.title: Blossom Facet Family
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Facet status of odd-set inequalities for complete-graph matching polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(n\geq3\) and let \(P_M(K_n)\subseteq\mathbb R^{E(K_n)}\) be the matching polytope of the complete graph. For every odd set \(S\subseteq V(K_n)\) with \(|S|\geq3\), the blossom inequality \[x(E(S))\leq\frac{|S|-1}{2}\] defines a facet of \(P_M(K_n)\). Thus the odd-set family supplies genuine non-degree facets even though every integral matching automatically satisfies each member.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In a complete graph, every odd-set inequality on at least three vertices defines a facet of the matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(E(S))\leq (|S|-1)/2\) is facet-defining for \(P_M(K_n)\).

knowledge_statements.title: Facet-Defining Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A standard graph-theoretic regime for an odd-set inequality to define a matching-polytope facet.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) and let \(S\subseteq V\) be odd with \(|S|\geq3\). If the induced graph \(G[S]\) is factor-critical and 2-vertex-connected, then the valid inequality \[x(E(S))\leq\frac{|S|-1}{2}\] defines a facet of the matching polytope \(P_M(G)\). Here factor-critical means that \(G[S]-s\) has a perfect matching for every \(s\in S\). In particular, complete induced subgraphs of odd order at least three satisfy this regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd-set inequality is facet-defining when its induced subgraph is factor-critical and 2-vertex-connected; odd complete subgraphs are standard examples.
assumptions_latex: \(S\subseteq V\) is odd, \(|S|\geq3\), and \(G[S]\) is factor-critical and 2-vertex-connected.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(E(S))\leq (|S|-1)/2\) defines a facet of \(P_M(G)\).

notation.meaning: Subgraph of G induced by S.

children.title: Redundant Odd-Set Constraints

knowledge_statements.title: Redundant Odd-Set Constraints
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A structural class of odd-set inequalities implied by vertex-degree constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(S\subseteq V\) be an odd set such that \(G[S]\) is bipartite with bipartition \((A,B)\), where \(|A|\leq|B|\). Every \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) satisfying \(x\geq0\) and \(x(\delta(v))\leq1\) for all \(v\in V\) also satisfies \[x(E(S))\leq\frac{|S|-1}{2}.\] Thus the odd-set inequality indexed by \(S\) is redundant in the matching-polytope system. For a singleton odd set, it reduces to \(0\leq0\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If an odd set induces a bipartite graph, its odd-set inequality follows from nonnegativity and the vertex-degree inequalities and is therefore redundant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x(E(S))\leq(|S|-1)/2\) is implied by nonnegativity and the vertex-degree constraints.

notation.meaning: A bipartition of the induced graph on S.

knowledge_statements.title: Cunningham–Marsh Total-Dual-Integrality Theory
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Total dual integrality of Edmonds' general matching-polytope system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), the system \(x_e\geq0\), \(x(\delta(v))\leq1\), and \(x(E(S))\leq(|S|-1)/2\) for all odd \(S\subseteq V\) is totally dual integral. Equivalently, for every integral weight vector \(w\in\mathbb Z^E\) for which the primal maximum is finite, the dual \[\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v+\sum_{S\text{ odd}}\frac{|S|-1}{2}z_S:\ y_u+y_v+\sum_{S\text{ odd}:\,u,v\in S}z_S\geq w_{uv},\ y,z\geq0\right\}\] has an integral optimum \((y,z)\). Consequently the system defines an integral polyhedron.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degree, nonnegativity, and odd-set system for general matchings is TDI, so every integral edge-weight objective admits an integral optimal dual solution.
assumptions_latex: \(w\in\mathbb Z^E\) and the primal optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The matching-polytope system is totally dual integral and its dual has an integral optimum for integral \(w\).

notation.meaning: Dual variable for the degree inequality at v.
Dual variable for the odd-set inequality indexed by S.

children.title: Odd-Set Separation
children.top_down_role: Detection of violated odd-set constraints for candidate fractional points.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Set Separation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong separation of odd-set inequalities through a minimum odd-cut computation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a rational vector \(x\in\mathbb Q^E\) satisfying \(x\geq0\) and \(x(\delta(v))\leq1\). Form an auxiliary graph \(H\) by adjoining a root \(r\), assigning capacity \(x_e\) to every original edge, and capacity \(1-x(\delta(v))\) to \(rv\). Find an odd-cardinality set \(S\subseteq V\) minimizing the cut capacity \(c_H(\delta_H(S))\). If its value is below \(1\), output \(x(E(S))\leq(|S|-1)/2\) as violated; otherwise certify that no odd-set inequality is violated. Indeed, \(c_H(\delta_H(S))=|S|-2x(E(S))\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Build a rooted capacitated graph and find a minimum odd cut; value below one identifies a violated odd-set inequality, otherwise none exists.
assumptions_latex: A polynomial-time minimum odd-cut routine is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a violated odd-set inequality or certifies that all such inequalities hold.

notation.meaning: Capacity of the auxiliary cut determined by S.
