children.title: Matching-Polytope Optimization
children.top_down_role: Linear optimization over general matching polyhedra.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Polytope Optimization
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear optimization over the general matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and rational weights \(w\in\mathbb Q^E\), solve \[\max\{w^Tx:x\in P_M(G)\}.\] Apply a polynomial-time strong separation oracle to the nonnegativity, degree, and odd-set inequalities and use the optimization-from-separation method. The returned optimum may be chosen as an extreme point; because \(P_M(G)\) is integral, it equals \(\chi^M\) for a matching \(M\). Thus the output matching satisfies \(w(M)=\max\{w(N):N\text{ is a matching of }G\}\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Optimize any rational linear objective over the matching polytope by separation; integrality ensures that an optimal extreme point is an actual matching.
assumptions_latex: A polynomial-time strong separation oracle for \(P_M(G)\) is available.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An optimal matching \(M\) maximizing \(w(M)\) is obtained in polynomial time.

children.title: Separation–Optimization Equivalence
children.top_down_role: Oracle-level relationship between polyhedral separation plus optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Separation–Optimization Equivalence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Oracle equivalence for rational, well-described polyhedra, specialized to matching polytopes.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) be a nonempty rational polytope with a known polynomial bound on facet encoding lengths. Strong separation over \(P\) and strong linear optimization over \(P\) are polynomial-time oracle equivalent: either oracle, together with the encoding bound, implements the other in time polynomial in \(d\), the input encoding length, and the oracle running time. Consequently, polynomial-time separation of the odd-set system yields polynomial-time weighted matching-polytope optimization, while a strong optimization oracle yields a strong separator for the same polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For a well-described rational polytope, strong separation and strong linear optimization reduce to one another in polynomial time; this applies to matching polytopes.
assumptions_latex: \(P\subseteq\mathbb R^d\) is a nonempty rational polytope.
A polynomial facet-complexity bound for \(P\) is known.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Strong separation over \(P\) is polynomial-time equivalent to strong linear optimization over \(P\).

notation.meaning: A rational polytope supplied through an oracle and encoding bound.

children.title: Minimum Odd-Cut Connection
children.top_down_role: Connection between odd-set separation plus minimum odd-cut structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Minimum Odd-Cut Connection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact representation of odd-set slack as a rooted auxiliary cut capacity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\), and let \(x\in\mathbb R^E\) satisfy \(x\geq0\) and \(x(\delta_G(v))\leq1\) for every \(v\in V\). Form a graph \(H\) by adjoining a root \(r\) to \(G\). Assign capacity \(c_e=x_e\) to each \(e\in E\) and capacity \(c_{rv}=1-x(\delta_G(v))\) to each root edge \(rv\). For every \(S\subseteq V\), \[c(\delta_H(S))=x(\delta_G(S))+\sum_{v\in S}\bigl(1-x(\delta_G(v))\bigr)=|S|-2x(E(S)).\] Therefore, when \(|S|\) is odd, the odd-set inequality indexed by \(S\) is violated exactly when the corresponding auxiliary cut has capacity less than \(1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The slack of an odd-set inequality is represented by an auxiliary rooted-cut capacity; a violation is exactly an odd-cardinality cut of capacity below one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: For odd \(S\subseteq V\), \(x(E(S))>(|S|-1)/2\) if and only if \(c(\delta_H(S))<1\).

notation.meaning: Graph obtained from G by adjoining root r and all root edges.

children.title: Fractional Matchings

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Degree-relaxation definition of a fractional matching in a general graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a fractional matching is a vector \(x\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^E\) satisfying \[\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\leq1\qquad\text{for every }v\in V.\] Its cardinality is \(x(E)=\sum_{e\in E}x_e\), and its weight under \(w\in\mathbb R^E\) is \(w^Tx\). The fractional matching polytope is \[P_{FM}(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^E:x(\delta(v))\leq1\text{ for every }v\in V\}.\] It is the degree relaxation obtained by omitting the odd-set inequalities from the matching-polytope description.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional matching assigns nonnegative edge values so that the total value incident to every vertex is at most one.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_{FM}(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^E:x(\delta(v))\leq1\text{ for every }v\in V\}\).

notation.meaning: Set of edges incident with v.

children.title: Fractional Covers

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Covers
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Vertex-cover LP dual to the maximum-cardinality fractional matching relaxation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), a fractional vertex cover is a vector \(y\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^V\) such that \[y_u+y_v\geq1\qquad\text{for every }uv\in E.\] Its value is \(y(V)=\sum_{v\in V}y_v\). More generally, for \(w\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^E\), a fractional cover of the edge requirements \(w\) is a vector \(y\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^V\) satisfying \(y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\) for every \(uv\in E\). The program \[\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^V,\ y_u+y_v\geq w_{uv}\text{ for every }uv\in E\right\}\] is the linear-programming dual of maximizing \(w^Tx\) over the fractional matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A fractional cover gives nonnegative vertex weights whose endpoint sum covers every edge requirement; its minimum-value program is dual to weighted fractional matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(y\in\mathbb R_{\geq0}^V\) is a fractional vertex cover exactly when \(y_u+y_v\geq1\) for every \(uv\in E\).

children.title: Matching–Cover Duality

knowledge_statements.title: Matching–Cover Duality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weighted LP duality between fractional matchings and fractional vertex covers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(c\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge 0}^{E}\). Then
\[
\max\left\{\sum_{e\in E}c_e x_e:x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E},\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le1\ \text{for every }v\in V\right\}
=
\min\left\{\sum_{v\in V}y_v:y\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{V},\ y_u+y_v\ge c_{uv}\ \text{for every }uv\in E\right\}.
\]
Both optima are attained. Thus the maximum weight of a fractional matching equals the minimum weight of a fractional vertex cover for edge demands \(c\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The maximum weight fractional matching equals the minimum fractional vertex-cover cost for the corresponding edge demands.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nu_f(G,c)=\tau_f(G,c)\), with both linear-programming optima attained.

children.title: Fractional Integrality Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Regimes separating integral behavior from genuinely fractional behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Fractional Integrality Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact integrality boundary for the degree-constrained fractional matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), define
\[
P_f(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E}:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}x_e\le1\ \text{for every }v\in V\right\}.
\]
Every extreme point of \(P_f(G)\) is integral if and only if \(G\) is bipartite. Consequently, degree and nonnegativity constraints describe the matching polytope precisely for bipartite graphs. If \(G\) is nonbipartite, a shortest odd cycle is chordless, and assigning \(1/2\) to its edges and \(0\) elsewhere yields a nonintegral extreme point of \(P_f(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The degree relaxation is integral exactly for bipartite graphs; an odd cycle produces a half-integral extreme point.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_f(G)\) is integral if and only if \(G\) is bipartite.

knowledge_statements.title: Half-Integral Extreme-Point Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Extreme-point classification for the fractional matching polytope with only degree constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, and let \(x\) be an extreme point of
\[
P_f(G)=\left\{z\in\mathbb{R}_{\ge0}^{E}:\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}z_e\le1\ \text{for every }v\in V\right\}.
\]
Then \(x_e\in\{0,1/2,1\}\) for every \(e\in E\). The edges with value \(1\) form a matching, while the edges with value \(1/2\) form a vertex-disjoint union of odd cycles disjoint from those value-one edges. Conversely, every vector having this structure is an extreme point of \(P_f(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every extreme fractional matching consists of disjoint unit edges and vertex-disjoint odd cycles whose edges have value one-half.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is half-integral, and its fractional support is a vertex-disjoint union of odd cycles.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd-Cycle Relaxation Gaps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp cardinality gap caused by omitting odd-set inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For the odd cycle \(C_{2k+1}\), where \(k\ge1\), the vector assigning \(x_e=1/2\) to every edge satisfies all fractional matching degree constraints and has value \((2k+1)/2\). Every integral matching has at most \(k\) edges, and a matching of size \(k\) exists. Hence
\[
\frac{\nu_f(C_{2k+1})}{\nu(C_{2k+1})}=\frac{2k+1}{2k}=1+\frac{1}{2k}.
\]
The ratio is maximized by the triangle, where it equals \(3/2\). The missing odd-set inequality is \(x(E(C_{2k+1}))\le k\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd cycle has fractional value one-half above its matching number; the triangle gives the largest cycle ratio, three-halves.

knowledge_statements.title: Algebraic Perfect-Matching Existence Testing
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact Tutte-matrix identity test for perfect-matching existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input a graph \(G\) on vertices \(1,\ldots,n\). Introduce commuting indeterminates \(z_{ij}\) for edges with \(i<j\), and initialize the skew-symmetric Tutte matrix \(T(G)\) by \(T_{ij}=z_{ij}\), \(T_{ji}=-z_{ij}\) when \(ij\in E(G)\), and \(T_{ij}=0\) otherwise. Compute whether \(\det T(G)\) is the zero polynomial. Output “perfect matching exists” exactly when it is nonzero. This is correct because
\[
G\text{ has a perfect matching}\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \det T(G)\not\equiv0.
\]
For odd \(n\), the determinant vanishes and the output is negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Construct the symbolic Tutte matrix and test whether its determinant is identically zero; nonvanishing is equivalent to a perfect matching.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite loopless undirected graph.
Polynomial arithmetic is over a field of characteristic different from \(2\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The algorithm returns yes if and only if \(G\) has a perfect matching.

notation.meaning: symbolic skew-symmetric Tutte matrix of G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The symbolic Tutte-matrix criterion is standard and the algorithm kind fits the existence-testing leaf, but the record has no citation. An authoritative source with a theorem or section/page locator is required before the determinant criterion can be accepted.

knowledge_statements.title: Randomized Algebraic Matching Construction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: One-sided-error construction by random Tutte evaluation and algebraic self-reduction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Input an even-order graph \(G
e\varnothing\) and a finite field \(\mathbb F_q\) of odd characteristic. Independently substitute uniform elements of \(\mathbb F_q\) for the Tutte variables, obtaining \(A
\). If \(\det A=0\), report failure and resample. Otherwise choose an edge \(uv\) with \(A_{uv}\ne0\) and \(\det A[V\setminus\{u,v\}]\ne0\), output \(uv\), delete \(u,v\), and repeat on the indicated principal submatrix until no vertices remain. The output edges form a perfect matching. If one initial evaluation is used, a graph having a perfect matching is rejected with probability at most \(n/q\); resampling gives a Las Vegas construction.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Randomly evaluate the Tutte matrix, then repeatedly select an edge whose complementary principal minor stays nonsingular.
assumptions_latex: Random field substitutions are independent and uniform.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A successful run outputs a perfect matching; when one evaluation is attempted, false failure has probability at most \(n/q\).

notation.meaning: random numerical evaluation of the Tutte matrix

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The construction requires an authoritative algorithm locator to verify the complementary-minor selection rule, reuse of one random evaluation, and the stated n/q bound. The Las Vegas claim must also be scoped to graphs promised to have a perfect matching, since perpetual resampling does not terminate on a graph without one.

children.title: Pfaffian Representations

knowledge_statements.title: Pfaffian Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pfaffian expansion of a skew-oriented weighted adjacency matrix.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G=(V,E)\) have \(V=\{1,\ldots,2m\}\), fix an orientation, and assign commuting weights \(w_e\). Define the skew-symmetric matrix \(K\) by \(K_{ij}=w_{ij}\) if \(i\to j\), \(K_{ij}=-w_{ij}\) if \(j\to i\), and \(K_{ij}=0\) if \(ij\notin E\). Then
\[
\operatorname{Pf}(K)=\sum_{M\in\mathcal M_{m perf}(G)}s_K(M)\prod_{e\in M}w_e,
\qquad
\det K=\operatorname{Pf}(K)^2,
\]
where \(s_K(M)\in\{-1,1\}\) is determined by the vertex order and orientation. Under a Pfaffian orientation, all nonzero matching terms have one common sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The Pfaffian of an oriented skew adjacency matrix is a signed generating function for perfect matchings, and its square is the determinant.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite graph on an even, linearly ordered vertex set.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{Pf}(K)\) is the signed perfect-matching polynomial and \(\det K=\operatorname{Pf}(K)^2\).

notation.meaning: set of perfect matchings of G

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The signed perfect-matching expansion and determinant-square identity fit the representation leaf, but no source is cited. A specific authoritative Pfaffian definition, proposition, or page locator is required, including support for the common-sign assertion.

children.title: Pfaffian Orientations
children.top_down_role: Orientation structures supporting Pfaffian matching representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Pfaffian Orientations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-orientation criterion using conformal even cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(G
\) be a graph having a perfect matching. An even cycle \(C\) is conformal, or nice, when \(G-V(C)\) has a perfect matching. An orientation of \(G\) is Pfaffian if every conformal even cycle \(C\) is oddly oriented: when either direction is chosen for traversing \(C\), an odd number of its edges point in that traversal direction. Equivalently, in the Pfaffian expansion of the associated skew adjacency matrix, all perfect matchings have the same sign.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A Pfaffian orientation directs every conformal even cycle oddly, making all perfect-matching terms in the Pfaffian share one sign.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and has at least one perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The orientation is Pfaffian exactly when every conformal even cycle is oddly oriented.

notation.meaning: graph obtained by deleting all vertices of C

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conformal-cycle definition and common-sign equivalence are standard and definition is the correct content kind, but the record supplies no inspectable citation. An authoritative definition or theorem locator is required.

children.title: Orientation–Sign Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility between orientation choices and Pfaffian sign behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Orientation–Sign Compatibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle-parity characterization of compatibility among perfect-matching signs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix an orientation and vertex order for a graph \(G\), and let \(M,N\) be perfect matchings. Their symmetric difference is a vertex-disjoint union of even cycles alternating between \(M\) and \(N\). The Pfaffian signs satisfy \(s_K(M)=s_K(N)\) if and only if the number of these alternating cycles that are evenly oriented is even. In particular, if every conformal alternating cycle is oddly oriented, then \(s_K(M)=s_K(N)\) for every pair of perfect matchings, so the Pfaffian matching terms do not cancel.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The relative signs of two perfect matchings are controlled by the orientation parities of their alternating symmetric-difference cycles.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) has a fixed orientation and linear vertex order.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(s_K(M)/s_K(N)=(-1)^r\), where \(r\) is the number of evenly oriented cycles in \(M\mathbin{\triangle}N\).

notation.meaning: sign of M in the Pfaffian expansion
symmetric difference of M and N
number of evenly oriented alternating cycles

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The relative-sign parity statement is convention-sensitive and has no citation. A source must confirm that, under the stated orientation convention, each evenly oriented alternating cycle contributes exactly one sign reversal and yields the displayed ratio.

children.title: Non-Pfaffian Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Graph regimes where the Pfaffian orientation interface ceases to apply.

knowledge_statements.title: Non-Pfaffian Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The complete bipartite graph \(K_{3,3}\) as a basic obstruction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The graph \(K_{3,3}\) has no Pfaffian orientation. Indeed, for every orientation of \(K_{3,3}\), the signs of its perfect matchings in the associated Pfaffian expansion cannot all agree. Consequently, its perfect-matching generating polynomial cannot be obtained, up to one global sign, as the Pfaffian of a skew adjacency matrix formed solely by signing its edge variables. Thus the cancellation-free Pfaffian representation available for planar graphs and other Pfaffian classes does not extend to all graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The graph K3,3 is non-Pfaffian, showing that cancellation-free orientation-based Pfaffian representations do not exist for every graph.
assumptions_latex: The representation uses one skew-symmetric signed entry for each edge of \(K_{3,3}\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: No orientation of \(K_{3,3}\) makes all perfect-matching Pfaffian terms have the same sign.

notation.meaning: complete bipartite graph with three vertices in each part

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The K_{3,3} obstruction is appropriate failure-boundary content, but the non-Pfaffian assertion and its representation consequence have no cited theorem or page locator. Authoritative support is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Bidirected-Graph Matching Representations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Matching feasibility under a bidirected incidence-sign representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A bidirected graph is a triple \(B=(V,E,\sigma)\), where every incidence \((v,e)\) has a sign \(\sigma(v,e)\in\{-1,1\}\); the two ends of an edge may have equal or opposite signs. Its underlying graph \(U(B)=(V,E)\) forgets \(\sigma\). A set \(M\subseteq E\) is a matching of \(B\) when no two edges of \(M\) share an endpoint. Therefore
\[
\mathcal M(B)=\mathcal M(U(B)),
\]
and incidence signs can carry orientation or algebraic information without changing matching feasibility. Any stronger signed-matrix correspondence requires an explicitly chosen bidirected representation convention.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bidirected incidence signs enrich an ordinary graph representation but do not alter which edge sets are matchings.
assumptions_latex: Every edge has two endpoint incidences.
Matching feasibility is defined solely by endpoint disjointness.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal M(B)=\mathcal M(U(B))\).

notation.meaning: sign assigned to the incidence of v with e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record only observes that endpoint-disjointness is unchanged after incidence signs are forgotten. It does not provide a bidirected algebraic matching representation and explicitly declines the stronger correspondence implied by the path. The selected representation kind therefore does not fit the actual statement or adequately fill this terminal container.

knowledge_statements.title: Matching-Covered Graphs
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Standard connected-graph definition via admissibility of every edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite loopless graph \(G=(V,E)\), with \(|V|\ge2\), is matching-covered if \(G\) is connected and every edge \(e\in E\) belongs to at least one perfect matching of \(G\). Equivalently, \(G\) is connected and the union of all its perfect matchings is exactly \(E\). An edge lying in a perfect matching is called admissible, so a connected graph is matching-covered precisely when every edge is admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching-covered graph is connected, has at least two vertices, and every edge lies in some perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) is matching-covered if and only if it is connected and every \(e\in E\) is admissible.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The connected admissible-edge definition is standard, internally consistent, and correctly classified as a definition, but the record has no source. A specific authoritative definition or page locator is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Factor-Critical Ear Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lovász’s odd-ear characterization, with closed ears permitted at the initial nontrivial extension.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite graph. Then \(G\) is factor-critical if and only if it has a spanning subgraph obtained from a single vertex \(G_0\) through a sequence \(G_0\subseteq G_1\subseteq\cdots\subseteq G_k\), where \(G_i\) is obtained from \(G_{i-1}\) by adjoining an odd-length ear whose internal vertices lie outside \(V(G_{i-1})\) and whose endpoints lie in \(V(G_{i-1})\). A closed ear, with coincident endpoints, is allowed when needed. Factor-critical means that \(G-v\) has a perfect matching for every \(v\in V(G)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph is factor-critical exactly when it can be built from one vertex by successively adjoining odd ears with new internal vertices.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is factor-critical}\iff G\text{ admits a spanning odd-ear decomposition from }K_1.\)

notation.meaning: The graph obtained by deleting vertex v and its incident edges.
The intermediate graph after i ear extensions.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Associated Maps for an M-Alternating Ear-Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines the matching-partner map and the nonmatching-ear neighbor map associated with a fixed alternating ear-decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be factor-critical, let \(M\) be a near-perfect matching in \(G\), and let \(r,P_1,\ldots,P_k\) be an \(M\)-alternating ear-decomposition. Functions \(\mu,\varphi:V(G)\to V(G)\) are associated with the decomposition if \(\mu(x)=y\) whenever \(\{x,y\}\in M\); \(\varphi(x)=y\) whenever \(\{x,y\}\in E(P_i)\setminus M\) and \(x\notin\{r\}\cup\bigcup_{j<i}V(P_j)\); and \(\mu(r)=\varphi(r)=r\). If \(M\) is fixed, \(\varphi\) alone is also called associated with the decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The associated map μ sends each matched vertex to its matching partner. For a vertex first introduced by an ear, φ sends it along the specified nonmatching edge of that ear. Both maps fix the initial vertex r; when M is fixed, φ alone may be called associated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(x)=y\text{ whenever }\{x,y\}\in M;\quad \varphi(x)=y\text{ whenever }\{x,y\}\in E(P_i)\setminus M\text{ and }x\notin\{r\}\cup\bigcup_{j<i}V(P_j);\quad \mu(r)=\varphi(r)=r.\)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Reconstruction of an M-Alternating Ear-Decomposition from Associated Maps
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reconstructs an M-alternating ear-decomposition from its associated matching-partner and ear-neighbor maps.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a factor-critical graph \(G\), a near-perfect matching \(M\), and maps \(\mu,\varphi\) associated with an \(M\)-alternating ear-decomposition, choose the vertex \(r\) with \(\mu(r)=r\), initialize \(X=\{r\}\), and use a stack to construct ears by following the prescribed \(\varphi\)- and \(\mu\)-links from vertices outside \(X\). Whenever both endpoints of the topmost constructed ear lie in \(X\), output it and add its vertices to \(X\). Once \(X=V(G)\), append every unused edge as a one-edge ear. The output is an \(M\)-alternating ear-decomposition \(r,P_1,\ldots,P_k\) of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The algorithm starts at the unmatched vertex fixed by μ, follows the associated φ and μ links to build ears, and holds them on a stack until both endpoints have been reached. It then appends unused edges as one-edge ears and outputs an M-alternating ear-decomposition.

children.title: Extendable-Graph Ear Decompositions
children.top_down_role: Ear structures associated with extendable graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Extendable-Graph Ear Decompositions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The one-or-two-ear form of the matching-covered ear-decomposition theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite matching-covered graph, meaning that \(G\) is connected, has at least two vertices, and every edge belongs to a perfect matching. Then there is a sequence \(K_2=G_0,G_1,\ldots,G_k=G\) of matching-covered graphs such that each \(G_i\) is obtained from \(G_{i-1}\) by adjoining either one odd ear or two vertex-disjoint odd ears, with all internal vertices new, and possibly adding edges having both ends already present. Thus no extension step requires more than two ears.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every finite matching-covered graph can be built from one edge through matching-covered extensions using at most two odd ears per step.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\) admits a matching-covered ear decomposition from \(K_2\) using at most two odd ears at each extension.

notation.meaning: The matching-covered graph after i extensions.
The two-vertex graph consisting of one edge.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The one-or-two-ear theorem is plausible and fits the container, but no citation is supplied. An authoritative theorem locator is required to confirm the precise matching-covered, edge-addition, and double-ear conventions.

children.title: Ear-Extension Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relations between ear additions and preservation of matching extendability.

assumptions_latex: \(P\) is an odd ear relative to \(H\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\cup P\) is factor-critical.

notation.meaning: An odd path ear or odd closed ear relative to H.
The graph formed by adjoining the ear P to H.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Correspondence between odd-ear extension and preservation of factor-criticality.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be a finite factor-critical graph. Let \(P\) be either an odd-length path with distinct endpoints in \(V(H)\) and all internal vertices outside \(V(H)\), or an odd-length cycle meeting \(H\) in exactly one vertex. Then \(H\cup P\) is factor-critical. Consequently, every intermediate graph obtained by successively adjoining such odd ears to \(K_1\) is factor-critical.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Adjoining an odd path ear, or an odd closed ear meeting the old graph at one vertex, preserves factor-criticality; hence every stage of such an ear decomposition is factor-critical.

children.title: Canonical Partitions
children.top_down_role: Canonical partition structures arising in graphs governed by perfect matchings.

knowledge_statements.title: Canonical Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Kotzig–Lovász canonical partition of an elementary factorizable graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite elementary graph with a perfect matching. For \(u,v\in V(G)\), define \(u\sim_G v\) when either \(u=v\), or \(u\ne v\) and \(G-u-v\) has no perfect matching. The relation \(\sim_G\) is an equivalence relation. Its equivalence classes form the canonical partition \(\mathcal P(G)=V(G)/{\sim_G}\), which is independent of the choice of a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Two vertices share a canonical class when they coincide or deleting both destroys all perfect matchings; these classes partition an elementary graph canonically.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite elementary graph having a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\sim_G\) is an equivalence relation and \(\mathcal P(G)=V(G)/{\sim_G}\).

notation.meaning: The canonical vertex equivalence relation of G.
The set of equivalence classes under the canonical relation.
G with u and v and their incident edges deleted.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The canonical relation and partition are standard and fit the definition container, but no source is cited. A precise locator is needed to confirm the adopted meaning of elementary graph and the domain on which the relation is asserted to be transitive.

children.title: Saturated Graph Structure
children.top_down_role: Structural organization specific to saturated graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Saturated Graph Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Saturation with respect to the existence of new perfect matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A finite factorizable graph \(G\) is saturated if, for every nonedge \(e=uv\) with distinct \(u,v\in V(G)\), the augmented graph \(G+e\) has a perfect matching containing \(e\). Equivalently, \(G-u-v\) has a perfect matching for every pair of nonadjacent vertices \(u,v\). Thus adding any missing edge strictly enlarges the set of perfect matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A factorizable graph is saturated when every added missing edge lies in a newly created perfect matching.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is finite and has a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is saturated}\iff \forall uv\notin E(G),\;G-u-v\text{ has a perfect matching}.\)

notation.meaning: The graph obtained by adding the nonedge e.
The graph obtained by deleting u and v.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition and its matching-deletion equivalence are coherent, but the specialized use of saturated requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Cathedral Structure
children.top_down_role: Cathedral-style organization of matching-covered structures.

knowledge_statements.title: Cathedral Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive cathedral representation of saturated graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every finite saturated graph \(G\) has a recursive cathedral representation. Its foundation \(F\) is a saturated elementary graph with canonical partition \(\mathcal P(F)\). For each class \(S\in\mathcal P(F)\), choose a possibly empty saturated graph \(T_S\), called a tower, take all these graphs vertex-disjoint, and join every vertex of \(S\) to every vertex of \(T_S\). The resulting graph is saturated; conversely, every saturated graph is obtainable by this construction, recursively decomposing each nonempty tower.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every saturated graph consists recursively of a saturated elementary foundation with saturated towers completely joined to designated canonical classes.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G=F\cup\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal P(F)}T_S\cup\bigcup_{S\in\mathcal P(F)}E(S,T_S)\), where each \(E(S,T_S)\) is complete.

notation.meaning: The elementary foundation of the cathedral representation.
The canonical partition of the foundation.
The saturated tower assigned to canonical class S.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation has the correct mathematical role for the cathedral-structure leaf, but no source supports the converse construction, recursive tower conditions, or attachment convention.

children.title: Partition–Cathedral Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Connections linking canonical parts to cathedral components.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition–Cathedral Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Canonical classes are exactly the attachment sites in the cathedral representation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be saturated and let \(F\) be the foundation in its cathedral representation. The admissible attachment sites for towers are precisely the classes \(S\in\mathcal P(F)\) of the canonical partition: each nonempty tower \(T_S\) is complete to \(S\), has no edge to \(V(F)\setminus S\), and is assigned to a unique class. Consequently, the foundation’s canonical partition determines the tower incidences, while the cathedral representation realizes every such incidence classwise.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The canonical classes of a cathedral foundation are exactly its tower attachment sites, and each tower attaches completely to one unique class.
assumptions_latex: \(F\) is the foundation of a cathedral representation of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N_G(V(T_S))\cap V(F)=S\) for every nonempty tower \(T_S\).

notation.meaning: The canonical partition of the foundation.
The tower assigned to class S.
The vertices outside X adjacent to at least one vertex of X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The classwise attachment statement fits the correspondence container, but its uniqueness and exact neighborhood assertion depend on the cathedral theorem and have no cited locator.

children.title: Tight-Cut Decomposition
children.top_down_role: Decomposition of matching-covered graphs along tight cuts.

knowledge_statements.title: Tight-Cut Decomposition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Recursive decomposition of matching-covered graphs by nontrivial tight cuts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a finite matching-covered graph \(G\). A cut \(\delta(X)\) is tight if every perfect matching \(M\) satisfies \(|M\cap\delta(X)|=1\); it is nontrivial when \(|X|,|V(G)\setminus X|>1\). While a current component has a nontrivial tight cut, replace it by the two graphs obtained by contracting respectively \(X\) and \(V(G)\setminus X\) to single vertices, deleting resulting loops but retaining parallel edges. Stop when no component has a nontrivial tight cut, and output the terminal matching-covered components.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly contract both shores of a nontrivial tight cut in a matching-covered graph until every resulting component is tight-cut indecomposable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output consists of matching-covered graphs having no nontrivial tight cut.

notation.meaning: The edges with exactly one endpoint in X.
A perfect matching of the current graph.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm correctly describes recursive tight-cut contraction and its kind fits the decomposition container. A source is required to support preservation of matching-coveredness and the loop and parallel-edge conventions.

children.title: Brick Components
children.top_down_role: Nonbipartite components arising from tight-cut decomposition.

knowledge_statements.title: Brick Components
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonbipartite terminal components of tight-cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A brick is a finite nonbipartite matching-covered graph having no nontrivial tight cut. Equivalently, in the standard structural characterization for matching-covered graphs, a brick is a nonbipartite graph that is \(3\)-vertex-connected and bicritical, where bicritical means that \(G-u-v\) has a perfect matching for every two distinct vertices \(u,v\). Brick components are the nonbipartite terminal graphs produced by tight-cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A brick is a nonbipartite matching-covered graph with no nontrivial tight cut; equivalently, it is 3-connected and bicritical.
assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite nonbipartite matching-covered graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is a brick}\iff G\text{ has no nontrivial tight cut}.\)

notation.meaning: G after deletion of distinct vertices u and v.
The edge cut determined by X.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The terminal-component definition is appropriate, but the asserted equivalence with 3-vertex-connectivity and bicriticality is a nontrivial structural theorem requiring a specific authoritative locator.

children.title: Brace Components
children.top_down_role: Bipartite components arising from tight-cut decomposition.

assumptions_latex: \(G\) is a finite bipartite matching-covered graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ is a brace}\iff G\text{ has no nontrivial tight cut}.\)

notation.meaning: The set of edges having exactly one endpoint in X.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Bipartite terminal components of tight-cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite bipartite matching-covered graph with bipartition \((A,B)\). A cut \(\delta(X)\) is nontrivial when \(|X|>1\) and \(|V(G)\setminus X|>1\), and it is tight when every perfect matching \(M\) of \(G\) satisfies \(|M\cap\delta(X)|=1\). The graph \(G\) is a brace if it has no nontrivial tight cut. Brace components are the bipartite terminal graphs produced by tight-cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A brace is a finite bipartite matching-covered graph with no nontrivial tight cut, and braces are the bipartite terminal components of tight-cut decomposition.
knowledge_statements.title: Brace Components

children.title: Decomposition Uniqueness
children.top_down_role: Canonical aspects of the resulting brick–brace component structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Decomposition Uniqueness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniqueness of tight-cut decomposition up to terminal-component isomorphism.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a finite matching-covered graph. Perform tight-cut decomposition by choosing nontrivial tight cuts in any order until no further such cut remains. The resulting terminal components are bricks and braces, and their multiset of isomorphism classes, counting multiplicities, is independent of every choice of tight cuts and contraction order. In particular, the number of brick components and the number of brace components are invariants of \(G\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Although tight cuts may be selected in different orders, every complete decomposition yields the same multiset of brick and brace components up to isomorphism.
assumptions_latex: Every decomposition continues until no nontrivial tight cut remains.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The multiset of terminal brick and brace isomorphism classes is uniquely determined by \(G\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem has the correct role and states the standard uniqueness target, but the invariance of the terminal multiset is nontrivial and no source or theorem locator is supplied.

children.title: Perfect-Matching Nonexistence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structural regimes in which perfect matchings do not exist.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(G\text{ has no perfect matching}\iff\exists S\subseteq V:\ q(G-S)>|S|.\)

notation.meaning: The graph obtained by deleting all vertices in S and their incident edges.
The number of odd-order connected components of G-S.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte-set certificates for nonexistence of a perfect matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite graph, and for each \(S\subseteq V\), let \(q(G-S)\) be the number of odd-order connected components of \(G-S\). Then \(G\) has no perfect matching if and only if there exists \(S\subseteq V\) such that \(q(G-S)>|S|\). Any such set \(S\) is a certificate of perfect-matching nonexistence.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A finite graph has no perfect matching exactly when deleting some vertex set leaves more odd-order components than the set has vertices; that set is a nonexistence certificate.
knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Matching Nonexistence Regimes

children.title: Perfect-Matching Barrier Certificates
children.top_down_role: Barrier-based certificates for absence of perfect matchings.

knowledge_statements.title: Perfect-Matching Barrier Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tutte-set certificate for finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph and let \(S\subseteq V\). Write \(q(G-S)\) for the number of connected components of \(G-S\) having odd order. If \[q(G-S)>|S|,\] then \(S\) certifies that \(G\) has no perfect matching. Indeed, a proposed certificate is verified by deleting \(S\), computing the connected components, and checking their orders and the displayed inequality; all these operations are polynomial in \(|V|+|E|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A vertex set whose deletion leaves more odd components than its size is a polynomially verifiable certificate that no perfect matching exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(q(G-S)>|S|\Longrightarrow G\text{ has no perfect matching}.\)

notation.meaning: number of odd-order components of the vertex-deleted graph

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: standard certificate direction of Tutte's perfect-matching theorem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate statement is mathematically standard, precise, and appropriately classified, but no inspectable citation supports either the Tutte obstruction or the polynomial-verification claim.

children.title: Deficiency–Barrier Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between matching deficiency and barrier structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Deficiency–Barrier Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Berge–Tutte deficiency formula for finite undirected graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\), let \(\nu(G)\) be its maximum matching cardinality and define its matching deficiency by \(\operatorname{def}(G)=|V|-2\nu(G)\). Then \[\operatorname{def}(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}\bigl(q(G-S)-|S|\bigr).\] Thus a set \(S\) attaining the maximum is a barrier, and \(G\) has a perfect matching exactly when every \(S\subseteq V\) satisfies \(q(G-S)\le |S|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum matching deficiency equals the largest excess of odd components over deleted vertices; maximizing sets are barriers, and zero deficiency characterizes perfect matchability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \( |V|-2\nu(G)=\max_{S\subseteq V}(q(G-S)-|S|).\)

notation.meaning: maximum cardinality of a matching in G
minimum number of vertices left unmatched by a maximum matching
number of odd-order components of G minus S

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The deficiency formula and perfect-matching equivalence are correctly formulated for finite undirected graphs, but the nontrivial theorem has no inspectable citation.

children.title: Failure of Naive Augmentation around Blossoms

knowledge_statements.title: Failure of Naive Augmentation around Blossoms
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Concrete obstruction to alternating-tree search without blossom contraction.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let the graph contain a stem \(r a,a v_0\), the cycle \(v_0v_1v_2v_3v_4v_0\), and edges \(v_3t\), with matching \(M=\{av_0,v_1v_2,v_3v_4\}\). The vertices \(r,t\) are exposed, and \[r,a,v_0,v_4,v_3,t\] is an \(M\)-augmenting path. During alternating-tree search, the odd cycle is exposed by an edge joining two even-level vertices. A naive procedure that simply rejects such edges can miss the augmenting path; contracting the odd cycle to its base preserves and reveals augmentability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An odd alternating cycle can hide an augmenting path from tree search that discards same-parity edges; blossom contraction removes this obstruction.
assumptions_latex: Edges not explicitly listed are irrelevant to the exhibited subgraph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is not maximum, although naive alternating-tree search may fail without blossom contraction.

notation.meaning: odd blossom cycle with base v_0

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: canonical obstruction handled by Edmonds blossom contraction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed path is indeed augmenting for the listed matching, but the assertion that a naive search misses it depends on an insufficiently specified search rule. A source supporting this exact example and failure mechanism is required.

knowledge_statements.title: Hypergraph Matching Tractability Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uniformity boundary between graph matching and three-dimensional matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For \(k=2\), maximum-cardinality matching in a \(k\)-uniform hypergraph is ordinary graph matching and is solvable in polynomial time. For \(k=3\), the decision problem asking whether a 3-uniform hypergraph has a matching of size at least \(K\) is NP-complete, even when the vertices are partitioned into three classes and every hyperedge contains one vertex from each class. Hence increasing edge size from two to three crosses a polynomial-time versus NP-complete boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Graph matching is polynomial-time solvable, whereas matching in 3-uniform tripartite hypergraphs is NP-complete through three-dimensional matching.
assumptions_latex: The hypergraph is represented explicitly by its vertex and hyperedge lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(k=2\) admits polynomial-time optimization, while the threshold problem for \(k=3\) is NP-complete.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical graph-matching and three-dimensional-matching complexity boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The graph-versus-3-dimensional-matching boundary is standard and the complexity-bound kind fits, but the polynomial-time and NP-completeness claims require specific authoritative locators.

children.title: Matroid Matching Boundary
children.top_down_role: Tractability limits associated with matroid matching formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Matching Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Representation boundary for vertex-independent matroid matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a graph \(G=(V,E)\) and a matroid \(\mathcal M\) on \(V\), matroid matching asks for a matching \(F\subseteq E\) maximizing \(|F|\) subject to the covered set \(V(F)\) being independent in \(\mathcal M\). If \(G\) is a disjoint union of prescribed pairs, this specializes to matroid parity. Consequently, exponential independence-oracle lower bounds for matroid parity transfer to this model, while explicitly represented linear instances admit algebraic polynomial-time regimes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid matching contains matroid parity, so oracle hardness transfers; explicit linear representations permit algebraic algorithms unavailable from independence queries alone.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Matroid parity is a special case of matroid matching, so its independence-oracle lower bounds apply to matroid matching.

notation.meaning: vertices incident with edges of F

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: reduction from matroid parity by taking a graph of prescribed disjoint pairs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The disjoint-pair specialization is plausible under the stated vertex-matroid model, but matroid-matching terminology and the scope of polynomial-time linear-representation algorithms vary. Exact model and algorithm citations are needed.

children.title: Matroid Parity Boundary
children.top_down_role: Tractability limits associated with matroid parity formulations.

knowledge_statements.title: Matroid Parity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Independence-oracle versus linear-representation boundary for matroid parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let a matroid \(\mathcal M\) have ground set partitioned into pairs \(P_1,\ldots,P_m\). Matroid parity maximizes \(|I|\) over index sets \(I\subseteq\{1,
ldots,m\}\) satisfying \(\bigcup_{i\in I}P_i\in\mathcal I(\mathcal M)\). In the independence-oracle model, no polynomial-query algorithm solves all instances: some families require exponentially many oracle queries. When \(\mathcal M\) is supplied by an explicit linear representation over a field, randomized algebraic polynomial-time algorithms are available in the field-operation model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Matroid parity is exponentially hard in the independence-oracle model but admits randomized polynomial algebraic algorithms from an explicit linear representation.
assumptions_latex: Oracle complexity counts independence queries; linear complexity counts field operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Oracle access alone has an exponential worst-case query barrier, whereas explicit linear representation yields a randomized polynomial-time regime.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: established oracle-versus-linear distinction for matroid parity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The oracle-versus-linear boundary needs exact lower-bound and algorithm locators, including deterministic or randomized qualifications and field assumptions. The index-set formula also contains a malformed ellipsis near the lower endpoint.

children.title: Linear-Representation Regimes
children.top_down_role: Complexity regimes governed by explicit linear matroid representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Linear-Representation Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Randomized algebraic regime for linearly represented matroid parity.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a matrix \(A\) over a field \(\mathbb F\), whose columns represent a matroid, together with a partition of the columns into pairs. Introduce independent random field values into the standard skew-symmetric parity matrix derived from \(A\) and the pairs, compute its generic rank by Gaussian elimination, and recover the maximum feasible number of pairs from that rank; self-reduction may recover an optimal pair set. Over a sufficiently large sampling field, polynomially many field operations give one-sided polynomially bounded error.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A linear representation converts matroid parity into randomized rank computations, yielding polynomial field-operation complexity and optional recovery by self-reduction.
assumptions_latex: \(A\) explicitly represents the input matroid over \(\mathbb F\).
The sampling field is sufficiently large, or a suitable extension field is used.
Complexity is measured in field operations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximum linear matroid parity is computable by a randomized polynomial number of field operations with one-sided bounded error.
review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical Lovász-style algebraic treatment of linear matroid parity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The claimed randomized algebraic regime is plausible, but the parity matrix, rank-to-optimum relation, field restrictions, recovery procedure, and meaning of the error guarantee are too underspecified to validate without a precise source.

children.title: Oracle-Model Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity boundaries arising under oracle access to matroid structure.

knowledge_statements.title: Oracle-Model Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Query lower bound for parity and matching under independence-oracle access.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In the independence-oracle model, an algorithm learns a matroid only through queries asking whether a supplied subset is independent. There exists a family of matroid parity instances on ground sets of size \(n\) for which every algorithm guaranteed to return an optimum requires \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) independence queries in the worst case. Since matroid parity embeds into matroid matching by using the prescribed pairs as the graph edges, the same absence of a polynomial-query algorithm applies to general matroid matching in this oracle model.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Exact matroid parity needs exponentially many independence queries in the worst case, and the reduction by disjoint pair edges transfers this barrier to matroid matching.
assumptions_latex: Only independence-oracle access to the matroid is available.
The algorithm must return an exact optimum on every instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The worst-case exact query complexity is \(2^{\Omega(n)}\) for matroid parity and, by reduction, for matroid matching.

notation.meaning: an exponential asymptotic query lower bound

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: known oracle lower-bound phenomenon for matroid parity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: A precise source is required to verify the stated 2^{Omega(n)} bound, the applicable deterministic or randomized oracle model, and the transfer to the particular matroid-matching model.

knowledge_statements.title: Optimization–Counting Complexity Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Maximum matching versus exact perfect-matching counting.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given an explicitly represented finite graph, a maximum-cardinality matching can be found in polynomial time. In contrast, exactly counting perfect matchings is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete, already for bipartite graphs: if \(A\) is the bipartite adjacency matrix, then the number of perfect matchings equals \[\operatorname{perm}(A)=\sum_{\pi\in S_n}\prod_{i=1}^n A_{i,\pi(i)}.\] Thus polynomial-time optimization does not imply polynomial-time exact counting for the same matching family.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Maximum matching is polynomial-time solvable, but exact perfect-matching counting is #P-complete even in bipartite graphs, where it equals a zero-one permanent.
assumptions_latex: Graphs and matrices are represented explicitly.
Counting requires the exact integer answer.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Maximum matching belongs to polynomial time, whereas exact bipartite perfect-matching counting is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete.

notation.meaning: permanent of the bipartite adjacency matrix

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: classical matching algorithms and Valiant permanent complexity theorem

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The optimization–counting contrast and permanent identity are standard and correctly scoped, but both the polynomial-time optimization claim and #P-completeness claim lack inspectable citations.

children.title: Degree-Constrained Factor Theory
children.top_down_role: Matching generalizations governed by vertex-degree requirements, including b-matchings, factors, parity factors, degree-set models, and companion edge-cover systems.

children.title: Bipartite b-Matchings
children.top_down_role: b-matching structures restricted to bipartite graphs.

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated vertex-capacitated matching in a bipartite graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(L\mathbin{\dot\cup}R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph and let \(b:V(G)\to\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\). A bipartite \(b\)-matching is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) satisfying \[|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\qquad(v\in V(G)).\] Equivalently, its incidence vector lies in \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b(v)\text{ for every }v\}\). The equality variant \(|F\cap\delta(v)|=b(v)\) for every vertex is a bipartite \(b\)-factor.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A bipartite b-matching selects edges so that each vertex is incident with at most its prescribed integer capacity; equality at every vertex defines a b-factor.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\subseteq E\) is a \(b\)-matching exactly when \(|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\) for all \(v\).

source_refs.locator: 2.4 Bipartite matchings p. 65

source_witnesses.locator: 2.4 Bipartite matchings p. 65

children.title: General-Graph b-Matchings
children.top_down_role: b-matching structures in graphs without a bipartiteness restriction.

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated vertex-capacitated matching in an arbitrary graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite undirected graph, not necessarily bipartite, and let \(b:V\to\mathbb Z_{\ge0}\). A general-graph \(b\)-matching is an edge set \(F\subseteq E\) such that \[|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\qquad(v\in V).\] Its incidence vector belongs to \(\{x\in\{0,1\}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b(v)\text{ for all }v\}\). When \(b(v)=1\) for every \(v\), this definition reduces to an ordinary matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A general-graph b-matching is an edge set respecting an integer incidence capacity at every vertex; ordinary matching is the all-ones special case.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(F\) is a \(b\)-matching exactly when \(|F\cap\delta(v)|\le b(v)\) for every \(v\in V\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The scoped edge-set definition is mathematically standard and the definition kind fits, but no inspectable source is supplied for the general-graph convention.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Necessary and sufficient component-parity condition for a perfect b-matching in an unrestricted graph with integral edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be a graph, \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\), and \(b:V(G)\to\mathbb N\). Then \((G,u)\) has a perfect \(b\)-matching if and only if, for every pair of disjoint sets \(X,Y\subseteq V(G)\), the number of connected components \(C\) of \(G-X-Y\) for which \[\sum_{c\in V(C)}b(c)+\sum_{e\in E_G(V(C),Y)}u(e)\] is odd is at most \[\sum_{v\in X}b(v)+\sum_{y\in Y}\left(\sum_{e\in\delta(y)}u(e)-b(y)\right)-\sum_{e\in E_G(X,Y)}u(e).\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated graph has a perfect b-matching exactly when, for every pair of disjoint vertex sets X and Y, the number of residual components having the specified odd parity is bounded by the stated combination of the b-values and capacities incident with X and Y.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: (G,u)\text{ has a perfect }b\text{-matching}\iff \forall X\cap Y=\varnothing,\quad q_b^u(G-X-Y;Y)\le b(X)+\sum_{y\in Y}\bigl(u(\delta(y))-b(y)\bigr)-u(E_G(X,Y))

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Defines capacitated b-matchings in arbitrary undirected graphs and identifies their simple, perfect, matching, factor, and degree-two specializations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G\) be an undirected graph, \(u:E(G)\to\mathbb N\cup\{\infty\}\), and \(b:V(G)\to\mathbb N\). A \(b\)-matching in \((G,u)\) is a function \(f:E(G)\to\mathbb Z_+\) satisfying \(f(e)\le u(e)\) for every \(e\in E(G)\) and \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}f(e)\le b(v)\) for every \(v\in V(G)\). It is simple if \(u\equiv1\), and perfect if \(\sum_{e\in\delta(v)}f(e)=b(v)\) for every vertex. When \(b\equiv1\), this is ordinary matching; a simple perfect \(b\)-matching is also called a \(b\)-factor. A perfect simple \(2\)-matching is an edge set incident with every vertex exactly twice.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-matching assigns nonnegative integer multiplicities to edges, subject to edge capacities and vertex degree bounds. Unit capacities give simple b-matchings, equality at every vertex gives perfect b-matchings, b=1 gives ordinary matchings, and simple perfect b-matchings are b-factors.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: f\text{ is a }b\text{-matching in }(G,u)\iff f:E(G)\to\mathbb Z_+,\ f(e)\le u(e)\ \forall e,\ \sum_{e\in\delta(v)}f(e)\le b(v)\ \forall v

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite-to-General Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Loss of degree-relaxation integrality outside bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For bipartite \(G\), every extreme point of \[P_b(G)=\{x\in[0,1]^E:x(\delta(v))\le b(v)\text{ for all }v\}\] is integral when \(b\) is integral. This fails for general graphs: on a triangle with \(b(v)=1\) at every vertex, the vector \(x_e=\tfrac12\) for all three edges is an extreme feasible point. It is excluded by the blossom inequality \(x(E(V))\le1\), illustrating why general-graph formulations require odd-set inequalities beyond degree constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Bipartite degree relaxations are integral, but a half-valued triangle is fractional in general graphs; odd-set inequalities repair the missing structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Bipartiteness ensures integrality of \(P_b(G)\); without it, degree constraints alone need not describe the \(b\)-matching polytope.

knowledge_statements.title: Simple b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Edge-simple, degree-upper-bounded b-matchings in a finite loopless graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless graph and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\). A simple \(b\)-matching is a set \(M\subseteq E\) satisfying \[|M\cap\delta(v)|\le b_v\qquad(v\in V).\] Equivalently, its incidence vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{E}\) satisfies \(x(\delta(v))\le b_v\) for every \(v\in V\). Thus each edge may be selected at most once, while a vertex may be incident with as many as \(b_v\) selected edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A simple b-matching selects each edge at most once and selects at most b_v edges incident with every vertex v.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\subseteq E\) is feasible exactly when \(|M\cap\delta(v)|\le b_v\) for all \(v\in V\).

knowledge_statements.title: Capacitated b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Integer edge-multiplicity model with vertex and edge capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a finite loopless graph, \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\), and \(u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\). A capacitated \(b\)-matching is a vector \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\) such that \[x(\delta(v))\le b_v\quad(v\in V),\qquad x_e\le u_e\quad(e\in E).\] The integer \(x_e\) is the multiplicity with which edge \(e\) is used. The model permits repeated use precisely when \(u_e>1\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A capacitated b-matching assigns each edge an integer multiplicity bounded by its edge capacity while respecting every vertex capacity.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x\) is feasible exactly when \(x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}\), \(x(\delta(v))\le b_v\), and \(x_e\le u_e\).

children.title: Capacity-Model Transition

knowledge_statements.title: Capacity-Model Transition
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Equivalence through unit capacities and parallel-edge expansion.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite loopless graph \(G=(V,E)\), the simple \(b\)-matchings are exactly the capacitated \(b\)-matchings with \(u_e=1\) for every \(e\in E\). More generally, replace each edge \(e\) by \(u_e\) parallel labeled copies of the same weight. Projection by \[x_e=\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}y_{e,i}\] maps simple \(b\)-matchings of the expanded multigraph onto capacitated \(b\)-matchings of \(G\), preserves all vertex degrees, and preserves linear objective values when every copy inherits the weight of \(e\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unit edge capacities recover simple b-matchings; replacing an edge by capacity-many parallel copies converts the capacitated model into a simple multigraph model.
assumptions_latex: Parallel labeled edges are allowed in the expanded graph.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x_e=\sum_{i=1}^{u_e}y_{e,i}\) gives a degree- and weight-preserving surjection between the two feasible families.

notation.meaning: indicator of the i-th parallel copy of e
projected multiplicity of original edge e

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The unit-capacity specialization and parallel-copy projection are mathematically plausible and fit the representation leaf, but no citation supports the stated surjection and preservation claims.

knowledge_statements.title: Weighted b-Matchings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Linear optimization over a specified b-matching feasibility regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) carry weights \(w\in\mathbb R^{E}\), and let \(\mathcal B\subseteq\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{E}\) be the feasible family of simple or capacitated \(b\)-matchings under the chosen convention. A maximum-weight \(b\)-matching is any \(x^\star\in\mathcal B\) satisfying \[w^\top x^\star=\max\{w^\top x:x\in\mathcal B\}.\] For the minimum-weight version, replace the maximum by a minimum. Negative weights are permitted unless an additional cardinality or degree-equality requirement changes whether unused edges are admissible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A weighted b-matching optimizes the sum of selected edge weights over the chosen simple or capacitated b-matching family.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(x^\star\in\operatorname*{argmax}_{x\in\mathcal B} w^\top x\).

notation.meaning: total weight counted with edge multiplicities

knowledge_statements.title: Bipartite b-Matching Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated integer-multiplicity b-matching polytope for bipartite graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(L\cup R,E)\) be a finite bipartite graph, let \(V=L\cup R\), and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\). The convex hull of its integer-multiplicity \(b\)-matchings is \[P_b(G)=\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b_v\ \text{for every }v\in V\}.\] In particular, the vertex-edge incidence matrix of a bipartite graph is totally unimodular, so every vertex of this polyhedron is integral for integral \(b\); no odd-set inequalities are required.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For bipartite graphs, nonnegativity and vertex-degree bounds completely describe the integer b-matching polytope.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(L\cup R,E)\) is finite and bipartite, with \(V=L\cup R\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(P_b(G)=\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b_v\text{ for all }v\in V\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: General-Graph b-Matching Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uncapacitated integer-multiplicity formulation with odd-set inequalities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be finite and loopless and let \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{V}\). The convex hull of integer-multiplicity \(b\)-matchings is \[P_b(G)=\left\{x\in\mathbb R_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b_v\ (v\in V),\quad x(E[U])\le\left\lfloor\frac{b(U)}{2}\right\rfloor\ (U\subseteq V,\ b(U)\text{ odd})\right\}.\] The odd-set inequalities supplement the degree system because every edge internal to \(U\) uses two units of the total vertex capacity \(b(U)\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In general graphs, degree bounds and nonnegativity require additional odd-set inequalities to describe the integer-multiplicity b-matching polytope.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed system equals \(\operatorname{conv}\{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}^{E}:x(\delta(v))\le b_v\text{ for all }v\in V\}\).

knowledge_statements.title: Total Dual Integrality for b-Matching Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: TDI criterion for a chosen rational b-matching inequality system.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A rational inequality system \(Ax\le d\) describing a \(b\)-matching polyhedron is totally dual integral if, for every integral objective vector \(c\in\mathbb Z^{E}\) for which the primal optimum is finite, the dual program \[\min\{d^\top y:A^\top y=c,\ y\ge0\}\] has an integral optimal solution \(y\). When additionally \(d\) is integral, total dual integrality implies that the polyhedron \(\{x:Ax\le d\}\) is integral. TDI is a property of the displayed system, not merely of the polyhedron it represents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A b-matching inequality system is TDI when every finite dual with an integral objective admits an integral optimal multiplier vector.
assumptions_latex: \(c\in\mathbb Z^{E}\) and the corresponding primal optimum is finite.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Ax\le d\) is TDI exactly when the displayed dual has an integral optimum for every such \(c\).
