knowledge_statements.scope_note: Uses the integral circulation-lattice interpretation of circuit sums.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite directed graph \(D=(V,A)\), every integral circulation \(z\in\ker(B)\cap\mathbb Z^A\) belongs to the integer lattice generated by signed simple-circuit vectors. Thus there are simple circuits \(C_1,\ldots,C_k\) and integers \(m_1,\ldots,m_k\) such that \[z=\sum_{i=1}^k m_i\chi^{C_i}.\] Consequently, the difference of two integral flows having the same boundary admits such an integer circuit-sum representation.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\alpha\chi^C\) is a real circulation but is not an integer sum of integral circuit vectors.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: a single-cycle graph gives an explicit lattice obstruction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates integral circuit lattices from their rational and real spans.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(D\) consist of one directed cycle \(C\). Its real circulation space is \(\{\alpha\chi^C:\alpha\in\mathbb R\}\), whereas its integer circuit lattice is \(\{m\chi^C:m\in\mathbb Z\}\). Hence, for every \(\alpha\in(0,1)\), the circulation \(\alpha\chi^C\) has a real circuit-sum representation but no representation with integer coefficients. Integrality of the represented circulation is therefore essential for an integer circuit-sum conclusion.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: On a single cycle, a fractional multiple of the cycle vector is a circulation but cannot be an integer circuit sum.

Replace each \(st\in M\) by a shortest \(s\)-\(t\) path in \(G\), retaining edge multiplicities. The resulting multiset has odd degree exactly at \(T\), and its cost equals \(\sum_{st\in M}d(s,t)\); this value is the minimum \(T\)-join cost.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Construct a Gomory-Hu cut tree for capacities \(x\). knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Define \[Q_T=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:x(\delta(S))\geq1\text{ for every }S\subseteq V\text{ with }|S\cap T|\text{ odd}\}.\] A direct polyhedral method minimizes \(c^\top x\) over \(Q_T\). Hence the linear-programming optimum equals the minimum combinatorial \(T\)-join cost.

assumptions_latex: \(G=(V,E)\) is a finite undirected graph, \(T\subseteq V\) has even cardinality, and \(c\in\mathbb Q_+^E\).
The T-join dominant \(Q_T\) is integral, and every restricted linear program and T-cut separation problem is solved exactly.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: When no violated \(T\)-cut remains, \(x^*\) is an optimal solution of the linear program over \(Q_T\); integrality of \(Q_T\) guarantees the existence of an optimal minimum-cost \(T\)-join incidence vector with the same objective value.

notation.meaning: T-join dominant defined by nonnegativity and T-cut inequalities.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \[Q_T=\{x\in\mathbb R_+^E:x(\delta(S))\geq1\text{ for every }S\subseteq V\text{ with }|S\cap T|\text{ odd}\}.\] Initialize a finite family \(\mathcal F\) of \(T\)-cut shores. Repeatedly minimize \(c^\top x\) subject to \(x\geq0\) and \(x(\delta(S))\geq1\) for every \(S\in\mathcal F\). Given an optimizer \(x^*\), compute a minimum-capacity \(T\)-cut. If its capacity is less than \(1\), add its shore to \(\mathcal F\) and repeat. Otherwise, \(x^*\in Q_T\), and comparison with the restricted relaxation shows that \(x^*\) is optimal over \(Q_T\). Integrality of \(Q_T\) guarantees an optimal integral extreme point, which is the incidence vector of a minimum-cost \(T\)-join, although the particular optimizer \(x^*\) returned by the restricted linear program need not itself be integral.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Repeatedly add a violated minimum T-cut to the restricted linear program. When no violation remains, the current solution certifies the exact optimum value; integrality guarantees an optimal T-join incidence vector with that value, though the current optimizer need not itself be integral.

assumptions_latex: The relaxation retains only \(x\geq0\) and omits all \(T\)-cut inequalities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The relaxation has optimum \(0\), while every feasible \(T\)-join has strictly positive cost whenever no zero-edge \(T\)-join exists.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Sharp failure after deleting the entire odd-cut inequality family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider the relaxation \(R=\{x\in\mathbb R^E:x\geq0\}\) obtained by deleting every inequality \(x(\delta(S))\geq1\) with \(|S\cap T|\) odd. The zero vector lies in \(R\), so \(\min\{c^\top x:x\in R\}=0\). If \(T\neq\varnothing\) and every edge has positive cost, each \(T\)-join uses at least one edge and has positive cost. Thus nonnegativity alone neither enforces parity correction nor gives a finite multiplicative approximation guarantee.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T=\{v\in V:\deg_G(v)\text{ is odd}\}\). Compute a minimum-cost \(T\)-join \(J\), duplicate its edges with multiplicity, and find an Euler tour of the resulting connected even-degree multigraph. Every closed postman walk must add a multiset whose odd-degree set is \(T\), so its added cost is at least \(\tau(G,T,c)\). Therefore \[\operatorname{OPT}_{\mathrm{CPP}}=c(E)+\tau(G,T,c),\] and the construction returns an optimal postman tour.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Duplicate a minimum join on the odd-degree vertices, then take an Euler tour; base edge cost plus join cost is optimal.

knowledge_statements.title: Rural Postman Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary between the undirected Chinese and rural postman problems.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph with nonnegative integer edge costs and let \(R\subseteq E\). The rural postman problem seeks a minimum-cost closed walk traversing every edge of \(R\). When \(R=E\), this is the polynomially solvable Chinese postman problem. When \(R\) is an arbitrary part of the input, the decision problem asking whether such a walk of cost at most \(B\) exists is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Requiring every edge yields the polynomial Chinese postman problem; allowing an arbitrary required-edge subset makes the decision problem NP-complete.

knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(R=E\) is polynomially solvable, whereas unrestricted \(R\subseteq E\) yields an NP-complete decision problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Windy Postman Boundary
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Complexity boundary created by direction-dependent traversal costs on undirected edges.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be a connected undirected graph in which traversing \(uv\in E\) from \(u\) to \(v\) costs \(c_{uv}\ge 0\), possibly with \(c_{uv}\ne c_{vu}\). A windy postman tour is a closed walk traversing every edge at least once. If \(c_{uv}=c_{vu}\) for every edge, the problem reduces to the polynomially solvable undirected Chinese postman problem; with arbitrary directional costs, its decision version is NP-complete.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Symmetric traversal costs give the ordinary polynomial postman problem, while arbitrary direction-dependent costs make the windy version NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: Directional costs and the decision bound are nonnegative integers.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Symmetric costs give a polynomial case; arbitrary \(c_{uv}\) and \(c_{vu}\) give an NP-complete decision problem.

knowledge_statements.title: Parity Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence criterion for an undirected \(T\)-join in a possibly disconnected graph.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and \(T\subseteq V\), a \(T\)-join is an edge set \(J\subseteq E\) whose odd-degree vertices are exactly \(T\). Hence any component meeting \(T\) oddly is a complete parity-infeasibility witness.

knowledge_statements.title: Component Infeasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Disconnected components impose independent parity constraints on joins.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(C\) be a connected component of an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\). Because no edge of \(G\) crosses from \(C\) to \(V\setminus C\), every edge set \(J\subseteq E\) has an even number of odd-degree vertices inside \(C\). Consequently, if a prescribed terminal set \(T\subseteq V\) satisfies \(\lvert T\cap C\rvert\) odd, no \(T\)-join exists, irrespective of edge costs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A component containing an odd number of prescribed terminals makes a T-join impossible, regardless of costs.
assumptions_latex: \(C\) is a connected component and \(T\subseteq V\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\lvert T\cap C\rvert\equiv 1\pmod 2\) implies that no \(T\)-join exists.

children.title: Componentwise Parity Certificates
children.top_down_role: Certificates combining terminal parity information with component placement.

knowledge_statements.title: Componentwise Parity Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A locally checkable certificate that a prescribed join cannot exist.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected graph \(G=(V,E)\) and terminals \(T\subseteq V\), an infeasibility certificate is a vertex set \(C\subseteq V\) satisfying \(\delta_G(C)=\varnothing\) and \(\lvert T\cap C\rvert\) odd. The certificate is verified by scanning the edges to check that none crosses \(C\), then counting terminals in \(C\). These conditions certify that no edge set can have odd-degree set exactly \(T\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An edge-isolated vertex set containing an odd number of terminals is a directly checkable certificate that no T-join exists.

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Length Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of shortest-path metric closure when traversal lengths may be negative.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Nonnegative edge lengths make shortest-path distances finite and permit path replacement in parity-correction reductions. With negative lengths, the same construction remains meaningful only when all relevant shortest-path values are finite, equivalently when no reachable negative-length closed walk can be inserted into the admissible walk model. In an undirected traversal model allowing repeated use in both directions, any negative edge creates a negative closed walk by immediate reversal, so the walk objective becomes unbounded below.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Negative lengths are admissible only when they create no repeatable negative closed walk; otherwise shortest-path closure and walk minimization fail.

Shortest-path values are defined as infima over admissible walks.

knowledge_statements.title: Metric-Closure Validity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Shortest-path matching representation of a minimum-cost undirected \(T\)-join.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(V,E)\) be connected with nonnegative edge lengths, and let \(T\subseteq V\) have even cardinality. Define \(d(u,v)\) as the minimum length of a \(u\)-to-\(v\) path. Then \(d\) is a finite metric on distinct vertices after identifying zero-distance vertices if necessary, and the minimum \(T\)-join cost equals the minimum weight of a perfect matching on the complete graph with vertex set \(T\) and edge weights \(d(u,v)\). Matching edges may be expanded into shortest paths.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With nonnegative lengths, a minimum T-join equals a minimum perfect matching on terminals weighted by shortest-path distances.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \[\min_{J\text{ a }T\text{-join}}\ell(J)=\min_{M\text{ a perfect matching on }T}\sum_{uv\in M}d(u,v).\]

children.title: Negative-Cycle Boundaries

knowledge_statements.title: Negative-Cycle Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Negative cycles are the sharp obstruction to finite walk-based shortest-path closure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a directed length graph, suppose a negative-length directed cycle \(Z\) is reachable from \(u\) and a target \(v\) is reachable from \(Z\). Repeating \(Z\) arbitrarily many times inside a \(u\)-to-\(v\) walk yields lengths tending to \(-\infty\). Thus the walk-based distance \(d(u,v)\) is not finite, and no finite metric-closure edge can represent that pair. If no relevant negative cycle exists, finite shortest-path distances may still be defined despite negative arcs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A negative cycle lying between a source and target makes their walk distance minus infinity and invalidates finite metric closure.
assumptions_latex: Shortest paths are interpreted over directed walks.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(u\leadsto Z\leadsto v\) and \(\ell(Z)<0\), then \(d(u,v)=-\infty\).

notation.meaning: infimum length of a directed u-to-v walk

knowledge_statements.title: Directed Parity Asymmetry
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Why undirected degree-parity correction does not directly model directed Eulerian augmentation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an undirected added edge, both endpoint degrees change parity. For a directed added arc \(uv\), however, the imbalance \(b(x)=d^+(x)-d^-(x)\) increases by one at \(u\) and decreases by one at \(v\). Consequently, specifying vertices of odd underlying degree is insufficient for directed Eulerian augmentation: feasibility requires correcting the signed imbalance vector, whose entries sum to zero in each weak component without external arcs. Undirected \(T\)-join parity conditions therefore cannot be transferred unchanged to directed graphs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Directed augmentation corrects signed in-out imbalances, not merely odd degrees, so undirected T-join criteria do not directly apply.
assumptions_latex: The graph is finite and directed.
Eulerian balance means equal indegree and outdegree at every vertex.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Directed Eulerian correction requires \(b(x)=0\) for every vertex, not only an even underlying degree.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) and \(W\) be disjoint finite agent sets of equal size. knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable-marriage preferences restricted to explicitly acceptable opposite-side agents.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U\) and \(W\) be disjoint finite agent sets. Each agent \(a\in U\cup W\) specifies a strict order over a subset \(A(a)\) of the opposite side. knowledge_statements.title: Unacceptable Partners
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Individual acceptability and its effect on feasible and blocking pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an agent \(a\) in a two-sided matching market, an opposite-side agent \(b\) is unacceptable when \(a\) strictly prefers remaining unmatched to being matched with \(b\). An individually rational matching contains no pair with either endpoint finding the other unacceptable. Under incomplete lists, omission of \(b\) from \(a\)'s list represents this relation. A pair can block an individually rational matching only when its members are mutually acceptable and each prefers the other to its current assignment or to being unmatched.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An unacceptable partner is worse than remaining unmatched; such pairs are infeasible and cannot constitute mutually acceptable blocking pairs.
assumptions_latex: Agents have strict preferences that include the unmatched outcome.

assumptions_latex: Every agent strictly ranks its acceptable neighbors.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite one-to-one deferred acceptance with strict incomplete lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initialize \(M=\varnothing\). While some unmatched proposer \(p\) has an acceptable receiver not previously proposed to, let \(p\) propose to its most-preferred such receiver \(r\). Receiver \(r\) tentatively retains its preferred agent among \(p\) and its current tentative partner, if any, rejecting the other; update \(M\) accordingly. Stop when no proposal is possible and output the tentative matching \(M\). Each edge in \(E_A\) is proposed along at most once, so termination occurs after at most \(|E_A|\) proposals, and the output is stable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unmatched proposers apply down their lists; receivers retain their best proposal. The process terminates after at most one proposal per acceptable edge and is stable.

knowledge_statements.title: Certificate Failure Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Limits of interpreting reduced preference lists as exact stable-partner certificates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a stable-marriage instance and let \(L_I(x)\) be each participant's reduced list. The equivalence \(y\in L_I(x)\) if and only if some stable matching pairs \(x\) with \(y\) requires the reduction procedure to be both sound and complete. If a pair occurring in a stable matching is deleted, list exclusion gives a false negative. If an unattainable pair remains, list membership gives a false positive. Thus arbitrary truncation, incomplete execution of the reduction rules, or applying strict-preference reductions unchanged to ties does not yield an exact stable-partner certificate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Reduced lists certify stable partners only when their reductions are sound and complete; erroneous deletion causes false negatives, while retention of impossible pairs causes false positives.

knowledge_statements.title: Distributive Lattice Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical lattice theorem for one-to-one stable marriage with strict complete preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite balanced stable-marriage instance with strict complete preferences, order stable matchings by \(M\preceq_U N\) when every member of \(U\) weakly prefers its partner in \(M\) to its partner in \(N\). The stable matchings form a distributive lattice. For stable \(M,N\), their meet assigns every member of \(U\) the better of its two partners, and their join assigns every member of \(U\) the worse; the induced assignments are stable matchings, with the opposite choices occurring for members of \(V\). The \(U\)-optimal and \(V\)-optimal stable matchings are the least and greatest elements.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under the side-U dominance order, stable matchings form a distributive lattice whose meet and join select each U-agent's better and worse partner, respectively.
assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) are finite, equally sized participant sets.
Every participant has a strict total order over the opposite side.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal S,\preceq_U)\) is a distributive lattice with extremal side-optimal stable matchings.

notation.meaning: componentwise preference order from side U's perspective

review_flags: Classical theorem, but no relevant stable-matching source locator was supplied.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and strict complete stable-marriage scope fit the lattice leaf. However, the distributivity theorem, coordinatewise meet/join description, and extremal-element orientation have no cited source or locator.

children.title: Rotation Structure
children.top_down_role: Rotation objects arising within the family of stable matchings.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotation Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exposed rotations in reduced tables for strict stable-marriage instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(M\) be a stable matching represented by its reduced preference table. An exposed rotation is a cyclic sequence \(\rho=((u_0,v_0),\ldots,(u_{k-1},v_{k-1}))\) of distinct pairs in \(M\) such that \(v_i\) is first and \(v_{i+1}\) is second on \(u_i\)'s reduced list, with indices modulo \(k\). Eliminating \(\rho\) replaces every pair \((u_i,v_i)\) by \((u_i,v_{i+1})\) and performs the consequent sound list deletions. The resulting reduced table represents a stable matching immediately below \(M\) in the side-\(U\) dominance order.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rotation is a cyclic set of current pairs whose members on one side can simultaneously move to their next reduced-list partners, producing another stable matching.
assumptions_latex: Preferences are strict and the reduced table is obtained by valid stable-marriage reductions.
\(M\) is the stable matching represented by the table.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating an exposed \(\rho\) transforms \(M\) into another stable matching.

notation.meaning: participants paired by the current stable matching

review_flags: Rotation convention and reduced-table update rules need an authoritative source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits Rotation Structure, but the precise exposed-rotation convention, consequent deletion rules, and immediate-cover assertion depend on a specific reduced-table formalism for which no source locator is supplied.

children.title: Rotation Posets
children.top_down_role: Precedence organization among rotations.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotation Posets
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Precedence order on rotations of a fixed strict stable-marriage instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\mathcal R\) be the rotations of a fixed stable-marriage instance. For distinct \(\rho,\sigma\in\mathcal R\), define \(\rho\prec\sigma\) when every valid rotation-elimination sequence starting at the side-\(U\)-optimal stable matching and containing \(\sigma\) eliminates \(\rho\) earlier. The transitive closure of this forced-precedence relation is a strict partial order; equivalently, its reflexive closure \(\preceq\) is a partial order. The ordered set \((\mathcal R,\preceq)\) is the rotation poset of the instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The rotation poset orders one rotation before another exactly when every valid elimination sequence using the latter must first eliminate the former.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite and has strict preferences.
\(\mathcal R\) is its set of rotations under a fixed side orientation.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\mathcal R,\preceq)\) is a partially ordered set encoding forced elimination precedence.

notation.meaning: set of rotations of the instance
rotation rho precedes or equals rotation sigma

review_flags: Forced-precedence characterization needs an authoritative rotation-poset source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the Rotation Posets leaf. The forced-precedence characterization and its equivalence to the standard rotation order require an authoritative locator; none is supplied. The statement also calls for clarification from a source because the universally quantified precedence relation appears already transitive before taking its transitive closure.

children.title: Closed Subsets of Rotations
children.top_down_role: Closed-set representations associated with stable outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Closed Subsets of Rotations
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Order ideals of the rotation poset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \((\mathcal R,\preceq)\) be a rotation poset. A subset \(C\subseteq\mathcal R\) is closed, or a down-set, when \(\sigma\in C\) and \(\rho\preceq\sigma\) imply \(\rho\in C\). Equivalently, \(C\) contains every forced predecessor of each rotation it contains. Consequently, any linear extension of the induced order on \(C\) lists its rotations in an order compatible with all precedence constraints; starting from the side-optimal matching, eliminating them in that order realizes the stable matching represented by \(C\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A closed rotation set contains every predecessor of each included rotation and can therefore be eliminated in any compatible topological order.
assumptions_latex: \((\mathcal R,\preceq)\) is the rotation poset of a strict stable-marriage instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\text{ is closed}\Longleftrightarrow (\forall\sigma\in C)(\forall\rho\preceq\sigma)\,\rho\in C\).
review_flags: The realization assertion requires a rotation-representation theorem source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The down-set definition fits the leaf, but the additional assertion that every compatible linear extension is a valid elimination sequence realizing a stable matching is a representation theorem, not merely definitional, and has no cited source locator.

children.title: Rotation-Elimination Reachability
children.top_down_role: Reachability relations among stable matchings induced by rotation elimination.

knowledge_statements.title: Rotation-Elimination Reachability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reachability between stable matchings through exposed-rotation eliminations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Associate with each stable matching \(M\) the closed set \(C(M)\) of rotations eliminated from the side-\(U\)-optimal matching to obtain \(M\). For stable matchings \(M,N\), there exists a valid sequence of exposed-rotation eliminations transforming \(M\) into \(N\) if and only if \(C(M)\subseteq C(N)\). When inclusion holds, the rotations in \(C(N)\setminus C(M)\) may be eliminated in any order that is a linear extension of the rotation poset restricted to that difference after its already-eliminated predecessors are removed.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: One stable matching reaches another by eliminating rotations exactly when its eliminated-rotation ideal is contained in the other's ideal.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite with strict preferences.
Stable matchings are oriented from the side-\(U\)-optimal matching by rotation elimination.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\leadsto N\Longleftrightarrow C(M)\subseteq C(N)\).

notation.meaning: closed set of rotations eliminated to obtain M
N is reachable from M by valid rotation eliminations

review_flags: Reachability equivalence needs an authoritative rotation theorem locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the reachability leaf, and the inclusion criterion is stated in the correct strict-preference setting. The bijective closed-set representation and the claim about permissible elimination orders need an authoritative rotation theorem locator.

children.title: Stable-Matching Enumeration
children.top_down_role: Systematic listing of stable outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Matching Enumeration
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Enumeration through the ideal representation of the rotation poset.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite strict stable-marriage instance, the map sending a stable matching \(M\) to its eliminated-rotation set \(C(M)\) is a bijection from the set \(\mathcal S\) of stable matchings to the order ideals \(\mathcal J(\mathcal R)\) of its rotation poset. Its inverse starts from the side-\(U\)-optimal matching and eliminates the rotations of an ideal in any compatible linear order. Hence enumerating stable matchings without duplication is equivalent to enumerating the order ideals of \((\mathcal R,\preceq)\), and \(|\mathcal S|=|\mathcal J(\mathcal R)|\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable matchings correspond bijectively to rotation-poset ideals, so they can be enumerated by generating each ideal exactly once.
assumptions_latex: The stable-marriage instance is finite and has strict preferences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S\cong\mathcal J(\mathcal R)\) and \(|\mathcal S|=|\mathcal J(\mathcal R)|\).

notation.meaning: family of order ideals of the rotation poset

review_flags: Bijection and enumeration representation require a stable-matching source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits this enumeration leaf. The bijection between stable matchings and rotation-poset ideals, including the inverse construction and exact cardinality identity, is nontrivial and has no cited source or locator.

children.title: Compact Rotation-Poset Encodings
children.top_down_role: Compressed representations of the stable-matching family using rotation precedence.

knowledge_statements.title: Compact Rotation-Poset Encodings
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Polynomial-size encoding of all stable matchings by rotations and precedence constraints.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a stable-marriage instance with \(n\) participants on each side and strict preferences, all stable matchings admit a rotation-poset encoding with at most \(n(n-1)/2\) rotations. A precedence digraph represents the order by reachability, and each stable matching is encoded by one down-closed Boolean vector \(x\in\{0,1\}^{\mathcal R}\) satisfying \(x_\sigma\le x_\rho\) whenever \(\rho\prec\sigma\). Thus a polynomial-size structure can represent a family of stable matchings whose cardinality may be exponential in \(n\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: At most quadratically many rotations and their precedence constraints compactly encode every stable matching as a down-closed binary vector.
assumptions_latex: There are \(n\) participants on each side with strict complete preferences.
Precedence arcs encode the rotation order by transitive reachability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|\mathcal R|\le n(n-1)/2\), and stable matchings correspond to feasible down-closed vectors \(x\).

notation.meaning: indicator that rotation rho is eliminated

review_flags: The quadratic rotation bound and polynomial precedence encoding need exact source certification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation role fits the compact-encoding leaf. The bound of at most n(n-1)/2 rotations and the existence of a polynomial-size precedence representation both require exact source certification; the supplied inventory contains no relevant stable-matching locator.

children.title: Output-Sensitive Generation
children.top_down_role: Enumeration regimes measured relative to the number of produced matchings.

knowledge_statements.title: Output-Sensitive Generation
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Duplicate-free generation via traversal of rotation-poset ideals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Input a strict stable-marriage instance and its rotation poset \((\mathcal R,\preceq)\). Initialize \(C=\varnothing\) and the matching to the side-\(U\)-optimal stable matching. Traverse the family of ideals by repeatedly adding an eligible rotation \(\rho\notin C\) whose predecessors all lie in \(C\), recursively outputting the matching obtained by eliminating \(\rho\), and undoing that elimination on backtracking. Use a canonical branching rule or visited-state suppression so that every ideal is output once. Stop after all ideals have been visited; the outputs are exactly all stable matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Traverse rotation-poset ideals, adding eligible rotations and backtracking, to output every stable matching once with work tied to the generated family.
assumptions_latex: The rotation poset and side-\(U\)-optimal matching are available.
Rotation elimination and its backtracking data are maintained consistently.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output set is exactly \(\{M_C:C\in\mathcal J(\mathcal R)\}\), with no duplicates.

notation.meaning: current order ideal of eliminated rotations
stable matching represented by ideal C

review_flags: A precise polynomial-delay or amortized bound requires a specific enumeration algorithm source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits the leaf, but the canonical branching rule is not specified, while visited-state suppression has materially different memory behavior. No explicit delay, total-time, or amortized output-sensitive bound is stated, and no enumeration-algorithm source locator is supplied. A source is needed to select and state a precise duplicate-free algorithm and its bound.

children.title: Stable-Matching Counting Complexity
children.top_down_role: Complexity boundaries for determining the size of the stable set.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Matching Counting Complexity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact counting complexity for strict complete stable-marriage instances.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The function problem that maps a finite stable-marriage instance with strict complete preference lists to the number of its stable matchings belongs to \(\#\mathrm P\): a proposed matching is polynomially checkable for perfectness and absence of blocking pairs. Moreover, exact counting is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete under polynomial-time counting reductions. Equivalently through rotations, the task counts the order ideals of a compactly represented rotation poset; therefore the polynomial-size representation does not imply a polynomial-time exact counting algorithm unless \(\mathrm{FP}=\#\mathrm P\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Counting stable matchings is #P-complete even though stability is efficiently verifiable and all solutions have a polynomial-size rotation-poset representation.
assumptions_latex: Instances have two equally sized sides and strict complete preferences.
Complexity is measured under polynomial-time exact counting reductions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\#\mathrm{StableMarriage}\) is \(\#\mathrm P\)-complete.

notation.meaning: function counting stable matchings of an input instance

review_flags: The #P-completeness theorem requires its original or authoritative secondary source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf. Membership in #P is adequately scoped, but #P-hardness and the exact reduction convention are source-dependent theorem claims. No original or authoritative secondary source with a theorem, section, or page locator is cited.

children.title: Egalitarian Stable Selection
children.top_down_role: Stable selection based on aggregate participant dissatisfaction.

knowledge_statements.title: Egalitarian Stable Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-total-rank stable matching under strict preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For each acceptable pair \((u,v)\), let \(r_u(v)\) and \(r_v(u)\) be partner ranks. The egalitarian stable-selection problem returns a stable matching minimizing \(E(M)=\sum_{(u,v)\in M}(r_u(v)+r_v(u))\). Starting from a side-optimal stable matching, assign each rotation the change in \(E\) caused by eliminating it. Minimize the resulting additive weight over closed rotation sets by a minimum-weight-closure reduction to an \(s\)-\(t\) minimum cut, then eliminate the selected ideal in topological order and output the resulting stable matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An egalitarian stable matching minimizes the total rank cost of all partners and can be selected through a minimum-weight closed set of rotations.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite with strict preferences and admits a stable matching.
Ranks are numerical positions in participants' preference lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: M^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{M\in\mathcal S} E(M)\) is obtainable by a minimum-weight-closure computation.

notation.meaning: total rank cost of stable matching M
rank assigned by participant x to partner y

review_flags: Polynomial minimum-weight-closure formulation requires an optimization-over-stable-matchings source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm role fits because the record gives a rotation-closure optimization procedure. The additive rotation-weight formulation and minimum-cut reduction require an authoritative source locator. In addition, conclusion_latex has a missing opening math delimiter before M^*, although statement_latex itself satisfies the explicit-delimiter rule.

children.title: Sex-Equal Stable Selection
children.top_down_role: Stable selection based on disparity between the two participant sides.

knowledge_statements.title: Sex-Equal Stable Selection
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable selection minimizing the absolute aggregate rank imbalance between the two sides.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(U,V\) be the two sides and let \(r_x(y)\) denote the rank of \(y\) in \(x\)'s preference order. For a stable matching \(M\), define \(C_U(M)=\sum_{u\in U}r_u(M(u))\) and \(C_V(M)=\sum_{v\in V}r_v(M(v))\). A sex-equal stable matching is any \(M^*\in\mathcal S\) minimizing the imbalance \(D(M)=|C_U(M)-C_V(M)|\) over all stable matchings. The definition compares aggregate dissatisfaction, not the total dissatisfaction minimized by egalitarian selection.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A sex-equal stable matching minimizes the absolute difference between the two sides' aggregate partner-rank costs.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite, bipartite, and has strict preferences.
\(\mathcal S\neq\varnothing\), and smaller numerical rank means greater preference.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^*\in\operatorname*{arg\,min}_{M\in\mathcal S}|C_U(M)-C_V(M)|\).

notation.meaning: aggregate rank costs of the two sides

review_flags: The standard objective definition needs a relevant stable-matching source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition role fits the leaf, and the plain and LaTeX statements consistently define the standard aggregate-rank imbalance objective. Nevertheless, the record supplies neither a source citation nor an explicit standard-field rationale, so an inspectable stable-matching source locator is required.

children.title: Egalitarian–Sex-Equal Tradeoffs
children.top_down_role: Compatibility or tension between aggregate welfare and side disparity.

assumptions_latex: A finite stable-marriage instance has two equally sized sides \(M,W\), strict complete preference orders, and stable matchings \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The two criteria satisfy \(B(\mu)=(E(\mu)+D(\mu))/2\), exposing their exact tradeoff on \(\mathcal S\).

notation.meaning: Total rank cost incurred by side M and side W under matching mu.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Exact algebraic relation among the three rank-sum objectives; it does not assert coincident minimizers.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For every \(\mu\in\mathcal S\), define \(E(\mu)=C_M(\mu)+C_W(\mu)\), \(D(\mu)=|C_M(\mu)-C_W(\mu)|\), and \(B(\mu)=\max\{C_M(\mu),C_W(\mu)\}\). Then
\[
B(\mu)=\frac{E(\mu)+D(\mu)}{2}.
\]
Consequently, for any \(\mu,\nu\in\mathcal S\), the implication \(E(\mu)\le E(\nu)\) and \(D(\mu)\le D(\nu)\) yields \(B(\mu)\le B(\nu)\). Thus a balanced optimum cannot be strictly dominated simultaneously in egalitarian cost and sex imbalance.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Balanced cost is half the sum of egalitarian cost and sex imbalance, so improving both criteria cannot worsen balance.
knowledge_statements.title: Egalitarian–Sex-Equal Tradeoffs

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algebraic identity and Pareto implication are correct and fit the tradeoff container, but the record has no inspectable source citation.

children.title: Selection Complexity Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Computational regimes governing these stable-selection objectives.

assumptions_latex: Instances use strict preference lists and rank-sum objectives encoded in binary.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Egalitarian selection is polynomial-time solvable, whereas exact sex-equal and balanced selection are NP-hard optimization regimes.

notation.meaning: Set of stable matchings of the input instance.
Side rank sums of a stable matching.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical strict stable-marriage optimization; complexity may change under restricted preference domains.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a strict stable-marriage instance, minimizing \(C_M(\mu)+C_W(\mu)\) over \(\mu\in\mathcal S\) is solvable in polynomial time by minimum-weight closure on the rotation poset. In contrast, minimizing \(|C_M(\mu)-C_W(\mu)|\), or deciding whether some \(\mu\in\mathcal S\) has \(|C_M(\mu)-C_W(\mu)|\le k\), is NP-hard. Minimizing \(\max\{C_M(\mu),C_W(\mu)\}\) is likewise NP-hard in the unrestricted strict model. Each decision version belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\), since stability and the displayed rank sums are polynomially verifiable.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Egalitarian stable matching is polynomial via rotations, while exact sex-equal and balanced selection are NP-hard in the unrestricted strict model.
knowledge_statements.title: Selection Complexity Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The complexity-bound role fits the leaf, but the polynomial-time and NP-hardness claims require stable-marriage-specific sources identifying the preference model, decision problems, and reductions.

children.title: Median Stable Selection
children.top_down_role: Stable outcomes selected through median positions across the stable family.

assumptions_latex: A finite strict stable-marriage instance is given together with an odd family \(\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_{2k+1}\) of stable matchings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The agentwise median partners form a stable matching \(\mu^{\mathrm{med}}\).

notation.meaning: Median stable matching selected from an odd family.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Agentwise median theorem for an odd multiset of stable matchings in the strict one-to-one model.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Order the partners \(\mu_1(a),\ldots,\mu_{2k+1}(a)\) according to each agent's strict preference \(\succ_a\), counting multiplicities, and let \(m_a\) be the \((k+1)\)-st partner. The assignments \(a\mapsto m_a\) are mutually consistent: there exists a matching \(\mu^{\mathrm{med}}\) satisfying \(\mu^{\mathrm{med}}(a)=m_a\) for every agent \(a\). Moreover, \(\mu^{\mathrm{med}}\) is stable. Hence the median operation is closed on the stable-matching lattice, although it need not minimize a rank-sum or balance objective.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For any odd collection of strict stable matchings, assigning every agent their median partner produces another stable matching.
knowledge_statements.title: Median Stable Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem is stated precisely for an odd multiset and fits the terminal container, but the nontrivial median-closure and mutual-consistency claims lack a cited theorem or section.

children.title: Balanced Stable Selection
children.top_down_role: Stable outcomes selected to control imbalance between participant sides.

assumptions_latex: A finite strict stable-marriage instance has nonempty stable set \(\mathcal S\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A balanced stable matching is any \(\mu^B\in\operatorname*{argmin}_{\mu\in\mathcal S}B(\mu)\).

notation.meaning: Sum of partner ranks borne by each side.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rank-sum minimax definition of balanced stable marriage, distinct from minimum-regret matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For \(\mu\in\mathcal S\), let \(C_M(\mu)=\sum_{m\in M}\operatorname{rank}_m(\mu(m))\) and \(C_W(\mu)=\sum_{w\in W}\operatorname{rank}_w(\mu(w))\), with rank \(1\) denoting the best partner. Define
\[
B(\mu)=\max\{C_M(\mu),C_W(\mu)\}.
\]
A balanced stable matching is a stable matching \(\mu^B\) for which \(B(\mu^B)=\min_{\nu\in\mathcal S}B(\nu)\). Ties between balanced stable matchings are permitted unless a secondary selection rule is specified.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A balanced stable matching minimizes the larger of the two sides' total partner-rank costs among all stable matchings.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced Stable Selection

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is internally consistent and distinct from minimum regret, but the use of “balanced stable matching” for this rank-sum minimax objective needs a stable-matching-specific terminology citation.

children.title: Median–Balance Compatibility
children.top_down_role: Regimes where median-based and balance-based choices agree or diverge.

assumptions_latex: The median matching \(\mu^{\mathrm{med}}\) and balanced objective \(B\) are defined for the same finite strict instance.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex:
Median and balanced selection coincide exactly when \(B(\mu^{\mathrm{med}})=\min_{
u\in\mathcal S}B(\nu)\).

notation.meaning: Minimum balanced value over stable matchings.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Instancewise compatibility criterion; median closure alone gives no balance optimality guarantee.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(B^*=\min_{
u\in\mathcal S}\max\{C_M(
u),C_W(
u)\}\). The median selection is compatible with balanced selection precisely when
\[
\max\{C_M(\mu^{\mathrm{med}}),C_W(\mu^{\mathrm{med}})\}=B^*.
\]
Equivalently, no stable matching \(
u\in\mathcal S\) satisfies \(C_M(
u)<B(\mu^{\mathrm{med}})\) and \(C_W(
u)<B(\mu^{\mathrm{med}})\) with at least one reduction sufficient to make \(B(
u)<B(\mu^{\mathrm{med}})\). Stability of the median does not by itself imply this condition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A median stable matching is balance-compatible exactly when its larger side cost attains the globally minimum balanced value.
knowledge_statements.title: Median–Balance Compatibility

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The main equality is a correct instancewise optimality condition and does not claim a general equivalence theorem. An inspectable source is nevertheless absent, and the explanatory reformulation should be checked against the intended literature terminology.

children.title: Balanced-Selection Complexity
children.top_down_role: Computational boundaries for balance-oriented stable selection.

assumptions_latex: Input is a finite stable-marriage instance with strict preference lists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Exact balanced stable selection is NP-hard, while a proposed threshold-feasible stable matching is polynomially verifiable.

notation.meaning: Threshold for the larger side rank sum.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Unrestricted strict stable-marriage model with total-rank minimax balance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The decision problem asking whether there exists \(\mu\in\mathcal S\) such that
\[
\max\{C_M(\mu),C_W(\mu)\}\le K
\]
belongs to \(\mathrm{NP}\): a matching certifies feasibility, and capacity, stability, and both rank sums are computable in polynomial time. In the unrestricted strict-preference model this decision problem is NP-hard, and therefore computing a balanced stable matching is NP-hard. This boundary concerns exact optimization; it does not preclude polynomial algorithms on restricted preference domains or approximation algorithms.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The threshold version of balanced stable selection is verifiable in polynomial time but NP-hard for unrestricted strict preferences.
knowledge_statements.title: Balanced-Selection Complexity

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Membership in NP is straightforward, but the exact NP-hardness boundary for the stated minimax rank-sum objective and unrestricted strict model requires a specific reduction or theorem citation.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Matching Polyhedra
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Rothblum-type formulation for perfect stable marriage with strict preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The stable-matching polytope is \(P_{SM}=\operatorname{conv}\{\chi^\mu:\mu\text{ is stable}\}\). For strict perfect stable marriage it is described by \(x_{mw}\ge 0\), the degree equations
\[
\sum_{w:mw\in E}x_{mw}=1,
\qquad
\sum_{m:mw\in E}x_{mw}=1,
\]
and, for every \(mw\in E\), the stability inequality
\[
x_{mw}+\sum_{w'\in P_m(w)}x_{mw'}+\sum_{m'\in P_w(m)}x_{m'w}\ge 1.
\]
This system is integral: its extreme points are exactly the incidence vectors of stable matchings.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Degree equations, nonnegativity, and one blocking-pair inequality per acceptable pair give an integral polyhedral description of strict stable marriage.
assumptions_latex: The bipartite graph is \(G=(M\cup W,E)\), preferences are strict, and every agent must be matched.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed linear system is integral and equals the convex hull of stable-matching incidence vectors.

notation.meaning: Incidence variable for acceptable pair mw.
Neighbors preferred by an agent to the indicated partner.

source_refs.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

source_witnesses.locator: 4.1 Linear inequality systems and polyhedra p. 136

children.title: Responsive Hospital Preferences
children.top_down_role: Hospital preference structures induced from rankings over individual residents.

assumptions_latex: Hospital \(h\) has capacity \(q_h\) and a strict order \(\succ_h\) over individual residents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The displayed replacement and cardinality rules define responsiveness of \(h\)'s preferences over feasible resident sets.

notation.meaning: Induced strict preference over feasible resident sets.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Classical responsive extension from individual rankings to feasible sets under a quota.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hospital's preference \(\succ_h^*\) over subsets of acceptable residents of size at most \(q_h\) is responsive to \(\succ_h\) when two conditions hold. For every feasible \(S\), every \(r\in S\), and every \(r'\notin S\),
\[
(S\setminus\{r\})\cup\{r'\}\succ_h^* S
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
r'\succ_h r.
\]
Moreover, if \(|S|<q_h\) and acceptable \(r\notin S\), then \(S\cup\{r\}\succ_h^*S\). Thus comparisons of feasible sets are governed by individual rankings and the desirability of filling vacant positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Responsive hospital preferences compare feasible staffs by individual rankings and prefer adding an acceptable resident whenever capacity remains.
knowledge_statements.title: Responsive Hospital Preferences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The replacement and vacancy-filling conditions give a coherent responsive-preference definition and fit the leaf, but no hospitals-residents source with a definition or section locator is supplied.

children.title: Hospital Capacity Constraints
children.top_down_role: Upper-capacity effects in many-to-one assignments.

assumptions_latex: There are finite resident and hospital sets, and each hospital \(h\) has integer capacity \(q_h\ge0\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: An assignment is capacity-feasible exactly when \(|\mu(h)|\le q_h\) for every hospital and incidence is mutually consistent.

notation.meaning: Hospital assigned to resident r, or the unmatched symbol.
Set of residents assigned to hospital h.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Feasibility conditions for many-to-one hospitals-residents assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
A hospitals-residents assignment \(\mu\) is capacity-feasible when each resident \(r\) is assigned either one acceptable hospital or \(\varnothing\), each hospital \(h\) receives a set \(\mu(h)\) of acceptable residents, and
\[
r\in\mu(h)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mu(r)=h,
\qquad
|\mu(h)|\le q_h.
\]
A hospital is undersubscribed when \(|\mu(h)|<q_h\) and full when equality holds. These constraints define feasibility only; stability additionally excludes acceptable resident-hospital pairs that would prefer to deviate.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Each resident receives at most one hospital, assignments are mutually consistent, and no hospital receives more residents than its capacity.
knowledge_statements.title: Hospital Capacity Constraints

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The feasibility conditions are precise and the condition kind fits the container, but the record lacks an inspectable hospitals-residents model citation.

children.title: Responsiveness–Capacity Interaction
children.top_down_role: How responsive choice structure interacts with available hospital capacity.

assumptions_latex: Hospitals have responsive preferences induced by strict resident rankings and capacities \(q_h\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A resident-hospital pair blocks exactly under the stated vacancy-or-replacement predicate.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Reduction of setwise hospital choice to vacancy or single-resident replacement under responsiveness.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a capacity-feasible assignment \(\mu\), an acceptable pair \((r,h)\) with \(\mu(r)\ne h\) blocks \(\mu\) if and only if \(r\) prefers \(h\) to \(\mu(r)\) and either
\[
|\mu(h)|<q_h,
\]
or there exists \(r'\in\mu(h)\) such that \(r\succ_h r'\). Responsiveness makes this individual vacancy-or-replacement test equivalent to the hospital preferring some feasible set obtained by admitting \(r\). Consequently, stability can be checked without enumerating all subsets of residents.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Under responsiveness, blocking occurs when a resident prefers a hospital that has a vacancy or prefers them to one current assignee.
knowledge_statements.title: Responsiveness–Capacity Interaction

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vacancy-or-replacement characterization is appropriate under responsive strict hospital preferences, but its equivalence to setwise hospital choice and the resulting stability check require a cited source.

children.title: Nonresponsive Preference Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Stability limits appearing when hospital preferences depart from responsiveness.

assumptions_latex: Hospitals may rank feasible resident sets directly rather than by a responsive extension of individual rankings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without substitutability, rejection may reverse after the available set expands, invalidating deferred-acceptance guarantees based on responsiveness.

notation.meaning: Hospital h's chosen subset from available residents S.
Two nested sets of available residents.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Substitutability is the operative boundary; arbitrary nonresponsive preferences need not violate it.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
The hospital choice function \(C_h\) is substitutable when, for all \(S\subseteq T\) and \(r\in S\),
\[
r\in C_h(T)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad r\in C_h(S).
\]
A nonresponsive preference can violate this condition: there may exist \(S\subseteq T\) and \(r\in S\) with \(r\in C_h(T)\) but \(r\notin C_h(S)\). Then a resident rejected from one menu can become chosen after alternatives are added. The monotone-rejection argument supporting classical deferred acceptance fails, so existence, side-optimality, and strategy properties cannot be inferred from the responsive model alone.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When hospital choice is not substitutable, adding candidates can reverse a rejection, and classical deferred-acceptance guarantees no longer follow.
knowledge_statements.title: Nonresponsive Preference Boundaries

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly distinguishes nonresponsiveness from failure of substitutability and uses an appropriate failure-boundary kind. The claimed consequences for deferred acceptance require a choice-function source with a specific locator.

children.title: Resident-Optimal Stable Assignments
children.top_down_role: Stable assignments most favorable to residents.

assumptions_latex: A finite hospitals-residents instance has strict resident preferences, responsive hospital preferences, and capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Resident-proposing deferred acceptance returns a stable assignment weakly preferred by every resident to every other stable assignment.
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resident-optimality theorem for responsive many-to-one matching with strict preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Run resident-proposing deferred acceptance: each unassigned resident proposes to the most-preferred hospital not yet rejecting them, and each hospital tentatively retains its \(q_h\) most-preferred proposers and rejects the rest. The process terminates with a stable assignment \(\mu^R\). For every stable assignment \(\nu\) and every resident \(r\),
\[
\mu^R(r)\succeq_r\nu(r),
\]
where being unmatched is included in the resident's order. Thus \(\mu^R\) is resident-optimal among all stable assignments; under strict preferences, every resident has the same assignment in all resident-optimal stable outcomes.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resident-proposing deferred acceptance produces a stable assignment that every resident weakly prefers to any other stable assignment.
knowledge_statements.title: Resident-Optimal Stable Assignments

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role and responsive many-to-one scope fit the leaf, but termination, stability, and resident-optimality are nontrivial claims requiring a specific deferred-acceptance theorem citation.

children.title: Hospital-Optimal Stable Assignments
children.top_down_role: Stable assignments most favorable to hospitals.

knowledge_statements.title: Hospital-Optimal Stable Assignments
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hospital-side optimum in the finite responsive hospitals–residents model with strict preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be a finite resident set, \(H\) a finite hospital set, and \(q_h\) the capacity of \(h\in H\). Let \(\mathcal S\) denote the nonempty set of stable assignments, and let \(\succeq_h\) be hospital \(h\)'s responsive preference over feasible resident sets. A stable assignment \(M^H\in\mathcal S\) is hospital-optimal if
\[
M^H(h)\succeq_h M(h)\qquad\text{for every }h\in H\text{ and every }M\in\mathcal S.
\]
Under strict responsive preferences, the hospital-proposing deferred-acceptance algorithm returns this assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hospital-optimal stable assignment is weakly preferred by every hospital to every other stable assignment; hospital-proposing deferred acceptance produces it.
assumptions_latex: Preferences are strict, acceptable partners are specified, and hospital preferences are responsive to resident rankings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^H(h)\succeq_h M(h)\) for all \(h\in H\) and \(M\in\mathcal S\).

notation.meaning: Residents assigned to hospital h by assignment M.
Hospital h's responsive weak preference over feasible sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition of hospital optimality is mathematically standard and fits the leaf, but the deferred-acceptance sentence adds a theorem-like algorithmic claim to a definition record. No citation or inspectable locator supports either claim; an authoritative hospitals-residents source is required, and the algorithmic assertion should be separated or the record reclassified before acceptance.

children.title: Opposed-Side Optimality
children.top_down_role: Preference opposition between resident-optimal and hospital-optimal outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Opposed-Side Optimality
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Opposition between resident and hospital welfare at the two lattice-extreme stable assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a finite hospitals–residents instance with strict resident preferences and strict responsive hospital preferences, let \(M^R\) and \(M^H\) be the resident-optimal and hospital-optimal stable assignments. For every stable assignment \(M\), every resident weakly prefers \(M^R\) to \(M\) and \(M\) to \(M^H\); simultaneously, every hospital responsively weakly prefers \(M^H(h)\) to \(M(h)\) and \(M(h)\) to \(M^R(h)\). Thus each side's optimal stable assignment is the opposite side's pessimal stable assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The resident-optimal stable assignment is hospital-pessimal, while the hospital-optimal assignment is resident-pessimal.
assumptions_latex: The hospitals–residents instance is finite and admits strict preferences.
Hospital preferences over feasible sets are responsive.
Being unmatched is worse than every acceptable partner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^R\succeq_R M\succeq_R M^H\) and \(M^H\succeq_H M\succeq_H M^R\) for every stable \(M\).

notation.meaning: Componentwise weak preference orders of residents and hospitals.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The opposed resident-side and hospital-side extrema are stated consistently for finite strict responsive preferences, and duality is an appropriate content kind. However, no source reference or locator is supplied for the side-optimality and opposite-side-pessimality theorem.

children.title: Coincident Optimal Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instances where resident-optimal and hospital-optimal assignments coincide.

knowledge_statements.title: Coincident Optimal Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Characterization of uniqueness by equality of the two side-optimal stable assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For a finite hospitals–residents instance with strict resident preferences and strict responsive hospital preferences, let \(M^R\) and \(M^H\) denote the resident-optimal and hospital-optimal stable assignments. Then
\[
M^R=M^H
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{the instance has exactly one stable assignment}.
\]
Indeed, every stable assignment lies between these two extremes in the resident preference order, equivalently between them in the reverse hospital order. Hence coincident extremes leave no distinct intermediate stable assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Resident-optimal and hospital-optimal assignments coincide exactly when the stable assignment is unique.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite with strict preferences.
Hospital preferences over feasible resident sets are responsive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^R=M^H\) if and only if \(|\mathcal S|=1\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The uniqueness characterization is mathematically appropriate for this leaf, but the sentences beginning with “Indeed” and “Hence” are proof text and must be removed before acceptance. An authoritative source with a precise theorem, section, or page locator is also required.

knowledge_statements.title: Assignment-Cardinality Invariants
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Hospital-by-hospital cardinality conclusion of the rural hospitals theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a finite hospitals–residents instance with strict resident preferences, hospital capacities, and strict responsive hospital preferences. If \(M\) and \(N\) are stable assignments, then every hospital receives the same number of residents in both assignments:
\[
|M(h)|=|N(h)|\qquad\text{for every }h\in H.
\]
Consequently the total number of assigned residents, \(\sum_{h\in H}|M(h)|\), is invariant over all stable assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every hospital has the same assigned cardinality in every stable assignment, so the total number of matched residents is invariant.
assumptions_latex: The hospitals–residents instance is finite with strict preferences.
Each hospital has a fixed integral capacity and responsive preferences.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|M(h)|=|N(h)|\) for all \(h\in H\), and therefore \(\sum_h|M(h)|=\sum_h|N(h)|\).

notation.meaning: Residents assigned to hospital h under M.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The hospital-by-hospital cardinality invariant is a correct theorem-level formulation of a rural hospitals conclusion under the stated finite strict responsive model. No source reference or inspectable rural-hospitals-theorem locator is provided.

children.title: Unmatched-Participant Invariance
children.top_down_role: Persistence of unmatched participant sets across stable assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Unmatched-Participant Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Resident-set invariance component of the rural hospitals theorem.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a finite hospitals–residents instance with strict resident preferences and strict responsive hospital preferences, let \(M\) and \(N\) be any stable assignments. Then a resident is unmatched under \(M\) if and only if that resident is unmatched under \(N\):
\[
\{r\in R:M(r)=\varnothing\}
=
\{r\in R:N(r)=\varnothing\}.
\]
Thus invariance holds for the identities of unmatched residents, not merely for their number.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: The same residents are unmatched in every stable assignment, not merely the same number of residents.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite with strict preferences.
Hospital preferences are responsive and capacities are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M(r)=\varnothing\Longleftrightarrow N(r)=\varnothing\) for every \(r\in R\).

notation.meaning: Hospital assigned to resident r, or the empty symbol if unmatched.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The identity of unmatched residents, rather than merely their number, is the appropriate theorem for this leaf under the stated model. The record has no authoritative citation or specific locator supporting this rural hospitals conclusion.

children.title: Undersubscribed-Hospital Invariance
children.top_down_role: Persistence of undersubscribed hospitals across stable assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Undersubscribed-Hospital Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong setwise invariance for a hospital that is undersubscribed in one stable assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Consider a finite hospitals–residents instance with strict preferences and responsive hospital preferences. Let hospital \(h\) have capacity \(q_h\), and suppose some stable assignment \(M\) satisfies \(|M(h)|<q_h\). Then for every stable assignment \(N\),
\[
N(h)=M(h).
\]
Hence an undersubscribed hospital has not only the same number of assignees but exactly the same resident set in every stable assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If a hospital is below capacity in one stable assignment, it receives exactly the same residents in every stable assignment.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite with strict preferences.
Hospital preferences are responsive and \(q_h\) is fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(N(h)=M(h)\) for every stable assignment \(N\).

notation.meaning: Resident set assigned to h under M.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The setwise invariance asserted for a hospital undersubscribed in one stable assignment is the standard strong rural hospitals conclusion and fits the leaf. It requires an authoritative source with a precise theorem, section, or page locator.

children.title: Vacancy-Pattern Invariance
children.top_down_role: Stable-assignment invariance of unfilled capacity patterns.

knowledge_statements.title: Vacancy-Pattern Invariance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Invariance of the hospital-wise vacancy vector across stable assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For each hospital \(h\) of capacity \(q_h\), define its vacancy under assignment \(M\) by \(v_M(h)=q_h-|M(h)|\). In a finite hospitals–residents instance with strict preferences and responsive hospital preferences, any two stable assignments \(M\) and \(N\) satisfy
\[
v_M(h)=v_N(h)
\qquad\text{for every }h\in H.
\]
Therefore the complete vector of unfilled positions, including which hospitals are undersubscribed and by how much, is stable-assignment invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Every hospital has the same number of vacant positions in all stable assignments, so the entire vacancy vector is invariant.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite with strict preferences.
Hospital capacities are fixed and hospital preferences are responsive.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((q_h-|M(h)|)_{h\in H}=(q_h-|N(h)|)_{h\in H}\) for all stable \(M,N\).

notation.meaning: Number of vacant positions at hospital h under M.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The vacancy-vector equality follows from hospital-by-hospital assignment-cardinality invariance and is correctly expressed as a property. No source reference or precise locator is supplied for the underlying theorem or this corollary.

children.title: Participant–Vacancy Coupling
children.top_down_role: Relationship between unmatched residents and unused hospital capacity.

knowledge_statements.title: Participant–Vacancy Coupling
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Conservation identity coupling unmatched residents to unfilled hospital positions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(R\) be the resident set, let hospital \(h\) have capacity \(q_h\), and define \(v_M(h)=q_h-|M(h)|\). For every feasible assignment \(M\), the number \(u_M\) of unmatched residents satisfies
\[
u_M=|R|-\sum_{h\in H}|M(h)|
=|R|-\sum_{h\in H}q_h+\sum_{h\in H}v_M(h).
\]
Thus, with the market size and capacities fixed, changes in total vacancies and unmatched-resident cardinality must coincide. Under stable assignments, both quantities are invariant.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Unmatched residents and total hospital vacancies obey a conservation identity; in stable assignments, both are invariant together.
assumptions_latex: \(M\) is a feasible many-to-one assignment with \(|M(h)|\le q_h\).
Each resident is assigned to at most one hospital.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(u_M-|R|+\sum_{h\in H}q_h=\sum_{h\in H}v_M(h)\).

notation.meaning: Number of residents unmatched under M.
Vacancies at hospital h under M.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The conservation identity is internally correct and matches the participant-vacancy coupling leaf. The final stable-assignment invariance assertion depends on rural hospitals results, but neither those results nor the identity are tied to a source or explicit standard-field rationale.

knowledge_statements.title: Substitutable-Choice Extensions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Choice-function condition extending responsive hospital preferences in matching with contracts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(X_h\) be the finite set of contracts involving hospital \(h\), and let \(C_h:2^{X_h}\to2^{X_h}\) satisfy \(C_h(Y)\subseteq Y\). The choice function \(C_h\) is substitutable if, for all \(Z\subseteq Y\subseteq X_h\) and \(x\in Z\),
\[
x\in C_h(Y)\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x\in C_h(Z).
\]
Equivalently, rejecting some available contracts cannot cause a contract retained in the smaller menu to become rejected merely because other contracts were removed. Responsive capacity choice is a special case.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Choices are substitutable when a contract chosen from a larger menu remains chosen from every smaller menu that still contains it.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(Z\subseteq Y\) and \(x\in Z\cap C_h(Y)\) imply \(x\in C_h(Z)\).

notation.meaning: Contracts hospital h chooses from menu Y.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed implication is a standard substitutes condition for a choice function and the condition content kind fits the extension topic. Because substitutability conventions vary across matching-with-contracts sources, a precise authoritative definition locator is necessary before accepting the formulation and claimed responsive-choice specialization.

top_down_textbook_witnesses.source: An Efficient Algorithm for the Stable Roommates Problem
top_down_textbook_witnesses.source_title: An Efficient Algorithm for the Stable Roommates Problem

children.title: Stable-Roommates Existence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance classes admitting stable roommate assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Roommates Existence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A concrete sufficient regime: strict preferences induced by one common master order.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \(V=\{v_1,\ldots,v_{2m}\}\) be a stable-roommates instance. Suppose every participant ranks all other participants according to the same strict master order \(v_1\succ v_2\succ\cdots\succ v_{2m}\), with the participant themself omitted. Then the matching
\[
M=\{\{v_1,v_2\},\{v_3,v_4\},\ldots,\{v_{2m-1},v_{2m}\}\}
\]
is stable. Moreover, it is the unique stable matching, since the first two remaining participants in the master order must be paired in any stable matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common strict master ranking guarantees a unique stable roommates matching obtained by pairing consecutive participants in that ranking.
assumptions_latex: All preference lists are complete and strict.
Every list is induced by the same master order after deleting its owner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M=\{\{v_{2i-1},v_{2i}\}:1\le i\le m\}\) is the unique stable matching.

notation.meaning: Roommate matching pairing consecutive master-order participants.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The common-master-order regime and consecutive-pair matching are mathematically plausible and theorem is an appropriate content kind. The clause beginning “since” gives proof text, which must be removed, and no authoritative stable-roommates source with a specific locator is supplied.

children.title: Stable-Roommates Nonexistence Regimes
children.top_down_role: Instance classes lacking stable roommate assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable-Roommates Nonexistence Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Four-participant strict complete instance having no stable roommate matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let the participants be \(V=\{1,2,3,4\}\), with strict preference lists
\[
1:2\succ3\succ4,\qquad
2:3\succ1\succ4,\qquad
3:1\succ2\succ4,\qquad
4:1\succ2\succ3.
\]
The three perfect matchings are \(\{12,34\}\), \(\{13,24\}\), and \(\{14,23\}\). They are blocked respectively by the pairs \(\{2,3\}\), \(\{1,2\}\), and \(\{1,3\}\). Consequently this complete strict stable-roommates instance has no stable matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A four-person cyclic-preference instance has three possible perfect matchings, each blocked by a specified pair, so no stable matching exists.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S=\varnothing\).

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The listed four-person instance is a valid counterexample, and the specified blocking pairs correctly correspond to its three perfect matchings. The matching enumeration and blocker verification amount to proof or certificate text under the no-proof rule, and the record also lacks a source with a specific locator.

children.title: Nonexistence Obstructions
children.top_down_role: Preference structures responsible for failure of stable assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Nonexistence Obstructions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A dominating directed three-cycle sufficient to obstruct stable-roommates existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
In a complete strict stable-roommates instance, suppose three participants \(a,b,c\) satisfy
\[
a:b\succ c\succ V\setminus\{a,b,c\},\qquad
b:c\succ a\succ V\setminus\{a,b,c\},\qquad
c:a\succ b\succ V\setminus\{a,b,c\},
\]
where each displayed outsider block may have any internal order. Then no stable perfect matching exists. Any perfect matching either pairs two members of \(\{a,b,c\}\), leaving the third paired outside, or pairs all three outside; in either case one pair from the directed cycle mutually prefers one another to its assigned partners and blocks the matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A preference-dominating directed cycle on three participants forces every perfect matching to contain a blocking pair.
assumptions_latex: The participant set is finite and even.
Preference lists are complete and strict.
The three-cycle participants rank both cycle peers above every outsider.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal S=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Participants forming the dominating directed preference cycle.
Set of stable perfect roommate matchings.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The dominating directed three-cycle is a valid sufficient nonexistence obstruction, and failure_boundary fits the leaf. The final two sentences explicitly argue all matching cases and therefore constitute proof text; they must be removed after an authoritative source and precise locator are supplied.

children.title: Existence Recognition Boundaries
children.top_down_role: Computational regimes for distinguishing solvable from unsolvable instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Existence Recognition Boundaries
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict, complete, finite stable-roommates instances; Irving’s recognition boundary.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a stable-roommates instance on an even set of \(n\) agents, each having a strict total order over all other agents. Irving’s two-phase procedure first performs proposal-driven reductions and then repeatedly eliminates exposed rotations. Every deletion made by the procedure preserves every stable matching still possible in the current table. The procedure terminates with a stable matching precisely when all final lists are singletons; it reports nonexistence precisely when a list becomes empty. With preference positions and deletions represented for constant-time access, existence and a stable matching, when one exists, are computable in \(O(n^2)\) time and space.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: For strict complete preferences, Irving’s quadratic-time procedure recognizes existence: singleton final lists yield a stable matching, while any empty list proves nonexistence.
assumptions_latex: Every agent strictly ranks all other agents.
Preference lists are represented to support constant-time deletion and comparison.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(I\) has a stable matching if and only if Irving’s procedure terminates without an empty list, and recognition takes \(O(n^2)\) time.
review_flags: Authoritative stable-roommates algorithm theorem and exact complexity locator required.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem role fits the existence-recognition leaf, but the preservation claim, terminal characterization, and quadratic time-and-space bound require an authoritative stable-roommates theorem and complexity locator.

children.title: Roommates Proposal Structure
children.top_down_role: Proposal relations arising in the initial roommates reduction regime.

knowledge_statements.title: Roommates Proposal Structure
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-one proposal dynamics for strict stable roommates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Initially every agent is free, has an undeleted preference list, and has proposed to nobody. A free agent \(x\) proposes to the highest-ranked person \(y\) on \(x\)'s list not previously proposed to. Agent \(y\) tentatively holds the most-preferred proposal received so far and rejects any previously held or newly received inferior proposal. A rejected proposer becomes free and continues downward through its list. Stop when every agent holds a proposal, or when some free agent has no untried name. The held proposals need not form a matching because an agent may simultaneously hold one proposal and have a different proposal held.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Free agents propose down their lists; each recipient retains only its favorite proposal. The phase stops when everyone holds one proposal or someone exhausts their list.
assumptions_latex: Each proposal is made at most once.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The output is either one held proposal at every agent or an exhausted-list failure signal.
review_flags: Exact phase-one formulation requires a stable-roommates source locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind and local scope fit, but the exact phase-one proposal, rejection, and stopping rules have no cited source locator.
