children.title: Preference-List Reduction
children.top_down_role: Removal of preference entries incompatible with retained proposal relations.

knowledge_statements.title: Preference-List Reduction
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Symmetric safe deletions induced by held proposals.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Whenever agent \(y\) holds a proposal from \(x\), delete every agent \(z\) ranked below \(x\) on \(y\)'s current list, and simultaneously delete \(y\) from each such \(z\)'s list. Rejections likewise delete the rejected pair symmetrically. After each deletion, any newly free proposer resumes proposing to its highest remaining untried choice. Continue until every agent holds a proposal and all successor deletions have been performed, or until a list becomes empty. The resulting table is symmetric: \(y\) occurs on \(x\)'s list if and only if \(x\) occurs on \(y\)'s list.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Held proposals remove all inferior alternatives at the recipient, with every deletion mirrored on the other list, until closure or an empty list.
assumptions_latex: The proposal process follows the roommates proposal structure.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: The procedure returns a symmetric reduced table or detects an empty list.

notation.meaning: a successor of the held proposer on the recipient's list

review_flags: Safe-deletion invariant and exact phase-one closure need an authoritative locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the reduction leaf, but the timing and safety of symmetric successor and rejection deletions require authoritative confirmation.

children.title: Reduced-List Certificates
children.top_down_role: Structural information preserved by the reduced preference lists.

knowledge_statements.title: Reduced-List Certificates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Locally checkable invariants of a phase-one reduced table.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A table \(T\) certifies completed proposal reduction when: every list is nonempty; list membership is symmetric; every agent holds exactly one proposal; and, whenever \(y\) is first on \(x\)'s list, \(x\) is last on \(y\)'s list. The certificate is checked by scanning the surviving entries and the held-proposal pointers. Moreover, the deletion invariant certifies that every stable matching of the original instance uses only pairs surviving in \(T\). Thus a singleton table directly specifies a stable matching by pairing each agent with its sole remaining entry.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A valid reduced table has symmetric nonempty lists and the first–last property; all original stable matchings use surviving pairs, and singleton lists specify one.
assumptions_latex: \(T\) results from completed proposal-driven safe deletions.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(T\) is a verifiable reduced-table certificate, and singleton lists in \(T\) define a stable matching.
review_flags: The precise reduced-table invariants and singleton conclusion require source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The certificate kind fits exactly, but the first–last invariant, stable-pair preservation claim, and singleton-table conclusion need a precise reduced-table source locator.

children.title: Empty-List Failure Signals
children.top_down_role: Reduction outcomes that expose nonexistence before rotation processing.

knowledge_statements.title: Empty-List Failure Signals
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Nonexistence boundary reached by stable-matching-preserving list reductions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a finite stable-roommates instance, let \(T_0,T_1,\ldots,T_m\) be preference tables produced from \(I\), and suppose every deletion from \(T_{j-1}\) to \(T_j\) preserves all pairs that can occur in a stable matching compatible with \(T_{j-1}\). If some agent \(x\) has an empty list in \(T_m\), then \(I\) has no stable matching. Thus an empty list is a sound failure signal when it is reached exclusively through certified safe deletions.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: If certified stable-matching-preserving reductions empty an agent’s list, the original instance has no stable matching.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is finite and every stable solution matches every agent.
For each \(j\in\{1,\ldots,m\}\), every deletion from \(T_{j-1}\) to \(T_j\) satisfies the stable-matching preservation invariant.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: If \(L_{T_m}(x)=\varnothing\) for some \(x\), then \(I\) has no stable matching.

notation.meaning: preference table after the j-th safe-reduction stage
agent x's list in the terminal table

review_flags: An authoritative locator is required for the deletion-safety invariant and empty-list nonexistence boundary.

knowledge_statements.title: Roommates Rotation Elimination
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Phase-two elimination of an exposed roommates rotation.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: In a reduced table, an exposed rotation is a cyclic sequence \(R=((x_i,y_i))_{i=0}^{r-1}\), with indices modulo \(r\), such that \(y_i\) is first on \(x_i\)'s list and \(y_{i+1}\) is second. Eliminate \(R\) by making each \(x_i\) displace \(x_{i+1}\) at \(y_{i+1}\): delete \((x_i,y_i)\), and delete symmetrically every pair \((y_{i+1},z)\) for which \(y_{i+1}\) ranks \(x_i\) above \(z\). Repeat until all lists are singletons, or stop with failure if a list empties. Each elimination preserves existence of a stable matching in the current table.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: An exposed rotation redirects each participant from its first to second choice and deletes newly dominated pairs; repeated elimination reaches singleton lists or failure.
assumptions_latex: The current table is a nonempty reduced table.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Eliminating \(R\) yields another reduced instance with the same stable-solvability status unless an empty list certifies nonexistence.

notation.meaning: first choice of the corresponding proposer

review_flags: Rotation indexing and elimination rule require confirmation against an authoritative presentation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The algorithm kind fits the rotation-elimination topic, but the rotation indexing, deletion rule, and preservation of solvability are convention-sensitive and require an authoritative locator.

children.title: Stable Partitions
children.top_down_role: Partition-based representations associated with roommates instances.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable Partitions
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable-permutation formulation for strict complete roommates preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(V\) be a finite set of agents with strict complete preferences, and let \(\pi\) be a fixed-point-free permutation of \(V\). The permutation \(\pi\) is a stable partition if: for every \(x\in V\), either \(\pi(x)=\pi^{-1}(x)\) or \(x\) prefers \(\pi(x)\) to \(\pi^{-1}(x)\); and there are no distinct \(x,y\in V\) such that \(x\) prefers \(y\) to \(\pi^{-1}(x)\) while \(y\) prefers \(x\) to \(\pi^{-1}(y)\). The cycles in the disjoint-cycle decomposition of \(\pi\) are the parts of the stable partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable partition is a fixed-point-free permutation whose successors dominate predecessors and whose predecessor assignments admit no mutually preferred pair.
assumptions_latex: Each agent strictly ranks every other agent.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\pi\) is stable exactly when it satisfies the successor condition and the no-blocking-pair condition.

notation.meaning: successor of x in the partition
predecessor of x in the partition

review_flags: Stable-partition conventions vary; the fixed-point-free strict-preference version needs a precise source.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits, but stable-partition successor/predecessor conventions vary, and no source supports this fixed-point-free formulation.

children.title: Stable Cycles
children.top_down_role: Cyclic components occurring within stable-partition representations.

knowledge_statements.title: Stable Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Cycle components in a stable partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\pi\) be a stable partition of \(V\). A stable cycle is a cycle \(C=(x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_{k-1})\) in the disjoint-cycle decomposition of \(\pi\), so that \(\pi(x_i)=x_{i+1}\) and \(\pi^{-1}(x_i)=x_{i-1}\), with indices modulo \(k\). If \(k>2\), stability requires every \(x_i\) to prefer its successor \(x_{i+1}\) to its predecessor \(x_{i-1}\), while no two agents prefer each other to their respective predecessors. A two-cycle represents a mutual partner pair because successor and predecessor coincide.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A stable cycle is a permutation cycle of a stable partition; longer cycles prefer successors to predecessors, while a two-cycle represents one partner pair.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(C\) inherits the successor and no-blocking conditions of \(\pi\).
review_flags: A source locator is required for the stable-cycle terminology and conventions.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits the leaf and is internally consistent with the preceding stable-partition convention, but the terminology and inherited conditions lack a source locator.

children.title: Odd Stable Cycles
children.top_down_role: Odd cyclic components linked to stable-matching nonexistence.

knowledge_statements.title: Odd Stable Cycles
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Odd-cycle obstruction in strict stable-roommates partitions.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a strict complete stable-roommates instance, a stable partition exists. Moreover, the odd cycles occurring in a stable partition are invariant: every stable partition contains the same odd-cycle components. Consequently, if one stable partition contains an odd cycle, the instance admits no stable matching, because partner pairs would give a stable partition consisting only of two-cycles. Conversely, if a stable partition contains no odd cycle, each even cycle can be resolved by selecting alternating cycle edges, producing a stable matching. Thus stable-matching existence is equivalent to the absence of odd cycles in a stable partition.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Odd cycles are invariant across stable partitions and exactly obstruct stable matchings; without them, alternating edges of even cycles produce a stable matching.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite, complete, and has strict preferences.
Stable partitions use the successor–predecessor convention.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stable matching exists if and only if a stable partition has no odd cycle.

notation.meaning: a cycle component of a stable partition

review_flags: The odd-cycle invariance theorem and converse construction require an authoritative theorem locator.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The theorem kind fits the obstruction leaf, but stable-partition existence, invariance of odd components, and the all-even converse are substantive claims requiring an authoritative theorem locator.

children.title: Partition–Matching Correspondence
children.top_down_role: Relationship between stable partitions and stable roommate assignments.

knowledge_statements.title: Partition–Matching Correspondence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Stable matchings represented through stable-partition cycles.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every stable matching \(M\) induces a stable partition \(\pi_M\) by setting \(\pi_M(x)=M(x)\); its cycle decomposition consists entirely of two-cycles. Conversely, let \(\pi\) be a stable partition having only even cycles. On each two-cycle retain its unique edge. On every cycle \((x_0,\ldots,x_{2r-1})\) of length at least four, choose either alternating edge set \(\{\{x_{2j},x_{2j+1}\}:0\le j<r\}\) or its complementary alternating set. The union over all cycles is a stable matching. Hence stable matchings correspond to stable partitions after resolving every even cycle into alternating pairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Stable matchings are stable partitions of two-cycles; an all-even stable partition yields a stable matching by choosing alternating edges on every longer cycle.
assumptions_latex: \(\pi\) is a stable partition with no odd cycle.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\mapsto\pi_M\) embeds stable matchings as two-cycle partitions, and alternating resolution maps all-even stable partitions to stable matchings.

notation.meaning: half the length of an even cycle

review_flags: The claim that either alternating resolution is stable needs exact source verification.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The representation kind fits exactly, but the claim that either alternating resolution of every even cycle yields a stable matching requires precise source verification.

knowledge_statements.title: Almost-Stable Roommates
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Minimum-blocking-pairs version of almost-stable roommates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I=(V,\succ)\) be a roommates instance and let \(M\) be a matching, with being unmatched treated as worse than every acceptable partner. An acceptable pair \(\{x,y\}\notin M\) blocks \(M\) when \(x\) strictly prefers \(y\) to \(M(x)\) and \(y\) strictly prefers \(x\) to \(M(y)\). Define \(b_I(M)\) as the number of blocking pairs. In the minimum-blocking-pairs almost-stable roommates problem, an almost-stable matching is a feasible matching \(M^*\) satisfying \(b_I(M^*)=\min_M b_I(M)\). It is stable exactly when this minimum equals zero.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In the minimum-blocking-pairs formulation, an almost-stable matching minimizes the number of mutually improving unmatched pairs; optimum zero is ordinary stability.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^*\) is almost stable when \(b_I(M^*)=\min_M b_I(M)\), and it is stable when \(b_I(M^*)=0\).

notation.meaning: number of blocking pairs of M in I

review_flags: Almost-stable roommates has several formulations; the intended optimization variant requires source confirmation.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition is coherent for the minimum-number-of-blocking-pairs variant, but “almost-stable roommates” has multiple formulations and the selected variant has no supporting locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Weak Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Weak stability for matching instances with ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let each agent \(x\) have a weak preference order \(\succeq_x\) over acceptable partners, and write \(y\succ_x z\) for strict preference. Treat being unmatched as strictly worse than every acceptable partner. A matching \(M\) is weakly stable if there is no acceptable pair \(\{x,y\}\notin M\) such that \(y\succ_x M(x)\) and \(x\succ_y M(y)\). Thus a pair blocks weak stability only when both agents strictly improve; indifference by either endpoint prevents that pair from being a weak blocking pair.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With ties, a matching is weakly stable when no acceptable unmatched pair would make both endpoints strictly better off.
assumptions_latex: Each preference relation is a weak order on acceptable partners.
Unmatched status is below every acceptable partner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is weakly stable if and only if no acceptable pair strictly improves both endpoints' assignments.

notation.meaning: strict part of agent x's preference order
x's assigned partner or unmatched status

review_flags: A matching-with-ties source locator is required despite the standard definition.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition kind fits and the formulation is mathematically standard and internally consistent, but no authoritative matching-with-ties section or definition locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Strong Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strong stability for one-to-one bipartite matching with ties and incomplete acceptability lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U\cup V,E)\) be bipartite, and let every vertex have a total preorder over its acceptable neighbors. For a matching \(M\), write \(M(x)=\bot\) when \(x\) is unmatched, with every acceptable neighbor strictly preferred to \(\bot\). An unmatched edge \(uv\in E\setminus M\) strongly blocks \(M\) when \(v\succeq_u M(u)\) and \(u\succeq_v M(v)\), and at least one of these two comparisons is strict. The matching \(M\) is strongly stable if it has no strongly blocking edge.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is strongly stable when no unmatched acceptable pair weakly prefers each other to its assignments with at least one strict preference.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(U\cup V,E)\) is a finite bipartite acceptability graph.
Each preference relation is a total preorder.
Unmatched status is worse than every acceptable partner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is strongly stable}\iff \nexists uv\in E\setminus M:\ v\succeq_u M(u),\ u\succeq_v M(v),\text{ and }(v\succ_u M(u)\lor u\succ_v M(v)).\)

notation.meaning: Partner of x under M, or the unmatched symbol.
Weak and strict preference of vertex x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The definition correctly distinguishes strong blocking by requiring both endpoints to weakly prefer the deviation and at least one endpoint to prefer it strictly. The mathematical and plain statements agree, but no source with an inspectable locator is supplied.

knowledge_statements.title: Super-Stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Super-stability for one-to-one bipartite matching with ties and incomplete acceptability lists.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(G=(U\cup V,E)\) be bipartite, and give each vertex a total preorder over its acceptable neighbors. Treat being unmatched, denoted \(\bot\), as strictly worse than every acceptable neighbor. For a matching \(M\), an edge \(uv\in E\setminus M\) super-blocks \(M\) if \(v\succeq_u M(u)\) and \(u\succeq_v M(v)\); thus neither endpoint need strictly improve. The matching \(M\) is super-stable precisely when no such edge exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A matching is super-stable when no unmatched acceptable pair regards each other as at least as good as their current assignments.
assumptions_latex: \(G=(U\cup V,E)\) is a finite bipartite acceptability graph.
Each preference relation is a total preorder.
Every acceptable partner is strictly preferred to \(\bot\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is super-stable}\iff \nexists uv\in E\setminus M:\ v\succeq_u M(u)\land u\succeq_v M(v).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The super-stability definition is mathematically precise and correctly permits both endpoint comparisons to be non-strict. The selected content kind fits the terminal container, but the record has no cited source or locator.

knowledge_statements.title: Maximum-Cardinality Stability with Ties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: The cardinality-maximization problem over weakly stable matchings in a tied-preference instance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given a finite bipartite acceptability graph \(G=(U\cup V,E)\) with total-preorder preferences, an unmatched edge \(uv\) weakly blocks a matching \(M\) when \(v\succ_u M(u)\) and \(u\succ_v M(v)\), where every acceptable partner is preferred to being unmatched. A matching is weakly stable when it has no weakly blocking edge. Maximum-cardinality stability with ties asks for a weakly stable matching \(M^*\) satisfying \[|M^*|=\max\{|M|:M\text{ is a weakly stable matching of the instance}\}.\]
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Find a weakly stable matching containing as many matched pairs as possible when preference lists may contain ties.
assumptions_latex: The acceptability graph is finite and bipartite.
Preferences are total preorders on acceptable partners.
Stability means weak stability unless another regime is stated.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M^*\in\operatorname*{argmax}\{|M|:M\text{ is weakly stable}\}.\)

notation.meaning: Number of matched edges in M.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record correctly defines the maximum-cardinality weakly stable matching problem with ties, and definition is an appropriate content kind for this optimization-problem container. An authoritative MAX-SMTI source with a specific definition, section, theorem, or page locator is still required.

children.title: Indifference Regimes
children.top_down_role: Tie structures that alter stable-matching optimization.

knowledge_statements.title: Indifference Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Comparison of weak, strong, and super-stability through their blocking predicates.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For an unmatched acceptable pair \(uv\), compare each proposed partner with the endpoint's current assignment. The weak, strong, and super-blocking predicates are respectively \[B_W(uv):=(v\succ_u M(u))\land(u\succ_v M(v)),\] \[B_S(uv):=(v\succeq_u M(u))\land(u\succeq_v M(v))\land((v\succ_u M(u))\lor(u\succ_v M(v))),\] and \[B_{SS}(uv):=(v\succeq_u M(u))\land(u\succeq_v M(v)).\] Hence \(B_W\Rightarrow B_S\Rightarrow B_{SS}\), so super-stability implies strong stability, which implies weak stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Permitting progressively more indifference in blocking pairs strengthens stability: super-stable implies strongly stable, which implies weakly stable.
assumptions_latex: Preferences are total preorders over acceptable partners.
Unmatched status is below every acceptable partner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{M:M\text{ is super-stable}\}\subseteq\{M:M\text{ is strongly stable}\}\subseteq\{M:M\text{ is weakly stable}\}.\)

notation.meaning: Weak and strict preference of endpoint x.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three blocking predicates and the resulting nesting of stability classes are internally consistent, and representation fits this comparative terminal container. No inspectable source supports the characterization.

children.title: Approximation Guarantees with Ties
children.top_down_role: Achievable approximation quality under specified tie restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Approximation Guarantees with Ties
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Approximation convention for maximum-cardinality weakly stable matching with ties.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) be the maximum cardinality of a weakly stable matching in tied-preference instance \(I\). For \(\rho\geq1\), an algorithm is a \(\rho\)-approximation if, on every instance in its stated tie regime, it returns a weakly stable matching \(M_A(I)\) in polynomial time such that \[|M_A(I)|\geq \frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{\rho}.\] The guarantee must state whether ties occur on one or both sides, whether lists are incomplete, and whether tie length is bounded, because these choices determine the applicable ratio.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A rho-approximation returns a weakly stable matching of size at least optimum divided by rho; the covered tie regime must be specified.
assumptions_latex: \(I\) is a finite tied-preference matching instance.
\(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) maximizes cardinality over weakly stable matchings.
Runtime is measured in the ordinary explicit-input model.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(|M_A(I)|\geq\operatorname{OPT}(I)/\rho\) for every instance \(I\) in the declared regime.

notation.meaning: Optimal weakly stable matching cardinality for instance I.
Multiplicative approximation factor, at least one.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives only the generic definition of a rho-approximation, not an approximation guarantee for any fixed tied-preference regime. Consequently, complexity_bound does not fit the actual content supplied. A sourced numerical ratio together with sidedness, completeness, tie-length restrictions, and the precise model is needed before a reliable replacement can be formulated.

children.title: Inapproximability Thresholds
children.top_down_role: Hardness limits on approximation quality.

knowledge_statements.title: Inapproximability Thresholds
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Formal hardness threshold for approximating maximum-cardinality weakly stable matching under a fixed tie regime.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a class \(\mathcal I\) of tied-preference instances and let \(\operatorname{OPT}(I)\) denote maximum weakly stable matching cardinality. A constant \(\alpha>1\) is an inapproximability threshold under assumption \(H\) if, for every \(\varepsilon>0\), no polynomial-time algorithm always returns a weakly stable \(M\) satisfying \[|M|\geq\frac{\operatorname{OPT}(I)}{\alpha-\varepsilon}\qquad(I\in\mathcal I),\] unless \(H\) fails. A numerical threshold is not transferable between classes that differ in sidedness, maximum tie length, completeness, or admissible preference structure.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A hardness threshold rules out every polynomial-time approximation better than the threshold, within a precisely fixed tie regime and complexity assumption.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal I\) fixes all relevant tie and acceptability restrictions.
\(H\) is an explicitly stated complexity assumption.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(H\Rightarrow\nexists\text{ polynomial-time }(\alpha-\varepsilon)\text{-approximation on }\mathcal I\text{ for every }\varepsilon>0.\)

notation.meaning: Complexity assumption underlying the hardness claim.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record defines a schema for an inapproximability threshold but supplies neither a numerical threshold nor a concrete instance class or complexity assumption. The failure_boundary kind fits the intended terminal container, but an actual threshold cannot be stated reliably without a regime-specific hardness source.

children.title: Tie-Structure Sensitivity
children.top_down_role: Dependence of approximation behavior on tie placement or tie length.

knowledge_statements.title: Tie-Structure Sensitivity
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Dependence of stability on strict refinements of tied preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(I\) be a one-to-one instance with total-preorder preferences, and let a strict refinement replace every tie by an arbitrary strict ordering without reversing strict comparisons. For any matching \(M\): \[M\text{ is weakly stable in }I\iff M\text{ is stable in at least one strict refinement of }I,\] and \[M\text{ is super-stable in }I\iff M\text{ is stable in every strict refinement of }I.\] Thus tie-breaking may preserve a weakly stable matching while failing to certify super-stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Weak stability corresponds to stability under some tie-breaking, whereas super-stability corresponds to stability under every tie-breaking.
assumptions_latex: The instance is finite, bipartite, and one-to-one.
A refinement orders tied alternatives but preserves all strict comparisons.
Stability after refinement uses ordinary strict-preference blocking.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\operatorname{WeakStable}(I)=\bigcup_{J\in\mathcal R(I)}\operatorname{Stable}(J)\) and \(\operatorname{SuperStable}(I)=\bigcap_{J\in\mathcal R(I)}\operatorname{Stable}(J)\).

notation.meaning: Set of all strict refinements of instance I.
Stable matchings of strict instance J.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: For finite one-to-one instances, the stated union and intersection characterizations under strict refinements are precise and match the plain statement. Property is an appropriate content kind, but the characterization lacks an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Lower Quotas
children.top_down_role: Minimum-assignment requirements imposed on individual institutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower Quotas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Individual lower-capacity requirements in a hospitals–residents assignment.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(R\) be residents, \(H\) hospitals, and \(E\subseteq R\times H\) acceptable pairs. Assign each hospital \(h\) integers \(0\leq \ell_h\leq u_h\). A matching \(M\subseteq E\) satisfies the lower and upper quotas at \(h\) when \[\ell_h\leq |M(h)|\leq u_h,\qquad M(h):=\{r\in R:rh\in M\}.\] It is quota-feasible when this holds for every hospital and each resident occurs in at most one edge. If closed hospitals are permitted, the usual alternative is \(|M(h)|=0\) or \(\ell_h\leq|M(h)|\leq u_h\).
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A lower quota requires each operating hospital to receive at least a prescribed number of residents, while its upper quota limits capacity.
assumptions_latex: Each resident may be assigned to at most one hospital.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is quota-feasible}\iff \forall h\in H,\ \ell_h\leq|M(h)|\leq u_h\), with the stated closure variant when applicable.

notation.meaning: Lower and upper quotas of hospital h.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The record blends two materially different lower-quota models: mandatory satisfaction at every hospital and the open-or-closed alternative. Its conclusion therefore does not define one fixed feasibility notion. A matching-specific source must determine which convention belongs in this container before the statement can be corrected.

children.title: Common Quotas
children.top_down_role: Shared assignment limits imposed across groups of institutions.

knowledge_statements.title: Common Quotas
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Capacity constraints shared by designated collections of hospitals or contracts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\) be the acceptable contracts and let \(\mathcal Q\subseteq2^E\) be a family of designated contract sets. Each \(Q\in\mathcal Q\) has integral bounds \(0\leq \ell_Q\leq u_Q\). A matching \(M\subseteq E\) satisfies the common quota on \(Q\) when \[\ell_Q\leq |M\cap Q|\leq u_Q.\] Individual hospital quotas are recovered by taking \(Q\) to be all contracts incident with one hospital; a quota spanning several hospitals restricts their aggregate assignments.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A common quota bounds the total number of selected contracts across a designated group, possibly spanning several hospitals.
assumptions_latex: \(\mathcal Q\) is a specified family of subsets of \(E\).
Every quota has integral bounds \(0\leq\ell_Q\leq u_Q\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ satisfies all common quotas}\iff \forall Q\in\mathcal Q,\ \ell_Q\leq|M\cap Q|\leq u_Q.\)

notation.meaning: Lower and upper common quotas for Q.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The contract-set formulation is coherent and definition fits the terminal container. However, common-quota models differ over whether lower bounds are admitted and how contract sets are induced by hospital groups, so the chosen formulation requires an authoritative source with a specific locator.

children.title: Laminar Common-Quota Systems
children.top_down_role: Nested common-quota structures with specialized feasibility behavior.

knowledge_statements.title: Laminar Common-Quota Systems
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Common quotas whose controlled contract sets form a laminar family.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A common-quota family \(\mathcal Q\subseteq2^E\) is laminar if, for every \(Q,Q'\in\mathcal Q\), \[Q\cap Q'=\varnothing\quad\text{or}\quad Q\subseteq Q'\quad\text{or}\quad Q'\subseteq Q.\] With bounds \(0\leq\ell_Q\leq u_Q\), a matching \(M\subseteq E\) is feasible for the laminar system when \(\ell_Q\leq|M\cap Q|\leq u_Q\) for every \(Q\in\mathcal Q\). The laminar sets can therefore be organized as a containment forest, with disjoint siblings and nested ancestor quotas.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A laminar quota system has only disjoint or nested quota groups, and a matching must satisfy every group's bounds.
assumptions_latex: Each member of \(\mathcal Q\) has integral lower and upper bounds.
Feasibility also includes the underlying matching constraints.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal Q\text{ is laminar}\iff \forall Q,Q'\in\mathcal Q,\ Q\cap Q'=\varnothing\lor Q\subseteq Q'\lor Q'\subseteq Q.\)

notation.meaning: Laminar family of quota-controlled contract sets.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The laminarity condition is correct and the feasibility statement is consistent with the preceding common-quota formulation. Definition is the correct mathematical role, but no matching-specific source or inspectable locator is supplied.

children.title: Joint Quota Feasibility
children.top_down_role: Compatibility of lower-quota requirements with shared quota restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Joint Quota Feasibility
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Simultaneous feasibility of matching constraints and all individual or common quotas.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(E\subseteq R\times H\) be acceptable contracts, and let \(\mathcal Q\subseteq2^E\) carry bounds \(\ell_Q,u_Q\). A set \(M\subseteq E\) is jointly quota-feasible exactly when \[\sum_{h:rh\in E}\mathbf 1_{rh\in M}\leq1\quad(r\in R),\qquad \ell_Q\leq\sum_{e\in Q}\mathbf 1_{e\in M}\leq u_Q\quad(Q\in\mathcal Q).\] Any required hospital capacities are included by placing their incident contract sets in \(\mathcal Q\). Thus feasibility means simultaneous satisfaction, not separate feasibility of each quota in isolation.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Joint feasibility requires one assignment per resident and simultaneous satisfaction of every individual and shared quota.
assumptions_latex: Quota bounds are integral and satisfy \(0\leq\ell_Q\leq u_Q\).
Hospital quota sets are included in \(\mathcal Q\) when required.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is jointly feasible}\iff M\text{ satisfies all resident-incidence and quota inequalities simultaneously}.\)

notation.meaning: Indicator that contract e is selected.
Family containing every applicable quota set.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The simultaneous incidence and quota inequalities correctly express joint feasibility under the stated contract-set model, and condition fits the terminal container. An authoritative matching-with-common-quotas source is needed to validate that this is the intended model and to support the claim.

knowledge_statements.title: Hospitals–Residents with Couples
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Contract model with singles, couples' joint preferences, and responsive hospital capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: An HRC instance consists of hospitals \(H\) with capacities \(q_h\), single residents \(S\), disjoint ordered couples \(C\subseteq R\times R\), acceptable hospital lists for singles, acceptable ordered hospital pairs for couples, and hospital rankings of residents. A feasible matching assigns each single to at most one hospital and each couple jointly to one listed pair \((h,k)\), while no hospital receives more than \(q_h\) residents. Under responsive hospital choice, stability excludes a single who can move to a hospital that would retain that resident, and excludes a couple preferring \((h,k)\) whose proposed members would both be retained by the affected hospitals after the joint move.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: HRC jointly assigns each couple to a hospital pair, respects capacities, and forbids accepted improving deviations by singles or couples.
assumptions_latex: Couples are disjoint pairs of residents.
Hospitals have responsive preferences and integral capacities.
Only listed resident–hospital and couple–hospital-pair assignments are acceptable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\text{ is stable}\iff M\text{ is feasible and has neither an accepted improving single deviation nor an accepted improving joint couple deviation}.\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The instance data and capacity constraints are broadly appropriate, but the stability clause is too compressed to determine all standard HRC blocking cases. In particular, deviations involving the same hospital, one member remaining at a current hospital, vacancies, and displacement of one or two assignees require explicit conventions. These source-sensitive details prevent a reliable mathematical replacement without an authoritative HRC definition.

assumptions_latex: \(U\) and \(V\) are finite disjoint agent sets with quotas \(q_a\in\mathbb Z_{\ge 0}\).
Each agent has a strict ranking of acceptable agents on the opposite side.
Preferences over feasible partner sets are responsive to the individual rankings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is stable if and only if it is individually rational and has no blocking pair.

notation.meaning: A feasible many-to-many matching, with partner set M(a) for agent a.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pairwise stability for finite many-to-many matching with quotas and responsive preferences.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A feasible matching \(M\) assigns each \(u\in U\) a set \(M(u)\subseteq V\) and each \(v\in V\) a set \(M(v)\subseteq U\), symmetrically, with \(|M(a)|\le q_a\). It is individually rational when every assigned partner is acceptable. An unmatched pair \((u,v)\notin M\) blocks \(M\) when each agent finds the other acceptable and, for each \(a\in\{u,v\}\), either \(|M(a)|<q_a\) or \(a\) prefers the other agent to its least-preferred member of \(M(a)\). The matching is stable precisely when it is individually rational and no such pair exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A quota-feasible many-to-many matching is stable exactly when all assigned partners are acceptable and no unmatched pair would mutually accept each other by using vacancies or replacing worse partners.
knowledge_statements.title: Many-to-Many Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: No citation or inspectable locator supports the many-to-many stability definition. The blocking condition also refers to the least-preferred member of M(a) without handling q_a=0, where M(a) is empty and no vacancy is available; an authoritative source is needed to fix the exact quota and blocking-pair convention.

assumptions_latex: \(d\ge 3\) and \(P_1,\ldots,P_d\) are finite disjoint participant classes.
Each participant strictly ranks acceptable \(d\)-tuples containing that participant.
Being unmatched is included as an outside option.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(M\) is stable if and only if no acceptable tuple \(t\notin M\) satisfies \(t\succ_i M(i)\) for every \(i\in t\).

notation.meaning: A matching consisting of vertex-disjoint acceptable d-tuples.
Participant i's assigned tuple, or the unmatched option.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: blocking-tuple definition of multidimensional stability
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Blocking-tuple stability in a finite, partite, multidimensional matching market.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(T\subseteq P_1\times\cdots\times P_d\) be the acceptable tuples. A matching \(M\subseteq T\) consists of pairwise participant-disjoint tuples. For a participant \(i\), let \(M(i)\) be its unique assigned tuple, or the unmatched option if none exists. A tuple \(t\in T\setminus M\) blocks \(M\) if every participant \(i\in t\) strictly prefers \(t\) to \(M(i)\). The matching \(M\) is multidimensionally stable when it is individually rational and admits no blocking tuple.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A multidimensional matching is stable when no acceptable cross-class tuple outside the matching is strictly preferred by every participant in that tuple to their current assignments.
knowledge_statements.title: Multidimensional Stability

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The blocking-tuple definition is mathematically coherent and the definition content kind fits the leaf, but no authoritative multidimensional-matching citation with a specific locator is supplied. The local inventory does not support this claim.

children.title: Strategic Properties of Stable Matching
children.top_down_role: Only stability-specific incentive properties are retained locally; general mechanism-design and market-design theory is cross-linked.

assumptions_latex: The market is a finite one-to-one bipartite matching market with strict preferences.
Proposers report preference lists to proposer-proposing deferred acceptance.
All other reports are held fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu_p(P_p,P_{-p})\succeq_p \mu_p(P'_p,P_{-p})\) for every proposer \(p\) and every report \(P'_p\).

notation.meaning: The proposer-proposing deferred-acceptance outcome under the displayed reports.

review_flags: standard_field_rationale: proposer strategyproofness of deferred acceptance
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Individual dominant-strategy result for one-to-one proposer-proposing deferred acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix the reports of every agent except proposer \(p\). Let \(P_p\) be \(p\)'s true strict preference order and let \(P'_p\) be any alternative report, including a truncation. If \(\mu_p(P_p,P_{-p})\) and \(\mu_p(P'_p,P_{-p})\) denote \(p\)'s assignments under proposer-proposing deferred acceptance, then \(\mu_p(P_p,P_{-p})\succeq_p\mu_p(P'_p,P_{-p})\). Thus truthful reporting is a weakly dominant strategy for every proposer, although the corresponding assertion need not hold for receivers.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: In proposer-proposing deferred acceptance, no proposer can obtain a strictly better partner by unilaterally misreporting preferences while all other reports remain fixed.
knowledge_statements.title: Proposer-Side Strategyproofness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The statement gives the standard individual strategyproofness theorem for the proposing side of one-to-one deferred acceptance, and theorem is the correct content kind. It nevertheless lacks an authoritative theorem citation and locator, so the precise domain, treatment of truncations, and dominant-strategy conclusion remain unsupported.

assumptions_latex: The market has proposers \(m_1,m_2,m_3\) and receivers \(w_1,w_2,w_3\), with being unmatched worst.
Proposer preferences are \(m_1:w_1\succ w_2\succ w_3\), \(m_2:w_2\succ w_1\succ w_3\), and \(m_3:w_1\succ w_2\succ w_3\).
Receiver preferences include \(w_1:m_2\succ m_1\succ m_3\) and \(w_2:m_1\succ m_2\succ m_3\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mu(w_1)=m_1\) truthfully, but reporting only \(m_2\) acceptable yields \(\mu'(w_1)=m_2\succ_{w_1}m_1\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Explicit receiver manipulation of one-to-one proposer-proposing deferred acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Give \(w_3\) any strict order with all proposers acceptable. Under truthful proposer-proposing deferred acceptance, \(w_1\) holds \(m_1\), \(w_2\) holds \(m_2\), and \(m_3\) eventually reaches \(w_3\), so \(\mu(w_1)=m_1\). If \(w_1\) instead reports only \(m_2\) acceptable, she rejects \(m_1\); then \(m_1\) proposes to \(w_2\), which rejects \(m_2\), and \(m_2\) proposes to \(w_1\). Consequently \(\mu'(w_1)=m_2\succ_{w_1}m_1\), demonstrating that receiver-side strategyproofness fails.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A receiver can profitably truncate her list: the induced rejection chain replaces her truthful partner with a strictly preferred proposer.
knowledge_statements.title: Receiver-Side Manipulation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The displayed preferences do produce the claimed profitable receiver truncation, and counterexample fits the manipulation-boundary leaf. However, no source or locator is supplied, and statement_latex contains a step-by-step deferred-acceptance derivation rather than only the knowledge statement.

assumptions_latex: The market is finite, one-to-one, and bipartite with strict preferences.
The mechanism is proposer-proposing deferred acceptance.
Receivers and proposers outside a deviating proposer coalition report truthfully.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists S,(P'_p)_{p\in S}\;\forall p\in S:\mu_p(P'_S,P_{-S})\succ_p\mu_p(P)\).
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Strict-improvement coalitional boundary for proposers under deferred acceptance.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There is no proposer coalition \(S\) and joint false report \((P'_p)_{p\in S}\) such that every member \(p\in S\) receives a partner strictly preferred, according to \(p\)'s true preferences, to the partner obtained under truthful reporting. This coalitional protection concerns unanimous strict improvement by coalition members; it does not assert receiver-side strategyproofness, nor does it exclude manipulations that benefit selected proposers while other coalition members serve as non-improving accomplices.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: No coalition of proposers can misreport so that every coalition member becomes strictly better off, but this does not exclude manipulations using non-benefiting accomplices.
knowledge_statements.title: Coalitional Manipulation Boundary

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The strict-unanimous-improvement boundary is plausible and failure_boundary fits the terminal container, but coalitional strategyproofness has several inequivalent weak/strict and accomplice variants. No authoritative theorem citation or locator supports the exact quantified version stated here.

assumptions_latex: There are three agents \(1,2,3\), and being unmatched is worse than every listed partner.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\nexists M\) such that \(M\) is a stable roommates matching for this instance.

notation.meaning: A matching on the three agents.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Small cyclic obstruction to stable-roommates existence.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Every matching \(M\) contains at most one pair. If \(M=\{\{1,2\}\}\), then \(\{2,3\}\) blocks because \(2\) prefers \(3\) to \(1\) and \(3\) prefers \(2\) to being unmatched. If \(M=\{\{2,3\}\}\), then \(\{1,3\}\) blocks. If \(M=\{\{1,3\}\}\), then \(\{1,2\}\) blocks. The empty matching is also blocked by every acceptable pair. Hence this stable-roommates instance has no stable matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Three cyclically oriented preferences form a stable-roommates obstruction: whichever pair is selected, another mutually improving pair blocks it.
knowledge_statements.title: Roommates Nonexistence Obstructions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The three-agent cyclic instance is a valid nonexistence counterexample and counterexample is appropriate for the obstruction leaf. No authoritative stable-roommates source with a locator is cited, and statement_latex includes the complete case analysis proving nonexistence.

assumptions_latex: Agents select sets of contracts through choice functions \(C_i\).
Stability means individual rationality together with absence of a set of contracts jointly chosen by all involved agents.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Without substitutability, stable outcomes need not exist, and deferred-rejection procedures need not converge to a stable outcome.

notation.meaning: Agent i's chosen subset from offered contract set X.
Finite sets of contracts with Y contained in X.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existence boundary for matching with contracts when choice functions violate substitutability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A choice function \(C_i\) is substitutable when, for all \(Y\subseteq X\) and \(x\in Y\), the implication \(x\in C_i(X)\Rightarrow x\in C_i(Y)\) holds. A violation occurs when some contract is chosen only in the presence of another contract, so removing alternatives reverses its acceptance. Once such complementarities are allowed, rejection is no longer monotone: a previously rejected contract may become desired after other contracts disappear. Consequently the standard deferred-rejection existence argument fails, and finite matching-with-contracts markets with non-substitutable choice functions can have no stable outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Non-substitutable choices make rejection nonmonotone. With such complementarities, deferred-rejection guarantees fail and some finite contract markets have no stable outcome.
knowledge_statements.title: Failure under Non-Substitutable Choice

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Failure_boundary fits the leaf, but non-substitutability alone does not identify which particular market lacks a stable outcome; the claim is only existential over markets admitting such choices. The separate conclusion that deferred-rejection procedures need not converge is not actually established by statement_latex. A matching-with-contracts source is required for the exact existence and algorithmic boundaries.

children.title: Couples in Matching Markets
children.top_down_role: Matching environments containing participants who submit joint preferences.

assumptions_latex: Applicants consist of singles and disjoint two-person couples.
Hospitals have finite capacities and strict rankings of individual applicants.
Each couple ranks ordered pairs of hospital assignments, including unemployment components.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: A stable outcome admits neither a blocking single-hospital pair nor a blocking couple-hospital-pair deviation.

notation.meaning: A couple with members a and b.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite hospitals-residents model with singles, two-person couples, and responsive hospital capacities.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: A matching \(M\) assigns each applicant to at most one hospital and assigns at most \(q_h\) applicants to each hospital \(h\). Members of a couple \(c=(a,b)\) are evaluated jointly through the ordered assignment \((M(a),M(b))\). A single blocks with \(h\) if both prefer one another to their current assignments after any necessary displacement. A couple blocks through \((h,k)\) if it prefers \((h,k)\) to its current ordered pair and hospitals \(h,k\), accounting for capacities, common-hospital placement, and displaced incumbents, would accept the relevant members. Stability excludes all such deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Couples rank joint hospital assignments. Stability requires feasibility and excludes profitable deviations by either one single or an entire couple with hospitals willing to accept them.
knowledge_statements.title: Couples in Matching Markets

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Definition is a suitable content kind for the model leaf, but the acceptance conditions for a couple assigned to the same hospital, capacity displacement, and interactions with incumbent couple members are left informal. No authoritative hospitals-residents-with-couples definition and locator is supplied.

children.title: Complementary Joint Preferences
children.top_down_role: Cross-position complementarities induced by joint choices.

assumptions_latex: A couple \(c=(a,b)\) has a strict preference relation over ordered hospital pairs.
The compared assignments are acceptable and may include \(\varnothing\).
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: Complementarity is witnessed when the preferred assignment of one member depends on the partner's assignment.

notation.meaning: The couple's strict preference relation over joint assignments.
Hospitals or unemployment assignments for the two members.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Preference-reversal condition expressing nonseparable joint preferences of a couple.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The couple's joint preference is complementary, in the preference-reversal sense, if there exist assignments \(h,h'\) for member \(a\) and \(k,k'\) for member \(b\) such that \((h,k)\succ_c(h',k)\) but \((h',k')\succ_c(h,k')\), or symmetrically with the members interchanged. Thus the ranking between \(a\)'s assignments \(h\) and \(h'\) changes with \(b\)'s assignment. Such a ranking cannot be represented by fixed, partner-independent ordinal rankings for both members.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: A couple has complementary joint preferences when one member's preferred hospital changes with the partner's assignment, preventing independent member rankings from representing the couple's choices.
knowledge_statements.title: Complementary Joint Preferences

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The preference reversal precisely witnesses nonseparability or context dependence, and condition fits the leaf. Calling every such reversal complementarity is terminology-dependent and may be broader than standard complementarity notions; no authoritative source with a specific locator resolves that issue.

children.title: Couples-Induced Nonexistence
children.top_down_role: Stable-assignment failures attributable to joint preferences.

assumptions_latex: Hospitals-residents markets may contain two-person couples with strict joint preference lists.
Hospitals have finite capacities and strict applicant rankings.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists I\) such that \(I\) is a finite couples market and \(\operatorname{Stable}(I)=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: A finite hospitals-residents instance with couples.
The set of stable matchings of instance I.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Existential nonexistence result for finite hospitals-residents markets with couples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: There exist finite hospitals-residents instances with strict preferences and couples for which no stable matching exists. Joint deviations can create a cycle: for every feasible matching \(M\), either a single applicant and hospital form a blocking pair or some couple and ordered hospital pair form a blocking deviation. Hence the existence guarantee supplied by deferred acceptance in the ordinary hospitals-residents model does not extend to unrestricted joint preferences of couples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Allowing couples can destroy existence: some finite strict-preference instances have a blocking single or couple deviation under every feasible matching.
knowledge_statements.title: Couples-Induced Nonexistence

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The existential nonexistence theorem matches the leaf and its content kind, but neither a concrete obstruction nor an authoritative theorem citation with an inspectable locator is provided. The supplied local inventory does not support couples-induced nonexistence.

children.title: Couples-Matching Hardness
children.top_down_role: Computational barriers associated with stability in markets containing couples.

assumptions_latex: The input is a finite hospitals-residents instance with singles, two-person couples, capacities, and explicit strict preference lists.
Stability uses blocking singles and blocking couples under the stated hospital capacities.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\textsc{HRC-Stable-Existence}\) is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete.

notation.meaning: The decision problem asking whether a stable matching exists in a couples market.
The class of decision problems verifiable in polynomial time.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Decision complexity for unrestricted finite hospitals-residents instances with couples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: The decision problem \(\textsc{HRC-Stable-Existence}\) asks whether the given market admits at least one stable matching. A proposed matching is a polynomial-size certificate: feasibility and all explicitly listed potential blocking deviations can be checked in time polynomial in the encoded preference lists. The problem is \(\mathrm{NP}\)-hard under polynomial-time many-one reductions and therefore \(\mathrm{NP}\)-complete. This statement concerns the unrestricted explicit-list model and makes no claim about stronger hardness under bounded capacities, bounded list lengths, or a bounded number of couples.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Deciding whether an unrestricted explicitly represented hospitals-residents market with couples has a stable matching is NP-complete; a proposed stable matching is polynomially checkable.
knowledge_statements.title: Couples-Matching Hardness

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Complexity_bound is the correct role for this leaf, but NP-completeness depends on the exact HRC stability definition and input encoding. No hardness theorem, reduction citation, or specific locator is supplied, and the generic complexity references in the inventory do not establish this result.

children.title: Tractable Couples Restrictions
children.top_down_role: Restricted couples settings with improved existence or computational behavior.

assumptions_latex: Every applicant is treated as a single agent with an independent strict preference list.
Hospitals have responsive preferences over applicants and finite capacities.
There are no joint couple deviations.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\textsc{HRC-Stable-Existence}\) restricted to \(|C|=0\) reduces to hospitals-residents and is solvable by deferred acceptance in polynomial time.

notation.meaning: The total number of acceptable applicant-hospital pairs.

knowledge_statements.scope_note: Tractable boundary obtained by eliminating joint couple preferences and deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Under the restriction \(|C|=0\), the couples model is exactly the ordinary hospitals-residents problem. Applicant-proposing deferred acceptance terminates after at most \(L\) proposals, returns a stable matching, and can be implemented in time polynomial in the explicit preference-list size. The same reduction applies when purported couples are replaced by two independent applicants and stability is defined only against individual applicant-hospital pairs. Thus tractability is recovered by removing the joint complementarity that permits couple-level blocking deviations.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: When couples and joint deviations are absent, the model reduces to ordinary hospitals-residents; deferred acceptance finds a stable matching after at most one proposal per listed pair.
knowledge_statements.title: Tractable Couples Restrictions

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The zero-couples reduction and deferred-acceptance claim are standard, but failure_boundary is not the best mathematical role for a positive algorithmic tractability statement; algorithm or complexity_bound would fit better. The plural leaf title suggests substantive tractable couples restrictions, whereas the record only removes all couples. No authoritative hospitals-residents algorithm citation and locator is supplied.

children.title: Lower-Quota Nonexistence
children.top_down_role: Stable-outcome failures caused by minimum-assignment requirements.

knowledge_statements.title: Lower-Quota Nonexistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: A minimal many-to-one instance where lower-quota feasibility excludes every stable matching.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let residents be \(R=\{r_1,r_2\}\), hospitals be \(H=\{h_1,h_2\}\), and set \(\ell_{h_i}=u_{h_i}=1\) for \(i=1,2\). The acceptable pairs are \((r_1,h_1)\), \((r_2,h_1)\), and \((r_2,h_2)\). Resident \(r_2\) prefers \(h_1\) to \(h_2\), and hospital \(h_1\) prefers \(r_2\) to \(r_1\); all other comparisons are immaterial. Quota feasibility forces the unique matching \(M=\{(r_1,h_1),(r_2,h_2)\}\). The pair \((r_2,h_1)\) blocks \(M\), because both endpoints prefer each other to their assigned partners. Hence no matching is simultaneously stable and lower-quota feasible.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Lower quotas force a unique feasible assignment, but that assignment is blocked; therefore a quota-feasible stable matching need not exist.
assumptions_latex: Preferences over acceptable partners are strict.
A full hospital may participate in a blocking pair by replacing a less-preferred assignee.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\{M:M\text{ is stable}\}\cap\{M:M\text{ satisfies all lower and upper quotas}\}=\varnothing\).

notation.meaning: Lower and upper quotas of hospital h.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The finite counterexample is internally correct and counterexample is the appropriate content kind, but no inspectable citation or explicitly marked standard-field rationale is supplied.

children.title: Common-Quota Nonexistence
children.top_down_role: Stable-outcome failures caused by shared quota restrictions.

knowledge_statements.title: Common-Quota Nonexistence
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Finite certificate of nonexistence under upper quotas shared by sets of contracts.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(X\) be a finite contract set and let \(\mathcal Q\subseteq 2^X\) carry common upper quotas \(q_Q\). Call \(M\subseteq X\) feasible when each agent signs at most one contract and \(|M\cap Q|\le q_Q\) for every \(Q\in\mathcal Q\). Fix the agents' strict preferences and the quota-constrained institutional choice rule \(C\). A nonexistence certificate is a function \(b\) assigning to every individually rational feasible \(M\) a contract \(b(M)\in X\setminus M\) such that its agent prefers \(b(M)\) to its assignment in \(M\) and \(b(M)\in C(M\cup\{b(M)\})\). Such a certificate exists exactly when no stable feasible matching exists.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Nonexistence is certified by exhibiting a quota-compatible blocking contract for every individually rational feasible matching.
assumptions_latex: The institutional choice rule \(C\) is fixed and explicitly evaluable.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\exists b\text{ as specified}\iff\nexists M\text{ that is individually rational, common-quota feasible, and stable}.\)

notation.meaning: Family of contract sets sharing quotas.

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: Certificate is an appropriate content kind, but the equivalence assumes that every unstable feasible matching has a singleton blocking contract. Common-quota choice models may instead permit setwise blocking, so an authoritative source must specify the choice and stability definitions and the hypotheses ensuring singleton witnesses.

children.title: Quota Feasibility Failures
children.top_down_role: Instances where quota requirements admit no feasible assignment.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota Feasibility Failures
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Lower- and upper-quota feasibility represented as a circulation problem, with a minimum-cut certificate of failure.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: For a finite bipartite acceptability graph with resident set \(R\) and hospital set \(H\), construct a network with arcs \(s\to r\) of bounds \([0,1]\), arcs \(r\to h\) of bounds \([0,1]\) for acceptable pairs, arcs \(h\to t\) of bounds \([\ell_h,u_h]\), and an arc \(t\to s\) of bounds \([0,|R|]\). Integral feasible circulations are in bijection with quota-feasible matchings. Apply the standard lower-bound transformation and introduce a super-source \(\sigma\) and super-sink \(\tau\). If \(D\) is the total capacity of the arcs leaving \(\sigma\), then a quota-feasible matching exists exactly when a maximum \(\sigma\)-to-\(\tau\) flow has value \(D\), equivalently when every arc leaving \(\sigma\) is saturated. If the maximum value is less than \(D\), a minimum \(\sigma\)-to-\(\tau\) cut of capacity less than \(D\) is a checkable certificate of infeasibility.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quota feasibility reduces to a lower-bounded circulation. After the standard transformation, feasibility holds exactly when all super-source demand arcs can be saturated; otherwise a minimum cut of capacity below the total demand certifies failure.
assumptions_latex: \(0\le \ell_h\le u_h\) are integers for every \(h\in H\).
Each resident may be assigned to at most one acceptable hospital.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\text{A quota-feasible matching exists}\iff \operatorname{maxflow}(\sigma,\tau)=D.\)

notation.meaning: Super-source and super-sink in the transformed network.
Total capacity of the arcs leaving the super-source.

children.title: Stability–Feasibility Conflict
children.top_down_role: Regimes where feasible assignments exist but stability remains unattainable.

knowledge_statements.title: Stability–Feasibility Conflict
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Separates combinatorial quota feasibility from preference-based stability.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Fix a finite matching instance with preferences and quotas. Let \(\mathcal F\) denote the matchings satisfying acceptability, assignment capacities, and all lower, upper, or common quotas, and let \(\mathcal S\) denote the stable matchings under the specified blocking rule. A stability–feasibility conflict occurs precisely when \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\) but \(\mathcal F\cap\mathcal S=\varnothing\). Equivalently, quota constraints are jointly feasible, yet every \(M\in\mathcal F\) admits a blocking pair or blocking coalition. Thus a feasibility certificate alone cannot certify the existence of a stable quota-feasible outcome.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Quotas are feasible but conflict with stability exactly when every quota-feasible matching has a blocking pair or coalition.
assumptions_latex: The feasible family \(\mathcal F\) and the applicable blocking rule are fixed.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\mathcal F\ne\varnothing\ \land\ \mathcal F\cap\mathcal S=\varnothing\iff (\forall M\in\mathcal F)(\exists B)(B\text{ blocks }M).\)

intermediate_metadata.review_comment: The failure-boundary role fits the leaf and the equivalence is definitional once stability is fixed. An inspectable source is still required to identify the applicable blocking objects and establish that instability is witnessed by a pair or coalition in the intended quota model.

children.title: Quota-Repair Regimes
children.top_down_role: Structured quota relaxations used to recover feasibility or stable outcomes.

knowledge_statements.title: Quota-Repair Regimes
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Pareto representation of integral lower-quota reductions and upper-quota expansions under a quota-independent stability rule.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Let \(H\) be finite and let \(\ell,u\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{H}\) satisfy \(\ell_h\le u_h\) for every \(h\in H\). Define the admissible repair set by \(\mathcal A=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{H}\times\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^{H}:\alpha\le\ell\}\), where a repair replaces the quotas by \(\ell'=\ell-\alpha\) and \(u'=u+\beta\). Suppose stability is determined by fixed preferences and a blocking rule independent of the quota values, and let \(\mathcal S(\ell',u')\) be the stable matchings feasible under \((\ell',u')\). The repair region is \(\mathcal R=\{(\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal A:\mathcal S(\ell-\alpha,u+\beta)\ne\varnothing\}\). If \((\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R\) and \((\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal A\) satisfy \(\widehat\alpha\ge\alpha\) and \(\widehat\beta\ge\beta\), then \((\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal R\). Thus \(\mathcal R\) is upward closed within \(\mathcal A\), and its Pareto-minimal elements are the undominated quota repairs.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: Among admissible integral repairs, further lowering lower quotas or raising upper quotas preserves existence when the stability rule itself is independent of quotas. The repair region is therefore upward closed, and its undominated points are the Pareto-minimal repairs.
assumptions_latex: \(H\) is finite and the original quotas are nonnegative integers with \(\ell_h\le u_h\).
Repair vectors are integral, nonnegative, and satisfy \(\alpha\le\ell\).
Stability depends only on the matching, fixed preferences, and a blocking rule independent of quota values.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \((\alpha,\beta)\in\mathcal R\land(\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal A\land(\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\ge(\alpha,\beta)\Rightarrow(\widehat\alpha,\widehat\beta)\in\mathcal R.\)

notation.meaning: Integral lower-quota reductions and upper-quota expansions.

knowledge_statements.title: Multidimensional Stability Hardness
knowledge_statements.scope_note: Three-sided matching with preferences over partner pairs and blocking triples.
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Consider three disjoint sets \(A,B,C\) of equal size. Each agent has a strict ranking of its acceptable pairs from the other two sets. A perfect three-dimensional matching partitions \(A\cup B\cup C\) into triples. A triple \((a,b,c)\) blocks a matching when each of \(a,b,c\) strictly prefers the other two agents to the pair assigned in its current triple. The decision problem asking whether a perfect matching with no blocking triple exists is NP-complete. Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}\) follows because perfection and the absence of blocking triples can be checked in polynomial time from an explicitly represented preference profile.
knowledge_statements.statement_plain: With three agent classes and preferences over partner pairs, deciding whether a perfect matching without a blocking triple exists is NP-complete.
assumptions_latex: Preferences are strict and explicitly represented.
A blocking triple requires unanimous strict improvement.
The requested outcome is a perfect three-dimensional matching.
knowledge_statements.conclusion_latex: \(\textsc{Perfect-3D-Stable-Matching-Existence}\text{ is NP-complete}.\)
